# OpenDFX for Printed Circuit Boards

By Chris Denney. Text licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Website: https://opendfx.org

Cite as: Denney, C. (2026). OpenDFX for Printed Circuit Boards (Version 1.0). https://opendfx.org

Generated from the book's source pages. Each page below starts with its address.

---

Source: https://opendfx.org/00-start-here/01-how-to-use-this-book/

## How to use this book

This book gives practical advice for designing printed circuit boards that are easy to make, assemble and test. It is written for the people who design boards: electrical engineers, layout designers and the people who order boards and parts. It is also written to be read by AI tools that help design boards.

Every piece of advice is a numbered recommendation. A recommendation is not a rule. Your board may have a good reason to do something else, and the book tries to say what you give up when you do. So the book prefers "avoid" to "never". For example, a polarity mark under a part is worse than one beside it, but it is better than no mark at all.

### How the book is ordered

The book follows the path a board takes through a factory, as D67 in [The path a board takes](https://opendfx.org/00-start-here/03-the-path-a-board-takes/) shows. It starts with the files you send, then the panel, bare-board fabrication, components, assembly, test, packing and shipping. It ends with working with a manufacturer.

If you would rather work through the advice in the order you meet it while designing, use [Appendix B: Index by design stage](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/02-design-stage-index/). Before you release a design, work through [Appendix A: Pre-release checklist](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/01-checklist/). [Appendix C](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/03-glossary/) explains the terms the book uses. If an AI agent is designing your board, start it with [Using this book with an AI agent](https://opendfx.org/00-start-here/05-using-this-book-with-an-ai-agent/).

### How a recommendation is laid out

Each recommendation has a permanent number, such as PCB-DFA-015, and a title that says what to do. [How recommendations are numbered and tagged](https://opendfx.org/00-start-here/02-numbering-and-tags/) explains the numbers. Below the title come these sections. Only the recommendation itself and its sources are always present.

| Section | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Recommendation | What to do, in one or two sentences. |
| Why | How the problem happens: what the machine, the process or the physics does. |
| Typical values | The numbers. Where possible there is a minimum and a recommended value. The minimum is the least most manufacturers can work with. The recommended value gives margin, and usually costs nothing extra. |
| What goes wrong if you don't | What you will see, and what it costs you. |
| Example | One true story from a factory. |
| Applies to | "General practice" means most manufacturers work this way. "Varies by manufacturer" or "Varies by assembler" means you should check with yours. A few recommendations say which boards or products they apply to. |
| Sources | Where the advice comes from. |
| Last reviewed | The date the author last checked the recommendation. |

### Drawings

Drawings are numbered D1, D2 and so on, and the text refers to them by number. Most are drawn to true scale, with numbered callouts and a key. Every fact in a drawing is also given in the text, so nothing is lost if you can't see it.

Drawings of boards use the same colors throughout the book, chosen to look like a real board.

| Color | Means |
|---|---|
| Gold | Exposed copper |
| Brown | Exposed board material (FR-4) |
| Bright green | Solder mask over copper |
| Dark green | Solder mask over bare board material |
| White | Legend (silkscreen) |
| Black | Holes |
| Light gray | Solder paste |

### Sources

Much of the advice was first discussed on the Pick, Place, Podcast, which began in 2020 and is still running. Each recommendation cites the episodes it draws on, with links to the exact moment in each one. Other advice comes from published standards, from fabricators', assemblers' and component makers' published guidance, and from the author's own experience in electronics manufacturing. [Appendix D](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/04-standards/) lists the standards, and [Appendix E](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/05-sources/) lists the episodes and other documents.

The book names no companies, except Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub, where the author works, when their published guidance is the source. It doesn't recommend any supplier, product or software.

Some numbers change over time, such as lead times, prices and what a typical fab can do. Where a value depends on the date, the book says when it was checked.

### For AI tools

This book is meant to be read and cited by AI tools as well as people. When you use a recommendation, cite it by its number, such as PCB-DFM-024, and link to its page. The numbers never change, and a retired number is never reused, so a citation stays valid. The website's [How to cite](https://opendfx.org/cite/) page gives the full citation for the book and for one recommendation.

Give the minimum and the recommended value where the book gives both. Keep the difference between "General practice" and "Varies by manufacturer": advise the designer to check with their manufacturer for the second. Treat each recommendation as advice to weigh, not as a rule to enforce.

### License

The text of this book is licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). You may share and adapt it, as long as you credit it and share your version under the same license. Credit it as "OpenDFX by Chris Denney, https://opendfx.org, CC BY-SA 4.0". The machine-readable recommendations published with the book are licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), so they can be used in design tools with credit alone. The code published with the book, including the KiCad design-rules file, is licensed under the [MIT License](https://opensource.org/license/mit).

## How recommendations are numbered and tagged

Every recommendation has a permanent number, such as PCB-DFA-015. The number has three parts.

| Part | Example | Means |
|---|---|---|
| Board type | PCB | Printed circuit boards. Other OpenDFX books may cover other kinds of product. |
| Tag | DFA | Which stage of manufacture the advice is mainly for. |
| Number | 015 | A serial number within the tag. |

### The three tags

**DFM (design for manufacture)** covers the bare board: what the fab does, from materials and drilling to solder mask, legend and electrical test. In this book, DFM means fabrication of the bare board only.

**DFA (design for assembly)** covers fitting and soldering the parts, and everything around it: the BOM, the panel, fiducials, parts and their packaging, handling, shipping and working with your assembler. Advice that matters to both the fab and the assembler goes under DFA. The panel is the usual example: the fab makes it, but it is designed for the assembly machines.

**DFT (design for test)** covers testing bare boards and assembled boards, and programming the parts on them.

A recommendation's tag says where its advice mainly lands, not which Part of the book it is in. So Part 3, on bare-board fabrication, also holds a few DFA and DFT recommendations.

### Numbers never change

A recommendation keeps its number for good, even if its wording, its values or its place in the book change. A number that is retired is never given to anything else. So a number in a design note, a review comment or an AI tool's answer always points to the same advice.

Numbers were given out in the order the recommendations were written, not in book order. That is why PCB-DFA-029, on chip footprints, comes before PCB-DFA-018, on solder paste, in the book. Use the number to find a recommendation, not to judge where it sits.

### Finding a recommendation

Each recommendation has its own heading, so it has its own link: the page's address followed by the number and title. [Appendix A](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/01-checklist/) lists every recommendation in book order, and [Appendix B](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/02-design-stage-index/) lists them by design stage.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

## The path a board takes

A board passes through several factories, or several departments of one factory, between your design files and a finished product. Each step has its own machines, and each machine has its own needs. Most of the advice in this book comes from meeting those needs. This page follows a board along the path, and points to the Part of the book that covers each step.

![D67: A flow diagram, not to scale. Six steps run left to right: the design package (Part 1), the panel (Part 2), bare-board fabrication (Part 3), assembly (Part 5), test and programming (Part 6), and packing and shipping (Part 7). Components and materials (Part 4) feed into assembly from above. A bar under every step shows working with a manufacturer (Part 8).](https://opendfx.org/00-start-here/images/board-path.svg)

*D67 is a flow diagram, not to scale. Six steps run left to right, each with the Part of the book that covers it. Components and materials feed into assembly from above, alongside the bare boards. A bar under every step shows working with a manufacturer, which runs through the whole path.*

### The design package

Everything starts with the files you send. The fab needs the copper, solder mask, legend and drill data, a netlist and a fabrication drawing. The assembler needs the placement file, the BOM, the paste layer and an assembly drawing. Anything missing or unclear turns into a question, and every question adds time. See [Part 1: The design package](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/).

### The panel

Once the order comes in, the manufacturer's CAM engineers prepare your data for production. Part of that work is placing your boards into a panel. The panel, not the single board, is what the fab makes and the assembly machines carry. It holds several copies of your board, or one board with extra material around it. It has rails for the machines to hold, and fiducials for their cameras to find. The boards are held in by V-scores or tabs until they are separated after assembly. The panel is set by the assembler's machines, so it is best designed with the assembler, before the bare boards are ordered. See [Part 2: The panel](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/).

### Bare-board fabrication

The fab builds the bare boards, in their panel. It images and etches the inner layers, presses them together with prepreg, drills the holes and plates them. Then it images and etches the outer layers, and adds solder mask, the surface finish and the legend. It cuts the panel's outline, with the V-scores or tabs that hold the boards in. Finally it tests every board for open and short circuits. See [Part 3: Bare board fabrication](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/01-materials-and-stack-up/).

### Components and materials

While the boards are being made, the parts are bought, or supplied by you. They arrive on reels, in tubes or in trays, and some must be kept dry until they are used. Parts that are hard to buy can delay a build more than any other step. See [Part 4: Components and materials](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/01-choosing-parts/).

### Assembly

The assembler prints solder paste onto the pads through a stencil and checks it. A pick-and-place machine fits the surface-mount parts, and a reflow oven solders them. Machines then inspect the joints with cameras, and with X-rays where joints are hidden. Through-hole parts are soldered after that, by machine or by hand. Some boards are then cleaned or coated, and finally the boards are separated from the panel. See [Part 5: Assembly](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/).

### Test and programming

The assembled boards are tested, and their programmable parts are loaded with firmware. Test can be a flying probe, a bed-of-nails fixture, boundary scan or a functional test that powers the board. Each needs a way to reach the board, which has to be designed in. See [Part 6: Test and programming](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/01-test-points/).

### Packing and shipping

Finished boards are packed against static and moisture, and shipped. The same care applies to boards and parts you store yourself. See [Part 7: Handling, packaging and shipping](https://opendfx.org/07-handling-packaging-and-shipping/01-static-protection/).

### Working with a manufacturer

All along the path, how you work with your manufacturer affects cost, lead time and quality. That includes how you get a quote, how you move from prototype to production, and when you bring the manufacturer into your design review. See [Part 8: Working with a manufacturer](https://opendfx.org/08-working-with-a-manufacturer/01-cost-and-lead-time/).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

## Classes and standards in one page

Most boards are made and inspected to IPC standards. IPC is the electronics industry's trade association, now called the Global Electronics Association. Its standards keep the IPC name, such as IPC-A-610, so the book calls them IPC standards. This page explains the three IPC classes, which the book refers to often, and lists the standards it uses most. [Appendix D](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/04-standards/) lists every standard the book mentions.

### The three IPC classes

The IPC standards sort products into three classes. The class sets what is acceptable in the bare board and in the assembly, such as the size of the annular ring, the thickness of plating in the holes and the shape of each solder joint.

| Class | Meant for | Share of what is built |
|---|---|---|
| Class 1 | General electronic products, where the main need is that the product works. | About 5% |
| Class 2 | Dedicated service products, which should work reliably for a long life but are not critical. Most commercial and industrial products are Class 2. | About 90% |
| Class 3 | High-performance products, which must keep working whenever they are called on, sometimes in harsh conditions. Examples are life-support medical equipment, aerospace and some automotive and military products. | The rest |

Class 3 limits are tighter, so Class 3 boards cost much more to make and inspect. One estimate is ten times as much or more. Some Class 3 limits can only be met if the design allows them. For example, a Class 3 annular ring needs pads big enough for it. So a board designed to Class 2 doesn't become a Class 3 board because the order says Class 3.

The book's recommendation is to build to Class 2 unless the product truly needs Class 3, and to design for Class 3 from the start if it does. See [PCB-DFT-003](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/11-bare-board-test/#pcb-dft-003-ask-for-ipc-class-2-unless-the-product-needs-class-3-and-know-class-3-is-a-design-standard-too).

State the class on the fabrication drawing, and on the assembly drawing if it differs. If you don't, the bare-board standard IPC-6012 defaults to Class 2. See [PCB-DFM-014](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-014-put-everything-the-gerbers-cant-say-on-the-fabrication-drawing).

### The standards the book uses most

| Standard | What it covers |
|---|---|
| IPC-2221 | How to design a printed board: the generic design standard, including test lands. |
| IPC-7351 | Land patterns (footprints) for surface-mount parts, and the zero-rotation convention for placement data. |
| IPC-6012 | What a finished rigid bare board must meet, class by class. |
| IPC-4761 | Ways of protecting vias: tenting, plugging and filling. |
| IPC-D-356 | The netlist format the fab uses to test bare boards. |
| IPC-A-610 | What an acceptable assembled board looks like, class by class. |
| J-STD-001 | The requirements for soldered assemblies, which go with IPC-A-610. |
| J-STD-020 and J-STD-033 | How moisture-sensitive parts are rated, and how they must be stored, handled and baked. |
| ANSI/ESD S20.20 | The requirements for a factory's static control program. |

Standards are revised every few years. The book names a revision where it quotes a value from one. Check that you are using the current revision, and say which one you mean when it matters.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

## Using this book with an AI agent

This book is written to be read by AI agents that design circuit boards, as well as by people. This page is for both. It tells an agent how to work through the book while it designs a board. It also tells the person directing the agent what to ask for, and what to expect back.

### Give the agent the book

There are three ways to give an AI tool the book. The simplest, for any chat tool, takes three steps: download one file, attach it to a new chat, and paste one prompt. The steps and the prompt are at [opendfx.org/ai](https://opendfx.org/ai/).

The first is the Agent Skill, which is a folder of instructions and files that many AI agents can load by themselves. Download it from [opendfx.org/opendfx-pcb-design.zip](https://opendfx.org/opendfx-pcb-design.zip). It holds a short version of this page, the recommendations data file, the KiCad design-rules file, the release checker, and a small script that prints the recommendations for each design stage. For a coding agent, put the skill's folder in your own PCB project, in the folder where your tool looks for skills. For a chat tool that supports skills, upload the zip file as the tool's documentation describes. Installing the skill doesn't install Python or KiCad, and it doesn't give the agent access to your computer.

The second is the whole book as one file, [opendfx.org/llms-full.txt](https://opendfx.org/llms-full.txt). Attach it to a chat, or add it to a project in any AI tool that accepts files. An uploaded file is a copy of the book on the day you downloaded it. When the book changes, download the file again, replace the old copy, and start a new chat. The [change log](https://opendfx.org/changelog/) lists what changed in each version.

The third is a block of instructions for your project, described in the next section. The agent then fetches only what it needs from the website while it works.

The whole book is long, so an agent that needs only part of it can fetch just that part. Every page of the book is also published as plain Markdown, at its web address with `.md` added in place of the final slash. For example, the page at `opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/` is also at `opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance.md`. Every recommendation is also published on its own as Markdown, at its permanent address with `.md` added, such as `opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-006.md`.

### Or add the book to your project's instructions

Many AI coding and design tools read a file of standing instructions from the project folder. Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, and Codex and many other agents read `AGENTS.md`. Cursor reads the files in `.cursor/rules/`, and GitHub Copilot reads `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. Paste the block below into whichever file your tool reads. This is the file in your own PCB project. OpenDFX's own `AGENTS.md` is for people changing the book, so don't copy it into your project.

```markdown
## PCB design: follow OpenDFX

When you design or review a printed circuit board in this project, follow
OpenDFX for Printed Circuit Boards by Chris Denney (https://opendfx.org).

- Read https://opendfx.org/llms.txt first. It explains how to use the book.
- Before you design, ask me who will make and assemble the board, how many
  will be built, the IPC class, the board thickness and copper weight, how
  through-hole parts will be soldered, and how the board will be tested.
  If I don't know, use the book's defaults and say which you used.
- Work stage by stage: parts, library, placement, routing, outline, release,
  production. At each stage, read that stage's recommendations from
  https://opendfx.org/data/recommendations.json (field design_stages).
  Fetch one recommendation as Markdown at https://opendfx.org/<ID>.md.
- Use the recommended values. Use a minimum value only where the design
  needs it, and tell me each place you did.
- In KiCad, run the design rule check with the OpenDFX rules file
  (https://opendfx.org/kicad/) after placement and after routing.
- Cite each recommendation by its ID and its address, such as
  PCB-DFA-006 and https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-006.
- Never replace or change an existing .kicad_dru rules file without asking me.
- If you can't read a file or a page, or can't run a check, say so and ask
  me for it. Don't answer as if you had read it.
- When a recommendation conflicts with something I need, tell me and let me
  choose.
- Mark a recommendation Met only when you can name the evidence: a file, a
  measurement, a report, or something I confirmed.
- When you finish, give me a table of every recommendation in the stages you
  worked on: ID, title, status (Met, Not met, Not applicable or Needs a
  person) and a note.
```

### Say what the agent can and can't do

Before it starts, the agent should check what the task needs, and only that. To answer a question about the book, it only needs to read the book. To review or change a board, it also needs the person's files. To run the checks, it also needs Python 3, and KiCad 10 for the design rule check.

If it can't do something the task needs, it should say so before it starts, and say whether that isn't available or hasn't been tried. It should then give the person the commands to run, and read the reports they send back. If it can't read a file or a page it needs, it should say so and ask for it, rather than answer as if it had read it.

### Start with the questions only the person can answer

Many recommendations depend on how the board will be built. So before it starts, the agent should ask the person these questions, and write the answers down.

1. Who will make the bare board, and who will assemble it?
   If they publish their own limits, their limits come first ([PCB-DFA-124](https://opendfx.org/08-working-with-a-manufacturer/03-design-reviews-and-communication/#pcb-dfa-124-bring-your-manufacturer-into-the-design-review-before-the-design-is-final)).
2. How many boards will be built, now and later?
   Volume decides many choices, such as panels, test fixtures and part packaging.
3. Which IPC class does the product need?
   Most products need Class 2 ([PCB-DFT-003](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/11-bare-board-test/#pcb-dft-003-ask-for-ipc-class-2-unless-the-product-needs-class-3-and-know-class-3-is-a-design-standard-too)).
4. How thick is the board, and how heavy is the copper?
   The book's trace and gap values are for 1 oz finished copper ([PCB-DFM-020](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/01-materials-and-stack-up/#pcb-dfm-020-size-traces-and-gaps-for-the-finished-copper-weight)).
5. How will any through-hole parts be soldered: by hand, by selective soldering or by wave soldering?
6. How will the board be tested: by flying probe, by a bed-of-nails fixture, or only by a functional test?

If the person doesn't know an answer, the agent should use the book's default and say which default it used.

### Give the agent your board

The more the agent can see, the more it can check. Give it the answers to the questions above, and the files for the work it is doing. For a review, that is usually the KiCad project folder, or the release folder of Gerber, drill, netlist, placement and BOM files. If the agent can't run KiCad or the release checker, run them yourself, and give it the reports. The design rule check's JSON report and the release checker's report are written to be read by an agent. Tell it what you know that the files can't show, such as what the assembler agreed.

Every fact shown in a drawing is also written in the text. If you want the agent to look at the drawing itself, give it the drawing's web link. If it can't view the drawing, attach the relevant PDF page or a PNG or JPEG of the drawing directly to the chat.

### Work through the design stage by stage

[Appendix B: Index by design stage](https://opendfx.org/09-appendices/02-design-stage-index/) lists every recommendation under the stage where it matters. The [recommendations data file](https://opendfx.org/data/recommendations.json) gives the same stages in the field `design_stages`. At the start of each stage, the agent should read that stage's recommendations in full, including the Why and the Typical values. Then it should do the work for that stage.

The stages, in order, are:

1. Parts and schematic.
2. Library and footprints.
3. Placement.
4. Routing and copper.
5. Board outline and panel.
6. Release.
7. Ordering and production.

Where a recommendation gives a minimum and a recommended value, the agent should use the recommended value. It should use the minimum value only where the design needs it, and tell the person each place it did.

### Check the board with KiCad's design rule check

For a board designed in KiCad, the agent should use the [OpenDFX design-rules file](https://opendfx.org/kicad/). If the project already has a rules file of its own, the agent should first follow the next section. It should run KiCad's design rule check after placing the parts, and again after routing. The command `kicad-cli pcb drc --format json --severity-all` gives a report that an agent can read.

Each report names the recommendation it comes from and gives its permanent address, such as opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-020. Before it changes the board, the agent should read that recommendation, so it fixes the cause and not only the symptom. Where the design really needs a minimum value, the agent should draw a small rule area named `OpenDFX minimum` there, rather than change the rules.

The design rule check can only see the board. It can't see the BOM, the drawings, the panel or the conversations with the manufacturer. So a clean check doesn't mean every recommendation is met.

### If the project already has a rules file

A KiCad project has one rules file, named after the project. If the project already has one, the agent should never replace it or change it without the person's agreement. Most OpenDFX rules only add checks, but three replace a Board Setup value or a setting: the board edge clearance, the silkscreen clearance, and how plated through-hole pads join copper pours. And when two rules of the same kind apply to the same item, KiCad uses the one later in the file. So the agent should list where the two files overlap, and propose a combined file for the person to review. If the person accepts it, the agent should try it on a copy of the project, refill the zones, and report any change in the check and in the copper. Otherwise it should leave the person's file as it is, and say which OpenDFX checks are then not run.

### Check the release files

Before the files go to the fab and the assembler, the agent should check them with the OpenDFX release checker, `check_release.py`. It comes with the Agent Skill, and it is also at [opendfx.org/check_release.py](https://opendfx.org/check_release.py). It reads the Gerber files, the drill files, the netlist, the placement file and the BOM exported from KiCad 10. It checks what those files can show, such as Gerber X2 files, separate drill files for plated and non-plated holes, a placement file in millimeters, and a BOM with a part number on every fitted line. Its help text lists the KiCad commands that export a release the way this book recommends. Its report uses the same statuses as the table below, so its rows can go straight into that table.

### Hand back a table of every recommendation

When the design is done, the agent should give the person a table with one row for every recommendation in the stages it worked on. Each row should have the recommendation's ID, its title, a status, and a note. The status should be one of these four.

| Status | Means |
|---|---|
| Met | The design follows the recommendation. The note names the evidence: a file, a measurement, a report, or something the person confirmed. |
| Not met | The design doesn't follow it. The note says why, and what the design gives up. |
| Not applicable | It doesn't apply to this board. The note says why. Missing evidence is never a reason. |
| Needs a person | Only a person can do it, such as agreeing a limit with the assembler, or the evidence is missing. The note says exactly what to check or do. |

For example:

| ID | Title | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| PCB-DFM-020 | Size traces and gaps for the finished copper weight | Met | Traces 0.15 mm wide or more on 1 oz copper. The KiCad check passed. |
| PCB-DFA-016 | Keep components back from breakaway edges, and ceramic capacitors further still | Met | Measured in KiCad: the nearest ceramic capacitor is 6 mm from the breakaway edge. |
| PCB-DFA-043 | Keep surface-mount parts away from through-hole pins on the solder side | Not met | Two pads of C12 are 2.4 mm from J1's pins, because the board outline is fixed. Inside an `OpenDFX minimum` area. |
| PCB-DFA-124 | Bring your manufacturer into the design review before the design is final | Needs a person | Send the design to the assembler for review before ordering. |

The agent should mark a recommendation Met only when it can name the evidence. Something the person confirmed is good evidence for what they can know, such as what the assembler agreed. But the note should say it came from the person, and not from a check the agent ran.

The person can then review the design by recommendation, instead of searching the board for problems. Every "Not met" and every `OpenDFX minimum` area is a place to look closely.

### Ask the person when the book and the design disagree

These are recommendations, not rules. When a recommendation conflicts with something the person needs, the agent should say so, and let the person choose. It shouldn't quietly break the recommendation, and it shouldn't quietly change the person's requirement.

Source: https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/

## Fabrication data

The fabrication data is everything you send a board fab so they can make the bare board: the copper and other layer images, the drill files, the board outline, a netlist, and a drawing with the notes the images can't carry. None of it goes straight onto a machine. A CAM engineer reads it all into CAM software, checks it, and rebuilds it into the fab's own production tools. So the goal is CAM input that is complete, consistent and impossible to misread.

Each time the CAM engineer has to ask you a question, it can cost about a day. Most of the recommendations below exist to remove those questions.

### PCB-DFM-008: Send one complete fabrication package, in one format, from one revision

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-008

**Recommendation:** Send the fab one archive per board, holding one set of fabrication data in a single format, all exported from the same revision of the design:
- one Gerber file per layer (every copper layer, both solder masks, both legends, both paste layers), in Gerber X2 if your tool supports it;
- drill files (see [PCB-DFM-011](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-011-separate-plated-and-non-plated-holes-and-use-an-unambiguous-drill-format));
- the board outline as its own file;
- an IPC-D-356 netlist (see [PCB-DFM-009](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-009-always-send-a-netlist-made-from-the-same-revision-as-the-gerbers));
- a fabrication drawing, plus the same specifications in a plain-text file (see [PCB-DFM-014](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-014-put-everything-the-gerbers-cant-say-on-the-fabrication-drawing)).

ODB++ or IPC-2581 can replace the Gerbers, drill files and netlist, if your fab says it reads them. Send one format or the other, not both.

Keep your native design files and schematic out of the fab package. Send them to your assembler, and to the fab only if asked, in a separate folder marked "reference only" (see [PCB-DFA-064](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/02-assembly-data/#pcb-dfa-064-always-send-the-xy-file-and-send-native-design-files-and-the-schematic-when-you-can)).

**Why:** Every file in the archive has to be opened and checked for instructions. Extra files waste that time, and two copies of the same board in different formats (Gerber and ODB++, say) force the CAM engineer to compare them and ask which one is right. Native design files need the same design software to open, and the fab builds from fabrication data, not from them. IPC-2581 and ODB++ carry the netlist and layer structure inside them, which is their advantage, but each design tool exports them a little differently and each CAM system reads them a little differently.

**Typical values:** Gerber files with the standard `.gbr` extension and Gerber X2 attributes. Even if top and bottom solder masks are identical, send both.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Questions, a day's delay for each, and occasionally a board built from the wrong one of two conflicting files.

**Example:** One assembler that imports IPC-2581 from several design tools found that each tool writes the same standard slightly differently, and had to handle each one separately. Practitioners have reported pads silently missing and thermal reliefs rotated after an ODB++ import, caught only by comparing against known-good artwork. Open your outputs in a viewer that is not part of your design tool before you send them.

**Applies to:** General practice. Which of Gerber, ODB++ and IPC-2581 to send varies by fab; ask yours.

**Sources:** *PCB Fabrication Data: Design to Fabrication Data Transfer*, V6 (Sept 2015), the guide published by the maintainers of the Gerber format: chapters 14 to 16 (one board per archive, nothing superfluous, no duplicate formats, both masks); Gerber Layer Format Specification, revision 2026.05; KiCad 10 documentation, fabrication outputs (Gerber, IPC-2581, ODB++, IPC-D-356); [“Building the factory of the future with CircuitHub CEO, Andrew Seddon”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440-building-the-factory-of-the-future-with-circuithub-ceo-andrew-seddon) (Aug 2026), [38:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440?t=2280)–39:00; [“The PCB assembly process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141-the-pcb-assembly-process) (Jun 2020), [08:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141?t=480); Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-009: Always send a netlist, made from the same revision as the Gerbers

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-009

**Recommendation:** Export an IPC-D-356 netlist from your design tool every time you export Gerbers, and send it with them. If you send ODB++ or IPC-2581, the netlist is already inside.

**Why:** The first thing a CAM engineer does is build a netlist from your Gerbers and drill files, and they re-check against it every time they edit the data. Your netlist comes from the schematic connections in your design tool, not from the images. Comparing the two catches a Gerber that didn't import correctly, a trace or hole deleted by mistake, and copper that shorts two nets you meant to keep apart. Without your netlist, the fab can only test the boards against a netlist built from your images, so a wrong image is built and passes electrical test anyway. Many design tools only regenerate the netlist when you tick a separate box, so it's easy to send an old one.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** An error in the data is built faithfully, passes the fab's electrical test, and is found only after the board is assembled. A stale netlist does the opposite: dozens of false mismatches, and questions back to you.

**Example:** CAM engineers report receiving netlists that contained only half the board, because the netlist was not re-exported after the layout changed. A fab's quoting engineer gives the classic case: if the Gerbers show a plated slot where there shouldn't be one, and there's no netlist, you get a plated slot.

**Applies to:** General practice. Fabs can work without a netlist; that doesn't make it a good idea.

**Sources:** *PCB Fabrication Data: Design to Fabrication Data Transfer*, V6 (Sept 2015), chapter 11, "Always include the netlist"; one large fab's published data guidance (checks the supplied IPC netlist against its own); [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=720)–19:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=540)–11:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-010: Tell the fab where you join nets on purpose

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-010

**Recommendation:** If your copper deliberately joins nets that stay separate in the schematic (a star point joining analog and digital ground, a net-tie, a shorting jumper), list them in your fabrication notes. Better still, use your design tool's net-tie feature so the netlist knows about them.

**Why:** The fab compares its netlist, built from the copper, with yours. A deliberate join looks exactly like a short.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** The netlist check fails, and the job stops while the CAM engineer asks you whether each join is meant to be there.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=1020)–18:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-011: Separate plated and non-plated holes, and use an unambiguous drill format

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-011

**Recommendation:** Put plated and non-plated holes in separate drill files. Export them as Gerber X2 drill files if your fab accepts them. If you send Excellon (NC drill) files, use one of the two safe formats, 2:4 inch or 3:3 metric, with the units and zero suppression stated in the header. Make the drill files from the same origin as the Gerbers, so the holes land on their pads.

**Why:** If plating isn't stated, the CAM engineer guesses from the copper: a hole through a pad is plated, a hole in bare laminate is not. A large hole you wanted plated, with no copper around it, comes back bare. Excellon has no standard way to say where the decimal point is, so the fab has to work out the number of digits and which zeros were left off. Formats with too few decimal places, such as 3:2 metric, round every hole position to the nearest 0.01 mm, which shifts holes off their pads. Gerber X2 drill files have none of these problems, and they also say which layers a blind or buried via spans.

**Typical values:** 2:4 inch or 3:3 metric for Excellon; avoid 3:2 metric, 5:1, 1:5 and other unusual formats. Metric is preferred where you have the choice. A format that writes every coordinate with a decimal point, such as KiCad's decimal format, can't be misread either, so it is also safe.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Holes plated that shouldn't be, or not plated that should, and drill files that need hand-work to line up with the copper.

**Applies to:** General practice. Many fabs still ask for Excellon. KiCad 10's drill dialog writes plated and non-plated holes to separate Excellon files by default, but its command-line export puts them in one file unless you ask for separate files.

**Sources:** [“The basics of the PCB drilling process w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552-the-basics-of-the-pcb-drilling-process-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552?t=1440)–28:00; [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [01:13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=4380)–01:15:00; *PCB Fabrication Data: Design to Fabrication Data Transfer*, V6 (Sept 2015), chapters 7 and 9; XNC drill format specification, revision 2021.11 (separate plated and non-plated files; metric recommended); KiCad 10 documentation, drill file options.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-012: Dimension the holes that matter, with their real tolerance

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-012

**Recommendation:** If a hole's size or position matters (a press-fit pin, a connector whose datasheet says +0.1/−0 mm, a hole sized for current, a mounting hole that must line up with an enclosure), dimension it on the drill drawing with its true tolerance. Design the hole to the middle of the allowed range, not to the nominal value. Don't create extra hole sizes just to split the difference; a drawing callout does the job.

**Why:** Fabs adjust hole sizes to suit their process: they drill plated holes larger to allow for plating, and may enlarge an awkward size within the standard tolerance without telling you. IPC-6012F says only holes dimensioned in the procurement documents are inspected for position; the rest are checked only through annular ring. A one-sided tolerance such as +0.1/−0 mm is invisible in the data: a 0.7 mm hole looks like any other 0.7 mm hole.

**Typical values:** IPC-6012F default finished hole tolerances, when the drawing says nothing: ±100 µm for plated component holes, +80 µm with no lower limit for via-only holes (they may be plugged), ±80 µm for non-plated holes. One large fab aims for the middle of any tolerance band you give it. Tighter than standard tolerances are possible, but cost more, because every hole has to be measured and out-of-range boards scrapped.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A connector that won't go in, or falls out; a press-fit pin that sits loose in a hole drilled too large.

**Example:** Small connectors whose datasheets call for 0.7 mm +0.1/−0 holes have repeatedly caused trouble when the footprint simply used a 0.7 mm hole, because the fab had no way of knowing the hole must never be smaller.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 1-2 and section 3.4.1; [“The basics of the PCB drilling process w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552-the-basics-of-the-pcb-drilling-process-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552?t=1080)–21:00; [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [42:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2520)–48:00; [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [01:00:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=3600)–01:11:00; one large fab's published hole-size guidance.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-013: Put your intent in the data, not in a note that contradicts it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-013

**Recommendation:** Make the layer files show the board you want. If you want vias tented, export the solder mask with no openings over them, rather than leaving openings and adding a note saying "tent all vias". Don't export component values or other assembly text onto the legend layer unless you want it printed. Keep title blocks, frames and notes out of the layer files; put them on the drawing.

**Why:** A CAM engineer treats the data as what you want. When a note contradicts the data, they have to stop and ask which one is right. A note like "tent all vias" also leaves them to decide which holes are vias, which is hard when a board has several via sizes and small component holes. Value text exported to the legend lands on pads and gets clipped off, or prints as an unreadable mass of overlapping text.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A question and a day's delay, or a board built to the data when you meant the note.

**Applies to:** General practice. Most design tools can tent vias in the export settings; in some it takes a design rule on hole size.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=1320)–24:00 and [55:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=3300)–01:00:00; [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=600)–14:00; *PCB Fabrication Data: Design to Fabrication Data Transfer*, V6 (Sept 2015), chapter 10, "Put only data in data files".

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-014: Put everything the Gerbers can't say on the fabrication drawing

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-014

**Recommendation:** Give every board a fabrication drawing that states, at least:
- performance class (IPC-6012 Class 2 or Class 3);
- base material, called out by grade and Tg (for example against an IPC-4101 slash sheet), not just "FR-4", and finished board thickness and its tolerance;
- copper weight for each layer;
- stack-up, and any controlled impedance as a table: structure, layers, target impedance, tolerance and reference planes;
- surface finish, solder mask color and legend color;
- via treatment (tented, plugged, filled);
- board outline with critical dimensions, cut-outs and slots, and the drill chart with tolerances;
- revision, date and author.

Put the same specifications in a plain-text file in the package too. If you order through a web form, make sure it matches the drawing.

**Why:** Gerbers only show shapes. Thickness, material, finish, class and impedance can only come from you. When the drawing is silent, IPC-6012F fills the gap with defaults the fab will build to, which may not be what you meant. Many fabs' software can read specifications from a plain-text file automatically; none can read them from a drawing. The same goes for the AI tools now used to check designs and prepare quotes: a text file is read exactly, a drawing has to be interpreted.

**Typical values:** IPC-6012F defaults when nothing is specified: Class 2; epoxy-glass laminate; ENIG finish for designs first released on or after 1 October 2023 (tin-lead for older ones); 1/2 oz starting copper on every layer; the hole tolerances in [PCB-DFM-012](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-012-dimension-the-holes-that-matter-with-their-real-tolerance). IPC-6012F gives no default board thickness tolerance; other dimensional tolerances fall back to the IPC-2220 design standards. Fabs commonly quote ±10% on thickness for boards 0.8 mm and thicker, but this varies, so state the tolerance you need. Controlled impedance is commonly held to ±10%, and ±5% on request.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards that are the wrong thickness, the wrong finish, or the wrong class, and no claim against the fab, because they built what was ordered. If controlled impedance isn't on the drawing, the fab doesn't control it, and a board that doesn't perform is still a good board as far as they're concerned.

**Example:** At one assembler that builds bare boards to what is entered on its order form, boards have come back the wrong thickness because the thickness wasn't set there. Wrong thickness can't be reworked: it means new bare boards and a new assembly.

**Applies to:** General practice. IPC-2611 and IPC-2614 cover fabrication documentation in full.

**Sources:** IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), section 1.3.3 and Table 1-2, Table 3-3, section 3.4; one fab's published fabrication-notes guide; *PCB Fabrication Data: Design to Fabrication Data Transfer*, V6 (Sept 2015), chapter 15; [“Understanding Controlled Impedance w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer, Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934-understanding-controlled-impedance-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Nov 2022), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=1020)–18:00; [“Impedance Control Demo w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746-impedance-control-demo-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Oct 2023), [25:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=1500)–27:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=660)–12:00; [“Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=2400)–43:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-015: Check a copied fabrication drawing line by line

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-015

**Recommendation:** When you start a new board from an old one's drawing or stack-up, read every note again. Remove impedance callouts, reference planes, finishes and special processes the new board doesn't need, and add the ones it does.

**Why:** Drawings are usually copied from the last project. Notes that were right for the old board stay on, and requirements for the new one get left off.

**Typical values:** Under IPC-6012F, a drawing first released before 1 October 2023 with no finish callout defaults to a tin-lead finish; one released after defaults to ENIG. State the finish rather than rely on the date.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Impedance requirements for traces that no longer exist, with questions to match, or a missing reference plane and a board that doesn't work even though it passed every inspection.

**Example:** One fab's engineers regularly find impedance callouts copied from an earlier drawing that don't apply to the new board, or reference planes left out.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Understanding Controlled Impedance w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer, Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934-understanding-controlled-impedance-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Nov 2022), [39:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=2340)–41:00; IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 1-2 and Table 3-3.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-016: Clear every design-rule error before you make the outputs

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-016

**Recommendation:** Run your design tool's design-rule check (DRC) and resolve every error, above all unconnected nets, before you export anything. Then compare the release with the previous one, so you know exactly what changed.

**Why:** Design tools will happily export Gerbers from a board with unrouted connections. Treat DRC errors like compiler warnings: each one is either fixed or understood. A comparison between versions (a schematic, layout or BOM diff, not just "this file changed") catches values and net names changed by accident.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A board with a missing connection, fixed with a wire on the prototype and a new revision afterwards.

**Example:** A first-time designer's board had a dead display because one power pin was never routed to the microcontroller. A mentor found it from the design files, and a single wire fixed the prototype.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Building a product at a big organization vs a startup w/ Barnacle Systems CTO, Darren Beckwith”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10360463-building-a-product-at-a-big-organization-vs-a-startup-w-barnacle-systems-cto-darren-beckwith) (Apr 2022), [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10360463?t=3120)–53:00; [“How sensors.AFRICA empowers citizens to fight against pollution w/ Jack McLeans”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7831030-how-sensors-africa-empowers-citizens-to-fight-against-pollution-w-jack-mcleans) (Feb 2021), [23:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7831030?t=1380)–24:00; [“The Benefits of Asynchronous Design Review for Engineers & Manufacturers w/ AllSpice.io”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11886751-the-benefits-of-asynchronous-design-review-for-engineers-manufacturers-w-allspice-io) (Dec 2022), [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11886751?t=1860)–34:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

## Assembly data

To build an assembled board, the assembler needs more than the bare-board data. They need to know which part goes where, which way round, and on which side: that comes from the placement (XY) file and the bill of materials ([The BOM](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/)). Anything the data can't show, such as how to bend a lead or how tight to make a screw, comes from an assembly drawing.

The assembler's programmers check every one of these against each other and against your copper and legend layers. Where they disagree, the job stops until someone asks you.

### PCB-DFA-064: Always send the XY file, and send native design files and the schematic when you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-064

**Recommendation:** Send a placement file (also called an XY, centroid or pick-and-place file) with every assembly order.
List every part location on the board, on both sides, with:
- reference designator (exactly as in the BOM);
- X and Y of the part's center, in mm;
- rotation in degrees;
- side (top or bottom);
- whether it's surface-mount or through-hole.

Keep do-not-place locations in the file; whether a location is fitted belongs in the BOM ([PCB-DFA-071](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/#pcb-dfa-071-mark-do-not-place-and-customer-supplied-lines-clearly)). Also send your native design files and the schematic, in a separate folder marked "reference only" (see [PCB-DFM-008](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-008-send-one-complete-fabrication-package-in-one-format-from-one-revision)).

**Why:** Gerbers show pads, not parts. Without the XY file, someone has to find and type in the position of every part by hand. Do-not-place locations stay in because a BOM change on a later order can fill them, and the assembler then already has their positions. With the schematic and design files, the assembler can answer their own questions about polarity, pin 1 and which part goes where, instead of putting the job on hold to ask you.

**Typical values:** Millimeters, with the origin and units stated in the header. Rotations positive counter-clockwise, as most assemblers expect. Plain text or CSV. Without the file, making placement data by hand takes about 3 minutes a part: about 5 hours for a 100-part board (one assembler).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A job put on hold while someone asks you a question the schematic would have answered; a four-day turn can become something like seven days. With no XY file at all, extra programming time and cost.

**Example:** One assembler says the XY file is the one file new customers most often don't know about, because a board soldered by hand on the bench never needs one. Assembly inspectors say the schematic is what they open when they can't work out a part's orientation from the placement viewer.

**Applies to:** General practice. Online assemblers vary in whether they want through-hole parts in the file; listing every location and marking the type works for all of them.

**Sources:** [Necessary Documentation](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/documentation) (Worthington Assembly); [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [06:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=360)–08:00; [“The PCB assembly inspection process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750-the-pcb-assembly-inspection-process) (Oct 2020), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750?t=1020)–20:00; [“The PCB assembly process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141-the-pcb-assembly-process) (Jun 2020), [08:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141?t=480); two large online assemblers' published file requirements (checked Nov 2026); KiCad 10 documentation, component placement files; Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-065: Draw footprints to the IPC zero rotation, and write your convention down

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-065

**Recommendation:** Draw every footprint in your library at the zero rotation shown in IPC-7351B, Figure 16-1, and write the convention into your library's rules so everyone who adds a footprint follows it. Expect the assembler to check every rotation anyway.

**Why:** The rotation in the XY file is the part's angle relative to how its footprint was drawn. If footprints are drawn in different orientations, the same rotation number means different things on different parts. The current standard, IPC-7352 (2023), no longer lists zero rotations; it says each organization's library standard should define them. IPC-7351B's figure is still the convention most libraries follow. Parts on reels sit in many orientations, depending on the maker, so the assembler always matches each reel to your footprint by hand; a consistent library means one correction per package type instead of one per part.

**Typical values:** IPC-7351B zero rotation, by package (drawn in D44):

| Package | Zero rotation |
|---|---|
| Chip resistors, capacitors, inductors; molded and MELF parts; aluminum electrolytics | Horizontal, pin 1 on the left. Pin 1 is the positive pin, or the cathode for diodes. |
| SOT, SOT-23, SOT-223, DPAK, SOIC, TSSOP, SON, DFN, QFP, QFN, chip arrays | Pin 1 at the upper left |
| BGA, LGA | Pin A1 at the upper left |
| PLCC, LCC, bumpered QFP with pin 1 at the center of a side | Pin 1 at the top center |

For example, a part that sits on its tape with pin 1 at the lower left is 90° counter-clockwise from its zero rotation.

![D44 is drawn to scale: six footprints at their IPC zero rotation: a horizontal 0603 chip with no polarity mark; a horizontal SOD-123 diode with the cathode on the left; a SOT-23 with pins 1 and 2 on the left, pin 1 at the top, and no mark; an 8-pin SOIC with pin 1 at the upper left; a 3 × 3 mm QFN with pin 1 at the top of the left side; a BGA with ball A1 at the upper left. Each has a cross at its center.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/zero-rotation.svg)

*D44 is drawn to scale and shows six footprints at the IPC-7351B zero rotation. The 0603 chip resistor or capacitor lies horizontal with no polarity mark, since it isn't polarized; the SOD-123 diode lies horizontal with its cathode, marked K, on the left. The SOIC, QFN and BGA, whose pads would fit either way round, each have a white pin-1 dot. The SOT-23 has pins 1 and 2 on the left, pin 1 at the top, and pin 3 on the right; it needs no mark, because its pads only fit one way. The 8-pin SOIC has pins 1 to 4 down the left side, pin 1 at the upper left. The 16-pin QFN has pin 1 at the top of the left side, and the BGA has ball A1 at the upper left. The cross at each part's center is the point the XY file gives; the rotation in the XY file is measured from this drawing.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** More time spent lining up rotations before the first board can be built, and more chances to place a part backwards.

**Example:** At one assembler, lining up rotations from customers' XY files commonly takes about half an hour per job. Because the rotations are at least consistent within a package type, the usual fix is "turn every 0402 by 90°", and the rest follow. LEDs are the hardest: each maker orients them differently in the tape and uses different polarity marks.

**Applies to:** General practice. If you use a different convention, that's fine; the assembler will work it out. Use one convention throughout the library.

**Sources:** IPC-7351B, section 16 and Figure 16-1; IPC-7352 (May 2023), section 7; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=420)–11:00; Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-066: Give every part a unique reference designator, placed next to its own part

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-066

**Recommendation:** Give every part on the board its own reference designator (R1, U4), with no duplicates and no suffixes like U4_1 and U4_2 left over from copied schematic blocks. Use only letters and numbers. If the legend shows reference designators, place each one where it clearly belongs to its own part.

**Why:** The reference designator is how everyone talks about a part: the BOM, the XY file, the inspection report and every email. Duplicates make every conversation ambiguous. Some inspection and programming software can't handle unusual characters in designators. Printed designators nudged around to fit can end up beside the wrong part, and the assembler uses them to check placement.

**Typical values:** Up to about 8 characters is safe; at least one inspection machine's software fails on longer ones.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A question that takes half an hour to answer instead of seconds; in the worst case, the wrong part soldered to a pad because its designator sat beside the neighboring footprint.

**Example:** One assembler's inspection machine crashes outright on some unusual designators; they now run their own check on every job for long or odd designators before it reaches the machine.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=2400)–43:00; [“Mastering Vias: Plugging, Filling, and Best Practices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518-mastering-vias-plugging-filling-and-best-practices) (Nov 2024), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518?t=1680)–30:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-067: Put everything the data can't show on an assembly drawing

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-067

**Recommendation:** Add an assembly drawing, or a short marked-up image, for anything the XY file and BOM can't express:
- through-hole leads that must be bent, with the angle and the direction;
- screws, nuts and other hardware, with a torque value;
- parts that must sit at a set height or stand-off, or be glued, sleeved or potted;
- areas to keep clear of coating, glue or labels;
- any special process or material, specified by what it must do rather than by brand.

**Why:** Placement data says where a part goes and which way it faces, not how its leads are formed or how tight a screw is. "Tight" means something different to every operator; a torque value can be set on a torque driver and checked. Assemblers are wary of choosing a torque for you, because they don't know your materials and loads. Branded solder pastes, wires and other materials get discontinued or go out of stock, and a drawing that names one product can stop a build.

**Typical values:** Torque in N·m (or in·lb), from the fastener maker, a calculation, or a pull test on a few samples.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts fitted the way the data shows, which may not be what you meant, and a second build to fix it.

**Example:** A customer wanted a through-hole LED bent at 90° and lined up with another feature, but sent no drawing; the LEDs were fitted the way the design appeared to call for, and the customer was disappointed. Screenshots and marked-up 3D renders of tricky areas help fabs and assemblers as much as formal drawings.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=1740)–31:00; [“Alternative Component Mounting”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=1980)–35:00; [“The nitty gritty details on solder”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11129008-the-nitty-gritty-details-on-solder) (Aug 2022), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11129008?t=2460)–44:00; [“Impedance Control Demo w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746-impedance-control-demo-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Oct 2023), [25:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=1500)–27:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

## The BOM

The bill of materials (BOM) lists every part on the board: what it is, how many, and where it goes. The assembler buys parts from it, programs machines from it alongside the XY file, and inspects against it. It's also a contract: a wrong value in the BOM gets built exactly as written.

A good BOM is one line per unique part, with enough information that a buyer who has never seen your design can order exactly the right thing, or a safe substitute.

### PCB-DFA-068: Give every BOM line the designators, quantity, maker and full part number

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-068

**Recommendation:** Give each line of the BOM at least:
- the reference designators it covers (matching the XY file and the legend exactly);
- the quantity per board;
- the manufacturer and the manufacturer's full part number, including any suffix for packaging, tolerance or termination;
- a short description (value, tolerance, voltage, package).

Useful extras: a line number (handy for listing alternates) and your own part number.

Send it as CSV or a spreadsheet. Use the part number exactly as the maker publishes it, the same in every document, and don't add commas or other characters to it.

**Why:** The assembler matches each line to the XY file by its designators, buys by the maker's part number, and checks what arrives against it. A distributor's own stock number, or a description alone, leaves the buyer to guess. One character in a part number can mean a different packaging (R for reel, T for tube), or a different part entirely. CSV files use commas to separate fields, so a comma inside a part number splits it into two.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Questions before parts can be bought, and parts received that don't match the BOM by one character, each of which has to be confirmed before it can be used.

**Example:** Some part makers do use commas in their part numbers; one assembler had to write software to quote every part number so that its files wouldn't break.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=2580)–46:00; [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=1440)–26:00; two large online assemblers' published BOM requirements (checked Nov 2026).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-069: Say which lines are locked to one part, and why; list alternates for the rest

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-069

**Recommendation:** Mark each BOM line as either "this exact part only" or "equivalents allowed". For a locked line, say which parameter makes it critical (for example, low ESR, a particular tempco, a qualified part). For the others, list one or more approved alternate part numbers, especially for anything that's scarce, single-source, or not a simple resistor or capacitor (LEDs, diodes, connectors).

**Why:** When a part is out of stock, the assembler's buyers need to know whether they may substitute, and what a good substitute must match. Many lines are more flexible than designers expect, and an alternate you've already approved can be bought at once. A locked line with a reason tells them what to protect, and stops them suggesting a substitute you'll have to refuse.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Emails back and forth, a job held waiting for a part, or a substitute chosen by someone who doesn't know which parameter mattered.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-1) (Jul 2020), [42:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=2520)–44:00; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=1020)–19:00; [“The Benefits of Asynchronous Design Review for Engineers & Manufacturers w/ AllSpice.io”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11886751-the-benefits-of-asynchronous-design-review-for-engineers-manufacturers-w-allspice-io) (Dec 2022), [46:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11886751?t=2760)–52:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-070: Check every value and part number before release, and check each part is still made

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-070

**Recommendation:** Before you release a BOM, check each value and part number character by character against what you meant, and check every part's lifecycle status and stock with a distributor. Replace parts that are obsolete or not recommended for new designs.

**Why:** Part numbers are long, and one character can change the value, the tolerance, or how the part is mounted. Libraries age: a BOM generated today from an old library can be full of parts that stopped being made years ago.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards built exactly to a wrong BOM, which don't work and have to be reworked; or a quote that can't be completed until obsolete parts are replaced.

**Example:** A customer's boards wouldn't power up; the BOM had the wrong value for 20 to 30 ceramic capacitors, one zero out. A one-character difference in another capacitor part number selects a version made for epoxy mounting instead of soldering; the two look identical and have the same electrical ratings. One assembler received a freshly generated BOM with 16 obsolete part numbers on it.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB assembly inspection process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750-the-pcb-assembly-inspection-process) (Oct 2020), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750?t=1740)–30:00; [“Alternative Component Mounting”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=660)–15:00; [“All about parts purchasing - part 1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-1) (Jul 2020), [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=2640)–46:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-071: Mark do-not-place and customer-supplied lines clearly

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-071

**Recommendation:** Give every location the BOM leaves empty its own line or column marked DNP (do not place), rather than deleting it. Mark parts you'll supply yourself as CONSIGNED, and confirm with the assembler that they'll use your parts and not buy their own. If you'll fit the through-hole parts yourself to save cost on a prototype, mark those lines DNP too.

**Why:** A location missing from the BOM looks like a mistake; one marked DNP is a decision. Assemblers buy from the BOM unless told otherwise, so a consigned part that isn't marked may be bought again, and the wrong one fitted. Through-hole parts are slow and costly to fit at low volumes, and leaving them off is a common, easy saving.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A question for every empty footprint, or parts fitted that you meant to leave off; a consigned, pre-programmed chip replaced with a blank one.

**Example:** A designer consigned pre-programmed bootloader chips, and the assembler bought and fitted blank ones instead; the boards had to be shipped back and forth to put it right.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How Joel Murphy went from visual artist to electronics design engineer”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659-how-joel-murphy-went-from-visual-artist-to-electronics-design-engineer) (Oct 2020), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659?t=1440)–25:00; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=1800)–31:00; Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-072: For small builds, keep the number of unique BOM lines down

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-072

**Recommendation:** When you'll build only a few boards at a time, use as few different part numbers as you can: one resistor value where several would do, the same capacitor for all decoupling, the same connector family throughout.

**Why:** Every unique part has to be loaded onto a feeder and set up on the machine, however many boards you build. On a run of a few boards, that set-up time is most of the cost.

**Typical values:** About 3 to 5 minutes to load each feeder. A 100-line BOM spread over 5 boards carries the set-up cost of all 100 feeders.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Prototype and small-batch prices that are much higher than they need to be.

**Applies to:** General practice; matters most for prototypes and small batches.

**Sources:** [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1140)–21:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*
