## Footprints and the component library

A footprint (also called a land pattern) is the set of copper pads, solder mask openings, paste openings and markings that a part is soldered to. Every footprint on a board comes from a library: one that came with the design software, one downloaded from a part maker or distributor, or one you drew yourself.

More assembly defects start in the library than anywhere else a designer controls. A tombstoned resistor, a bridged QFN or an LED soldered backwards usually traces back to a footprint, not to the factory. This page covers what a good footprint looks like. The paste layer inside each footprint is covered in [PCB-DFA-019](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/).

### PCB-DFA-029: Use proven footprints for chip resistors and capacitors

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-029

**Recommendation:** Use the footprints in the table below for chip resistors and capacitors. They are strongly recommended for industrial and consumer products. You can adjust them, but do it knowingly, and keep the gap between the pads (see the warning below).

**Why:** For small chip parts, the gap between the two pads matters most. If the pads sit too far apart, the part's metal ends don't both rest on solder: one end lifts while the other wets, and the part stands up on end (tombstoning), or one end looks soldered but never wetted (head-in-pillow). Many library footprints have gaps that are too wide for 0402 and smaller parts.

**Typical values:** Footprints proven over millions of placements at one assembler (Worthington Assembly, Rev E). All dimensions in mm; pad length runs along the part, pad width across it.

| Size (inch / metric) | Pad length × width | Pitch (pad center to center) | Gap between pads | Solder mask expansion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 008004 / 0201 | 0.20 × 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.10 | 0 (untested footprint) |
| 01005 / 0402 | 0.25 × 0.23 | 0.41 | 0.16 | 0.025 maximum |
| 0201 / 0603 | 0.25 × 0.35 | 0.55 | 0.30 | 0.05 maximum |
| 0402 / 1005 | 0.60 × 0.70 | 1.00 | 0.40 | |
| 0603 / 1608 | 0.70 × 1.00 | 1.40 | 0.70 | |
| 0805 / 2012 | 0.90 × 1.40 | 1.80 | 0.90 | |

⚠️ **If you change these, keep the gap.** On 0201 parts, a gap just 0.1 mm wider than shown causes serious tombstoning and head-in-pillow problems, and 0402 parts are nearly as sensitive. 0603 and larger parts are much more forgiving.

![D9: Enlarged and drawn to scale: the recommended 0402 footprint, two pads 0.6 by 0.7 mm on a 1.0 mm pitch with a 0.4 mm gap, the part's metal ends fully on the pads; beside it, a footprint with a 0.7 mm gap where the part's ends only just reach the pads.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/chip-footprint.svg)

*D9 is enlarged and drawn to scale. On the left is the recommended 0402 footprint: two copper pads 0.6 mm long and 0.7 mm wide, 1.0 mm apart center to center, leaving a 0.4 mm gap. The 1.0 × 0.5 mm part sits with both metal ends fully on the pads. On the right, the gap is 0.7 mm, and the part's metal ends only just reach the pads, which is how tombstoning and head-in-pillow start.*

The other sizes in the table, each enlarged and drawn to scale:

![D12: Enlarged and drawn to scale: the recommended 008004 (0201 metric) footprint, two pads 0.2 by 0.2 mm on a 0.3 mm pitch with a 0.1 mm gap, the 0.25 by 0.125 mm part's metal ends on the pads.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/chip-footprint-008004.svg)

*D12. 008004 (0201 metric): pads 0.2 mm long and 0.2 mm wide, 0.3 mm pitch, 0.1 mm gap; the part is 0.25 × 0.125 mm. Solder mask expansion 0 (untested footprint).*

![D13: Enlarged and drawn to scale: the recommended 01005 (0402 metric) footprint, two pads 0.25 by 0.23 mm on a 0.41 mm pitch with a 0.16 mm gap, the 0.4 by 0.2 mm part's metal ends on the pads.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/chip-footprint-01005.svg)

*D13. 01005 (0402 metric): pads 0.25 mm long and 0.23 mm wide, 0.41 mm pitch, 0.16 mm gap; the part is 0.4 × 0.2 mm. Solder mask expansion 0.025 mm maximum.*

![D14: Enlarged and drawn to scale: the recommended 0201 (0603 metric) footprint, two pads 0.25 by 0.35 mm on a 0.55 mm pitch with a 0.3 mm gap, the 0.6 by 0.3 mm part's metal ends on the pads.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/chip-footprint-0201.svg)

*D14. 0201 (0603 metric): pads 0.25 mm long and 0.35 mm wide, 0.55 mm pitch, 0.3 mm gap; the part is 0.6 × 0.3 mm. Solder mask expansion 0.05 mm maximum.*

![D22: Enlarged and drawn to scale: the recommended 0402 (1005 metric) footprint, two pads 0.6 by 0.7 mm on a 1.0 mm pitch with a 0.4 mm gap, the 1.0 by 0.5 mm part's metal ends on the pads.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/chip-footprint-0402.svg)

*D22. 0402 (1005 metric): pads 0.6 mm long and 0.7 mm wide, 1.0 mm pitch, 0.4 mm gap; the part is 1.0 × 0.5 mm.*

![D15: Enlarged and drawn to scale: the recommended 0603 (1608 metric) footprint, two pads 0.7 by 1.0 mm on a 1.4 mm pitch with a 0.7 mm gap, the 1.6 by 0.8 mm part's metal ends on the pads.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/chip-footprint-0603.svg)

*D15. 0603 (1608 metric): pads 0.7 mm long and 1.0 mm wide, 1.4 mm pitch, 0.7 mm gap; the part is 1.6 × 0.8 mm.*

![D16: Enlarged and drawn to scale: the recommended 0805 (2012 metric) footprint, two pads 0.9 by 1.4 mm on a 1.8 mm pitch with a 0.9 mm gap, the 2.0 by 1.25 mm part's metal ends on the pads.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/chip-footprint-0805.svg)

*D16. 0805 (2012 metric): pads 0.9 mm long and 1.4 mm wide, 1.8 mm pitch, 0.9 mm gap; the part is 2.0 × 1.25 mm.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Tombstoned and half-soldered small parts, found at inspection and reworked by hand, or missed and found in the field.

**Example:** Since about 2017, every tombstoning problem at one assembler has traced back to the footprint. The usual cause was a default library footprint, or one downloaded and never checked.

**Applies to:** Industrial, consumer and similar products. Mission-critical designs (space, aviation and similar) should follow the IPC land-pattern rules their customers require. These footprints are offered as a downloadable KiCad library; the 0402 and 0201 are also available for two other design tools.

**Sources:** [Discrete Component Footprint Recommendations, Rev E](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/s/Discrete-Component-Footprints-Rev-E.pdf) (Worthington Assembly, PDF) and its [KiCad library](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/s/Worthington_Assemblypretty.zip); [The Perfect 0402 Footprint](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/perfect-0402-footprint) and [The Perfect 0201 Footprint](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/perfect-0201-footprint) (Worthington Assembly); [“The selective soldering process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971-the-selective-soldering-process) (Jan 2021), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971?t=300)–08:00; [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=1620)–29:00; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [01:36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=5760)–01:39:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

---

### PCB-DFA-030: Use one footprint per package size, not one per part maker

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-030

**Recommendation:** Keep one footprint for each chip size (one 0402, one 0603, and so on) and use it for every resistor and capacitor of that size, whoever makes the part.

**Why:** Assemblers design stencil openings and program inspection machines footprint by footprint. Two parts of the same size from two makers, each with its own downloaded footprint, look like two different footprints and need two sets of work.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Extra engineering time on every new job, and more chances for a mistake.

**Example:** Designs regularly arrive with as many as 16 different 0402 footprints on one board.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Building the factory of the future with CircuitHub CEO, Andrew Seddon”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440-building-the-factory-of-the-future-with-circuithub-ceo-andrew-seddon) (Aug 2026), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440?t=1440)–26:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

---

### PCB-DFA-031: Check every footprint you didn't draw yourself, against the datasheet and a real part

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-031

**Recommendation:** Check every downloaded or library footprint before you use it. Compare it with the part maker's recommended land pattern, and print it 1:1 and lay a real part on it, or measure the part with calipers. Read the datasheet drawing carefully: many leadless parts are drawn from the bottom, and a footprint drawn from a bottom view comes out mirrored.

**Why:** Downloaded footprints are often wrong: off grid, the wrong pad sizes, or mirrored. Datasheet drawings are often made by people who never handled the part, and part tolerances only show up over many builds.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A part that doesn't fit, a mirrored chip that can't be fitted at all, or a board respin.

**Example:** One assembler catches a footprint drawn from a bottom view about once a month.

**Applies to:** General practice. Treat a new footprint as proven only after it has been soldered about 100 times.

**Sources:** [“Building the factory of the future with CircuitHub CEO, Andrew Seddon”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440-building-the-factory-of-the-future-with-circuithub-ceo-andrew-seddon) (Aug 2026), [23:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19621440?t=1380)–24:00; [“How Joel Murphy went from visual artist to electronics design engineer”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659-how-joel-murphy-went-from-visual-artist-to-electronics-design-engineer) (Oct 2020), [01:03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659?t=3780)–01:05:00; [“How to build and manage a great team w/ Eli Hughes of Tzero Labs (Part 1)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6828622-how-to-build-and-manage-a-great-team-w-eli-hughes-of-tzero-labs-part-1) (Dec 2020), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6828622?t=540)–11:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

---

### PCB-DFA-032: Put a solder mask dam between every pad of a fine-pitch part

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-032

**Recommendation:** Give every pad of a fine-pitch part (0.5 mm pitch and finer) its own solder mask opening, so a thin strip of mask (a dam) separates each pad from the next. Never use one large mask opening around a whole row of pads. If your fab says the dams are too thin, ask what they can do rather than accept their removal. What's easy for the fab may make the assembler's work very difficult.

**Why:** During reflow, solder flows wherever there's bare copper. A dam between the pads keeps each joint separate. Without it, the solder runs together along the row into one long bridge.

**Typical values:** 0.25 mm (10 mil) between copper pads, made up of 0.075 mm (3 mil) of mask registration on each side and a 0.1 mm (4 mil) dam in the middle. Green solder mask can hold a 0.075 mm (3 mil) dam, but 0.1 mm is recommended for every color. Where the pitch is too fine for 0.25 mm between pads (0.4 mm pitch, for example), trim the copper pads, or use a fab that images solder mask with a laser, which needs less registration: 0.2 mm copper and a 0.3 mm opening leaves the same 0.1 mm dam. Never give up the dam itself.

![D10: Enlarged and drawn to scale: three pads of a 0.5 mm-pitch part, 0.25 mm wide and 0.25 mm apart, each in its own mask opening 0.075 mm larger on each side, leaving a 0.1 mm solder mask dam between them; below, the same pads in one large opening with no dams.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/mask-dam.svg)

*D10 is enlarged and drawn to scale. At the top, three copper pads of a 0.5 mm-pitch part, each 0.25 mm wide, with 0.25 mm between them. Each pad has its own solder mask opening, 0.075 mm larger than the pad on each side, which leaves a 0.1 mm strip of mask, the dam, between neighboring pads. At the bottom, the same pads share one large opening, with bare board between them and nothing to stop solder bridging from pad to pad.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Solder bridges across a whole row of pins, which then have to be cleared by hand on every board.

**Applies to:** General practice. Laser-imaged solder mask varies by fab; check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Gloves not Mittens”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842-gloves-not-mittens) (Jun 2026), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=1260)–23:00 and [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=1560)–28:00; [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=2160)–41:00; [“An EDA Tool Walks Into a CM w/ Fusion 360 Electronics Product Manager, Ben Jordan”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9171908-an-eda-tool-walks-into-a-cm-w-fusion-360-electronics-product-manager-ben-jordan) (Sep 2021), [56:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9171908?t=3360)–58:00; [“An overview of bare PCB fabrication w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663-an-overview-of-bare-pcb-fabrication-w-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2020), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663?t=720); [Solder Mask Dams Between Fine Pitch Devices](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/blog/2021/11/19/solder-mask-dams-between-fine-pitch-devices) (Worthington Assembly, 2021).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

### PCB-DFA-033: Set the solder mask expansion of fine-pitch pads yourself

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-033

**Recommendation:** For parts of 0.5 mm pitch and finer, set the solder mask expansion of each footprint by hand instead of using your design software's default. Where a pad connects to a copper pour, set its mask opening so the exposed copper matches the other pads of the same part.

![D26: Drawn to scale, plan view of the corner of a 0.5 mm-pitch QFN, three times. Every pad has the same mask opening. On the left, the two ground pads at the corner each have a single trace to a via, and bare FR4 shows around them inside their openings, like every other pad. In the middle, the ground pads are tied straight into a copper pour, and copper fills their openings, so they look larger than the other pads. On the right, the ground pads join the pour through thin thermal spokes, and they look like the other pads again.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/pour-pad-mask.svg)

*D26 is drawn to scale. Every pad has the same mask opening, 0.075 mm larger than the pad. Around a pad with a single trace, the opening shows bare FR4 and only a sliver of trace. Where a pad is tied straight into a pour, the opening shows copper instead, so the pad looks as big as its opening. A thermal relief keeps the pour back from the pad and joins it with thin spokes, so the pad looks like its neighbors again. The pour clearance, relief gap and spoke width are example values.*

**Why:** Default mask expansions suit coarse parts and swallow the dam on fine-pitch ones. A pad inside a copper pour is defined by its mask opening, not by its copper, so a default expansion makes that pad bigger than its neighbors, and the part gets uneven solder.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Missing dams, uneven pads, and an assembler who has to guess what you meant.

**Applies to:** General practice. Above 0.5 mm pitch the default is usually fine.

**Sources:** [“Gloves not Mittens”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842-gloves-not-mittens) (Jun 2026), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=420)–11:00 and [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=1260)–23:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

---

### PCB-DFA-034: Make pin 1 impossible to miss

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-034

**Recommendation:** Make pin 1 of every IC a square or rectangular pad, with the other pads rounded. Put a pin-1 mark in silkscreen right beside pin 1, outside the part's body, where it can still be seen after the part is placed. Avoid putting a pin-1 or polarity mark under the part: once the part is placed, the information is lost. A mark under the part is still better than no mark at all. Use one kind of mark throughout the board, and don't use a symbol (such as an asterisk) that could mean something else. Parts that aren't polarized (chip resistors and ceramic capacitors), and parts whose pads only fit one way (SOT-23, SOT-23-5, SOT-223, DPAK), don't need a mark.

**Why:** The assembler sets the orientation of every part from your data, then checks it by eye against the board. A mark hidden under the part disappears once it's placed; an ambiguous mark gets read the wrong way.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts placed backwards, often on every board in the batch.

**Example:** A designer used an asterisk beside a diode as a footnote marker, because the reference designator wouldn't fit. The assembler read it as the diode's polarity mark, and every board in the batch was built with that diode backwards.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=2940)–51:00; [Your Manufacturer Is Stupid: Help Them](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/s/KiCon-Presentation.pdf) (KiCon 2019 talk, Worthington Assembly, PDF).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

---

### PCB-DFA-035: Mark diode and LED polarity so it can't be misread

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-035

**Recommendation:** Name diode and LED pins K (or C) for the cathode and A for the anode, not 1 and 2. Mark the cathode in silkscreen beside the cathode pad, not under the part: a K, or a short bar about as long as the pad is wide (one mark is enough). On through-hole diodes and LEDs, make the cathode the square pad (pin 1). Check the silkscreen mark against the schematic and the datasheet.

**Why:** Part makers mark polarity inconsistently: some LEDs are marked only underneath, some makers mark the anode on one part and the cathode on another, and some datasheets call the pins 1 and 2 without saying which is which. Some designers use the square pad for the anode, so a square pad alone isn't proof. A pin name, a visible mark and the schematic that agree leave nothing to guess.

![D11: Drawn to scale: an 8-pin IC footprint with a rectangular pin-1 pad and a silkscreen dot right beside pin 1, beside one with identical pads and the dot inside the part's outline; two 0603 LEDs on the recommended 0603 footprint, one marked with a K and one with a short bar beside the cathode pad, beside the same footprint with the bar under the part, where it is hidden once the part is placed.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/polarity-marks.svg)

*D11 is drawn to scale, with dashed lines showing each part's outline. Top left: an 8-pin IC footprint with a rectangular pin-1 pad, rounded other pads, and a silkscreen dot right beside pin 1, outside the part, so it's still visible after placement. Top right: the same footprint with all pads alike and the dot inside the outline, hidden once the part is placed. Bottom left: two 0603 LEDs on the recommended 0603 footprint (0.7 × 1.0 mm pads, 0.7 mm gap); one is marked with the letter K beside the cathode pad, the other with a short bar beside the cathode pad, about as long as the pad is wide. One mark per LED is enough. Bottom right: the same footprint with the cathode bar under the part, hidden once the part is placed. Any mark under a part, pin-1 dot or cathode bar, is lost as soon as the part is placed.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** LEDs and diodes fitted backwards, which inspection machines can't always catch.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [47:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=2820)–53:00; [“The PCB assembly inspection process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750-the-pcb-assembly-inspection-process) (Oct 2020), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750?t=780)–14:00 and [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750?t=3120)–53:00; [Your Manufacturer Is Stupid: Help Them](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/s/KiCon-Presentation.pdf) (KiCon 2019 talk, Worthington Assembly, PDF); the common library convention that pin 1 of a diode is the cathode (checked Nov 2026).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

---

### PCB-DFA-036: Draw the real outline of each part in silkscreen, including anything that hangs over the edge

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-036

**Recommendation:** Give every footprint a silkscreen outline of the part's real body. It doesn't have to be detailed, just accurate. Draw the overhang of any part that hangs past the board edge (connectors, antennas, modules) in silkscreen, past the edge, as it would look if it could print over empty space. Don't trim it to the board outline; the fab trims silkscreen that falls outside the board itself. Attach a 3D model where you can.

![D27: Drawn to scale, plan view of a connector footprint at a board edge, twice. On the left, the connector's silkscreen outline stops at the board edge. On the right, the outline continues 3 mm past the edge, over the area outside the board, showing the overhang.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/overhang-outline.svg)

*D27 is drawn to scale. On the left, the silkscreen outline stops at the board edge, so nothing shows that the connector hangs 3 mm past it. On the right, the outline is drawn as if silkscreen could print outside the board. The fab trims it, but sees it first, and leaves room for the overhang in the panel. The example connector is 9 mm wide, 6 mm deep on the board and 3 mm past the edge.*

**Why:** The assembler lays out the panel and checks for collisions from your data. An outline of the real body shows how much room a part needs; an overhang drawn past the edge tells them to keep the next board in the panel clear. The fab trims silkscreen that falls outside the board, and it sees the overhang first: the drawing is the warning that tells them to adjust the panel.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A connector that collides with the next board in the panel or a rail, found only after the boards are made.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How Loci Controls automates landfill methane gas collection”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5509702-how-loci-controls-automates-landfill-methane-gas-collection) (Sep 2020), [01:11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5509702?t=4260); [Your Manufacturer Is Stupid: Help Them](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/s/KiCon-Presentation.pdf) (KiCon 2019 talk, Worthington Assembly, PDF).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

---

### PCB-DFA-037: Size plated through-holes and their pads from the lead

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-037

**Recommendation:** Size each plated hole from the part's largest lead, and each pad from the hole. For a square or rectangular lead, measure corner to corner. If the datasheet gives a hole tolerance like "+0.1 / −0 mm", make the hole 0.1 mm larger than the datasheet's recommended size (for a recommended 1.0 mm hole, make it 1.1 mm).

**Why:** A hole sized to the nominal lead can be too tight for the largest leads in a batch; a pad sized without allowance for drilling and registration can lose its ring of copper.

**Typical values:** Hole = largest lead diameter + a hole allowance. Pad = hole + 2 × (0.05 mm minimum annular ring + a pad allowance). The allowances depend on the IPC density level; level A is the easiest to build and the usual choice when there's room.

| IPC density level | Hole = lead + | Pad = hole + 2 × (0.05 + …) | Example: 0.5 mm lead |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (least dense, easiest to build) | 0.25 mm | 0.3 mm | 0.75 mm hole, 1.45 mm pad |
| B (moderately dense) | 0.20 mm | 0.25 mm | 0.70 mm hole, 1.30 mm pad |
| C (most dense, hardest to build) | 0.15 mm | 0.2 mm | 0.65 mm hole, 1.15 mm pad |

![D23: Enlarged and drawn to scale, three steps: measure the lead (a 0.5 mm round lead across, a rectangular lead corner to corner); the hole is the lead plus 0.25 mm, 0.75 mm; the pad is the hole plus twice 0.35 mm, 1.45 mm.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/pth-sizing.svg)

*D23 is enlarged and drawn to scale, for density level A. First, measure the lead: a round lead across its diameter (0.5 mm here), a rectangular lead corner to corner. Second, the hole is the largest lead plus 0.25 mm: 0.75 mm, leaving 0.125 mm around the lead. Third, the pad is the hole plus 0.35 mm of copper on each side (a 0.05 mm minimum ring plus 0.3 mm allowance): 1.45 mm.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts that won't go into their holes, or that need forcing, and pads with too little copper around the hole.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [Determining Plated-Thru-Hole Sizes](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/determining-platedthruhole-sizes) (Worthington Assembly); [“The basics of the PCB drilling process w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552-the-basics-of-the-pcb-drilling-process-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552?t=1080)–21:00, for asymmetric hole tolerances; IPC-2221 and IPC-2222 (hole and pad sizing, via EDA vendors' summaries, checked Nov 2026).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-03*

### PCB-DFM-007: Don't put copper on non-plated holes

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-007

**Recommendation:** Remove the copper pad from every hole that isn't plated, and give its solder mask opening a proper clearance. Where the hole sits in a copper pour, keep the pour back from the hole's edge.

![D28: Drawn to scale, plan view of a 3.2 mm non-plated hole in a ground pour, twice. On the left, the pour runs right up to the hole, so a ring of copper shows at its edge, like the ring of a plated hole. On the right, the pour is kept 0.2 mm back, so a ring of bare FR4 shows instead. Enlarged views below show the edge of the hole in each.](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/images/nonplated-hole.svg)

*D28 is drawn to scale, with the edge of the hole enlarged below each view. The mask opening is 0.1 mm larger than the hole in both. On the left, the pour runs up to the hole, so copper shows at its edge and the hole looks plated. On the right, the pour is kept 0.2 mm back, so bare FR4 shows and the hole is clearly not plated.*

**Why:** A copper ring on a non-plated hole leaves the fab guessing whether the hole should be plated. A pour that runs right up to the hole shows as a ring of copper at its edge, which looks just like the ring of a plated hole. A mask opening only a hair larger than the hole leaves a sliver of mask too thin to hold.

**Typical values:** Copper pour kept at least 0.2 mm (8 mil) from the edge of the hole, the minimum fabs list; more with heavy copper, so check with your fab. Mask clearance of about 0.1 mm (4 mil) around the hole, not 0.025 mm (1 mil).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Questions from the fab, a delay, or a hole plated that shouldn't be.

**Example:** Designs arrive with pads on half their non-plated holes and none on the other half.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“An overview of bare PCB fabrication w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663-an-overview-of-bare-pcb-fabrication-w-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2020), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663?t=720); [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=2460)–43:00; fab capability tables for copper to non-plated holes (checked Nov 2026).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

Source: https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/

## Why boards are built in panels

A panel (sometimes called an array) is a larger board made up of several copies of your board, or one board with extra material around it, so the factory can handle it more efficiently. Assembly machines are built to carry boards of a certain size along two edges. Moving many boards at once is also much faster: every pass through the printer, the placement machine and the oven builds the whole panel. Most designers never draw a panel themselves, but the board they design can influence how difficult the board will be to panelize and process through the factory.

### PCB-DFA-001: Let your manufacturer design the panel, and approve it before you order bare boards

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-001

**Recommendation:** Don't panelize the board yourself. Send a single board and let the assembler's engineering team design the panel around their own equipment. If you buy bare boards separately and send them to an assembler, get the assembler to approve the panel drawing before you place the board order.

**Why:** Every factory's machines, conveyors, board racks and clamps are slightly different, and only the factory knows what works best on its line. A panel that suits one assembler can be awkward or unbuildable for another.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards arrive that the assembler can't run without extra handling. Sometimes it costs more to handle them than to order new boards. One assembler estimates that only about two out of five "we already bought the boards" requests can be accommodated, usually at extra cost.

**Example:** A customer arrived with bare boards and parts already in hand for a board half an inch by one inch, too small for the factory's machines to hold. It could not be built as designed.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** Pick, Place, Podcast: [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=660)–12:00; [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=2940)–51:00; [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=300).

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-002: Make sure small boards can be panelized, and never send them loose

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-002

**Recommendation:** If your board is shorter than about 100 mm (4 in) in the direction of travel, expect it to be built in a panel, and make the panel at least 100 mm long. Don't order loose single boards for automated assembly.

**Why:** Assembly lines are a row of machines joined by conveyors. Each conveyor end may leave a gap of up to 19 mm, so two machines side by side can leave 38 mm, and real-world alignment brings that to about 50 mm. A board has to be longer than twice the gap: anything shorter hangs more than halfway off one conveyor before it reaches the next, tips and falls. PCBA cleaning machines are also built for panels; a single small board needs to be set inside of a cage or some kind of fixture instead.

**Typical values:** 19 mm allowed gap per conveyor end · about 50 mm (2 in) real gap between machines · boards and panels at least 100 mm (4 in) long in the direction of travel. From the SMEMA conveyor interface standard (IPC-SMEMA-9851) and one factory's experience.

![D29: Drawn to scale, plan view of the end of one machine's conveyor and the start of the next, about 50 mm apart. A 15 by 10 mm board on its own has left the first conveyor and has nothing under it. The same board in a 120 by 50 mm panel, longer than twice the gap, rests on both conveyors at once.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/small-board-panel.svg)

*D29 is drawn to scale. Machines sit about 50 mm apart on the line. A 15 mm board on its own is far shorter than that gap and has nothing under it as it crosses. A panel has to be longer than twice the gap: anything shorter hangs more than halfway off one conveyor before it reaches the next, and tips. Twenty-four of the same board in a 120 by 50 mm panel rest on both conveyors at once.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards drop between machines, or parts near the edge have to be hand-soldered instead of machine-placed.

**Example:** Conference badges, 3 × 4 in, arrived as loose single boards on a tight deadline. They fell through the gaps between conveyors. The team had to mask off and hand-solder the edge components that got covered by the machine clamps.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Conveyers, An Episode You Didn't Know You Needed”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13980495-conveyers-an-episode-you-didn-t-know-you-needed) (Nov 2023), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13980495?t=1920)–37:00; [“Back from the Dead and Back from APEX”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19107985-back-from-the-dead-and-back-from-apex) (May 2026), [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19107985?t=2160)–37:00; [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=300).

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-003: Expect panels of about 200 × 150 mm, and plan quantities in whole panels

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-003

**Recommendation:** Assume your assembler will aim for a panel about the size of a sheet of letter or A4 paper. Order quantities, first articles and delivery batches in multiples of the number of boards on a panel.

**Why:** The panel is the unit the factory works in. Setting up a run (stencil, feeders, oven profile) builds at least one full panel, so even a request for "one first article" usually means one panel's worth.

**Typical values:** About 200 × 150 mm is a common target size. One factory's example; other factories differ.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Odd quantities leave partly built panels, and a one-up panel of a large order means every board is handled one at a time.

**Example:** A customer ordered more than 2,000 boards on a one-up panel. Switching to a three-up panel on the next order made the run dramatically faster. Another long-running customer orders in batches that match the panel: first 27 boards (a 3 × 3 panel), later 10 after a redesign to a 10-up panel.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“When to request first articles”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335-when-to-request-first-articles) (Dec 2021), [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335?t=960)–17:00; [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), story near the end; [“How Small Manufacturers Manage Large Volume Orders”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426-how-small-manufacturers-manage-large-volume-orders) (Apr 2023), [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=660)–13:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-004: Keep panels stiff: small panels for thin boards, and no long floppy rows

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-004

**Recommendation:** If your board is thinner than the standard 1.6 mm, expect smaller panels. Avoid board shapes that force a long, narrow panel held only at its short ends. For large, heavy, double-sided panels, ask whether the assembler will need a support fixture in the reflow oven.

**Why:** A panel behaves like a beam: the longer and thinner it is, the more it sags, and a heavy load makes it worse. In the reflow oven, a double-sided panel can't lie on a belt, so it hangs by its edges on narrow rails while the board is at its softest.

**Typical values:** 1.6 mm is the standard thickness. Oven pin rails grip only about 3 mm of board edge. Sag problems seen on panels over 200 mm.

![D30: End-on views of a 1.6 mm panel on the oven's pin rails, which grip about 3 mm of each edge. A panel 200 mm across the rails sags in the middle; one 100 mm across sags one sixteenth as much. The sag is exaggerated by the same factor in both.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/panel-sag.svg)

*D30 is drawn to scale except for the sag, which is exaggerated by the same factor in both views. The oven's pin rails grip only about 3 mm of each edge, so the panel spans the gap between them unsupported. Sag grows with the fourth power of that span: twice the span, sixteen times the sag.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Bowed panels cause trouble in optical inspection and selective soldering, and in the worst case a panel drops off the oven rails. The assembler has to build custom support tooling, which adds cost and time to your job.

**Example:** A 16 in (about 400 mm) long, 5 × 2 panel held only at its short ends flexed "like a diving board". Panels fell apart just from being picked up, and the job needed custom tooling.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1320)–23:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=2460)–42:00; [“Custom tooling to the rescue”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740-custom-tooling-to-the-rescue) (Jul 2022), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740?t=600)–12:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

Source: https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/02-rails-tooling-holes-fiducials/

## Rails, tooling holes and fiducials

Machines carry a panel by its two long edges, so most panels get a strip of extra material along each one called a **rail**. Rails give the conveyors and clamps something to hold. They also carry the panel's **global fiducials** and, at some factories, its **tooling holes**, which locate it on pins. Global fiducials are small copper targets the machines' cameras use to find exactly where the panel is. It's beneficial for your board to have its own fiducials, but not essential if there is not enough real estate. They cost about five minutes of design time and help every machine on the line.

![D1: Drawn to scale: a 140 × 110 mm panel of four 70 × 45 mm boards, with 10 mm rails along the top and bottom long edges, three global fiducials and four optional tooling holes on the rails, dashed V-score lines between the boards and rails, and two fiducials on each board near opposite corners.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/panel-anatomy.svg)

*D1 is drawn to scale. It shows a 140 × 110 mm panel of four boards, each 70 × 45 mm, in two rows of two. A 10 mm rail runs along each long edge, parallel to the direction of travel. Three global fiducials sit on the rails, one on the top rail and two on the bottom rail. Each rail may also have a 3/16 in tooling hole near each end (many factories no longer use them). Every board carries its own two fiducials near opposite corners. Dashed V-score lines run edge to edge, separating the boards from each other and from the rails.*

### PCB-DFA-005: Expect rails along the long edges unless you design them out

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-005

**Recommendation:** Assume your assembler will add a rail of about 10 mm along each long edge of the panel and will put the global fiducials there. If you can keep every component and exposed copper well clear of the board edges (see [PCB-DFA-015](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfa-015-keep-parts-and-exposed-copper-at-least-3-mm-from-the-edges-5-mm-if-you-can)), tell your assembler: they may be able to skip the rails.

**Why:** Conveyors and machine clamps grip the board edge. Rails give them a strip to hold that carries nothing of yours. Skipping rails saves panel material and a depaneling step, but needs a board designed for it from the start.

**Typical values:** About 10 mm per rail is common. For one assembler, 95–99 % of jobs need rails. A large panel may also get a 10 mm rail down the middle so the reflow oven's center support has somewhere to sit. Some assemblers, Worthington Assembly among them, put 10 mm rails on all four sides and between the boards, with the global fiducials on the short-edge rails (D48, [PCB-DFA-076](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/02-rails-tooling-holes-fiducials/#pcb-dfa-076-make-each-fiducial-show-which-side-and-which-corner-it-is)). Tooling holes in the rails are now largely a legacy feature: one assembler used 3/16 in (about 4.8 mm) holes for years and, as of 2026, has stopped using them altogether. Others still use them, in various sizes.

**Example:** One designer laid out a 2 × 2 panel with no rails at all: edge clearances and fiducials designed in, nothing to break off, zero waste.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1140)–20:00 and [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1860); [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=1020)–23:00; [“What are fiducials and why you should use them”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1620)–28:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-006: Make fiducials simple copper dots, round or square, with a clear ring around them

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-006

**Recommendation:** Make each fiducial a round copper dot 1 mm in diameter, with the solder mask pulled back to a circle 2 mm in diameter, so a 0.5 mm ring of bare board surrounds it. You can use squares too. But crosses and other shapes are less common. A clever practice is to use rounds on the top side and squares on the bottom side. Silkscreen labels are not necessary.

**Why:** Cameras need a high-contrast target. Glossy solder mask next to the dot, especially white or yellow, reflects light and confuses them. Modern vision systems don't need unusual shapes, and every assembler recognizes a plain dot as a fiducial.

**Typical values:** 1 mm dot · 2 mm mask opening. Common industry practice.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** The machine can't find the board. The operator has to teach it by hand, and placement accuracy can suffer.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“What are fiducials and why you should use them”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [23:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1380)–26:00; [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=1620)–31:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-007: Put at least two fiducials on each board, far apart, on every side that has surface-mount parts

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-007

**Recommendation:** Place two fiducials near opposite corners of the board itself, not only on the panel rails. Use three on large boards. If both sides of the board carry surface-mount parts, put fiducials on both sides. Keep the center of every fiducial's copper dot about 5 mm in from the edge of the panel.

**Why:** Two fiducials give the machine position and rotation. A third lets it correct for the board stretching or shrinking slightly. Fiducials on the board itself mean it can still be built if it comes out of its panel, and an operator can fix a setup mistake at the machine without calling an engineer. Most machines clamp the outer 3 mm or so of the panel edge, so any part of a fiducial inside that strip will probably be covered.

![D2: Drawn to scale, enlarged: a 1 mm copper fiducial dot inside a 2 mm solder mask opening, its center 5 mm from the panel edge, outside the shaded 3 mm clamp zone.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/fiducial-detail.svg)

*D2. The close-up is enlarged and drawn to scale. A copper dot 1 mm in diameter sits in a solder mask opening 2 mm in diameter, leaving a 0.5 mm ring of bare board. The outer 3 mm of the panel edge is shaded: that's where machine clamps grip. The center of the copper dot is 5 mm in from the panel edge, so the clamps can't hide it.*

**Typical values:** 2 minimum, 3 preferred · center about 5 mm in from the panel edge; clamps cover the outer ~3 mm. If the board runs without rails, its own edge is the panel edge, so give the fiducials more room: one rail-less design used about 10 mm.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Most designs arrive without fiducials (about 19 out of 20 at one factory), so assemblers add them to the rails. That works, but only while the board stays in its panel.

**Example:** A conveyor fault once broke a panel into its individual boards. Because each board had its own fiducials, the machine was reprogrammed and the boards were built anyway.

**Applies to:** General practice. Very small boards (about 10 × 15 mm) have been built successfully without fiducials by putting them in a panel.

**Sources:** [“What are fiducials and why you should use them”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=600)–14:00, [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1020)–23:00, [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1560)–28:00 and [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1860); [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [01:07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=4020).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-008: If there's room, add local fiducials beside expensive or very fine-pitch parts

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-008

**Recommendation:** If there's room and it's easy, add a pair of fiducials right beside high-value BGAs, very fine-pitch parts and dense clusters of very small parts, such as 0201 and 01005. This is a low priority. Leave them out if they get in the way of anything else on the board.

**Why:** Local fiducials let the placement machine re-check its position right at that part, instead of relying on fiducials far away across the panel. But modern placement machines are accurate enough with the board's own fiducials. They also use their own cameras to find each part's leads or balls before placing it. So on most boards today, local fiducials add little.

**Example:** A board carrying a single FPGA worth about $6,000 has fiducials at the corners of the BGA.

![D31: Drawn to scale, plan view of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA on a board, with its inner balls fanned out to vias and its outer ring escaping straight out. A local fiducial, FID1 and FID2, sits just outside two opposite corners of the BGA.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/local-fiducials.svg)

*D31 is drawn to scale. A pair of local fiducials just outside two opposite corners of the BGA lets the machine correct its position right where the accuracy matters. Each is a 1 mm copper dot in a 2 mm mask opening. The board's own fiducials sit at its corners, outside this view.*

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“What are fiducials and why you should use them”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1680)–30:00; Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-009: Don't use drilled holes instead of fiducials

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-009

**Recommendation:** Use etched copper fiducials for machine alignment, even if the board already has tooling or mounting holes.

**Why:** Holes are drilled in a separate step from copper etching, so they never line up with the pads quite as precisely. Fiducials are etched at the same moment as the pads they help place.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“What are fiducials and why you should use them”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=1140)–20:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-076: Make each fiducial show which side and which corner it is

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-076

**Recommendation:** Give the panel three global fiducials of different sizes, 1, 2 and 3 mm, and make them round on the top side and square on the bottom side. Put them on the rails at three corners: the 1 mm at one corner, and the 2 mm and 3 mm at the two ends of the opposite long edge. Give each the clear ring of bare board described in [PCB-DFA-006](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/02-rails-tooling-holes-fiducials/#pcb-dfa-006-make-fiducials-simple-copper-dots-round-or-square-with-a-clear-ring-around-them).

**Why:** A machine's camera finds each fiducial by its shape and size. If every fiducial is the same, a panel loaded the wrong way round, or upside down, still shows the camera what it expects, and the machine prints or places on the wrong side or rotated by 180°. With three sizes and a different shape on each side, the camera finds a 1 mm dot where it expected a 3 mm one, or a square where it expected a circle, and stops before anything is built.

**Typical values:** Copper dots 1, 2 and 3 mm, each in a solder mask opening about twice its size. Round on the top side, square on the bottom. At one assembler: on the short-edge rails, centered in the 10 mm rail and 15 mm from the long edges (D48).

![D48 is drawn to scale: the top and bottom of a 150 by 110 mm panel of four boards with 10 mm rails on all four sides and between the boards. Each side has a 1 mm, a 2 mm and a 3 mm fiducial on the short-edge rails, round on top and square on the bottom; the long-edge rail carries the side and the part number in silkscreen. An enlarged row shows the six fiducials.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/panel-style.svg)

*D48 is drawn to scale: a 150 × 110 mm panel of four 60 × 40 mm boards, with 10 mm rails on all four sides and between the boards, seen from the top and from the bottom. On each side, three fiducials sit on the short-edge rails, centered in the rail and 15 mm from the long edges: 1 mm at the upper left, 2 mm at the lower left and 3 mm at the lower right. They are round on the top side and square on the bottom side, as the enlarged row shows. The rail along the long edge opposite the 2 and 3 mm fiducials carries "Top" or "Bottom" and the board's part number in silkscreen (PCB-DFA-077).*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A panel loaded rotated or upside down that the machine accepts anyway: paste printed on the wrong side, or parts placed 180° out across the whole panel.

**Applies to:** Varies by assembler; this is Worthington Assembly's panel style. Many assemblers design the panel themselves ([PCB-DFA-001](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/#pcb-dfa-001-let-your-manufacturer-design-the-panel-and-approve-it-before-you-order-bare-boards)); if yours does, ask for this.

**Sources:** Worthington Assembly Panel Design Guidelines v1.1; Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-077: Print the board's part number and the side on the panel rails

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-077

**Recommendation:** Put the board's part number and the word "Top" or "Bottom" in silkscreen on a rail on each side of the panel. At one assembler, both go on the long-edge rail opposite the 2 mm and 3 mm fiducials (D48).

**Why:** Anyone handling a panel, at any station, can see at a glance what board it is and which side is facing them. That catches the wrong job on a machine, or a panel turned over, before it's built.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards that look alike mixed up between jobs, or a panel run on the wrong side.

**Applies to:** Varies by assembler; this is Worthington Assembly's panel style.

**Sources:** Worthington Assembly Panel Design Guidelines v1.1; Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFT-001: Give the board its own tooling holes if it will go into a test fixture

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-001

**Recommendation:** If the board will be tested in a fixture (for example a bed-of-nails or functional test fixture), include tooling holes on the board itself so the fixture can locate it. Don't rely on the board outline.

**Why:** Tooling holes on the rails are gone once the board leaves the panel. A routed edge is accurate to within about 0.1 mm, but a V-scored edge varies a lot more, so it's a poor reference for a fixture.

**Typical values:** There's no single standard, but one contract manufacturer's guide is a good starting point. Make each tooling hole 3 mm to 4 mm in diameter. A 2 mm hole is possible if you really need it. Drill them to a tolerance of +0.05 mm, −0.0 mm, and don't plate them. Use two holes per board, ideally in diagonally opposite corners, as far apart as you can, and at least 3 mm from the edge of the board. Keep an area at least 5 mm in diameter around each hole free of parts and tracks on the underside, so the board sits flat and the tooling pins can't short anything. Check the size and position with whoever builds the fixture.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [01:07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=4020); one contract manufacturer's technical paper, "Design guidelines for in-circuit testability" (2020).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

Source: https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/03-breakaway-methods/

## Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites

After assembly, the boards have to come out of the panel. There are two common ways to hold them in so they can be separated later:

- **V-score:** the fab cuts a V-shaped groove part-way through the board from both sides, in straight lines that run the full width of the panel.
  The boards are later separated by pushing a round knife along the groove or by snapping them by hand.
  Fast and cheap, but it only works on straight edges.
- **Tab routing:** the fab routes a slot around each board, leaving small tabs that hold it in place.
  Tabs with a row of small holes are called **mouse bites**, and they leave small stubs on the edge after breaking.
  Some assemblers have automated routers for depaneling these, leaving a clean edge.
  Though these machines are generally rare among most manufacturers.
  Ask your assembler about their capabilities.

| Feature | V-score | Tab routing (mouse bites) |
|---|---|---|
| Board shape | Straight edges only, scored edge to edge | Any shape |
| Cost | Lower | Higher (extra routing, slower to separate) |
| Edge finish | Clean, but less precise | Precise routed edge, with small stubs at each tab |
| Edge accuracy | Varies more | About ±0.1 mm on the routed parts |
| Typical tab width | Not applicable | About 3–6 mm |

Your design decides which one your assembler can use.

### PCB-DFM-001: Use straight-edged, rectangular board outlines when you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-001

**Recommendation:** Keep the board outline rectangular, or at least made of straight edges, unless the product really needs another shape.

**Why:** A straight-edged board can be V-scored, which is the cheaper and faster method. Any curved or irregular edge forces tab routing, which needs a slower router pass and leaves stubs that may need filing or sanding.

![D32: Drawn to scale, two 80 by 70 mm panels. Four rectangular boards are separated by V-score lines that run straight across the whole panel. Four round boards are each cut out by a routed slot and held by four tabs with mouse bites.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/outline-shapes.svg)

*D32 is drawn to scale. Rectangular boards are separated by V-score lines that run straight across the whole panel. Round boards each need a routed slot all the way round and tabs with mouse bites to hold them in.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Higher board cost, slower depaneling, and manual finishing of the tab stubs.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=1740); [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=780)–15:00; [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=2100)–40:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-010: Keep overhanging parts away from breakaway edges, and draw the overhang on the silkscreen

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-010

**Recommendation:** Avoid connectors, antennas or modules that hang past the board edge on an edge that will be V-scored or tabbed. Never put overhangs on opposite edges facing each other across the panel. If an overhang is unavoidable, show its full outline on the silkscreen or assembly drawing so the panel designer can leave room.

**Why:** Separating a V-score means bending the panel along the groove, and an overhanging part blocks that bend. The panel designer usually works from the board outline and won't read every datasheet; a visible outline makes them check and add a cut-out (relief) in the panel at that spot.

**Typical values:** Example: a coax connector overhanging by 7 mm needed about 10 mm of clearance. Some fiber optic connectors overhang the edge by more than 1 in (25 mm).

![D24: Drawn to scale, plan views with side views below. Boards A and B meet at a V-score, and a coax connector on board A hangs 7 mm past it, over board B; bent to snap the score, board B meets the connector before the score breaks. With board A's edge routed and held by tabs, and a routed relief cut-out leaving 10 mm from its edge, nothing is in the way.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/overhang-vscore.svg)

*D24 is drawn to scale. On the left, a coax connector on board A hangs 7 mm past the V-score, over board B. The side view shows board B bent up to snap the score: it meets the underside of the connector before the score can break. On the right, board A's edge is routed and held by tabs with mouse bites, and a routed relief cut-out leaves 10 mm from board A's edge. The connector's silkscreen outline includes the part past the edge, so the panel designer can see it.*

![D25: Drawn to scale, three side views of two boards joined by a V-score. A connector on board B's top hangs 7 mm over board A, and a connector on board A's underside hangs 7 mm under board B. Bending board B up drops its own connector onto board A; bending it down lands board B on board A's connector. The score can't be snapped either way.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/overhang-facing.svg)

*D25 is drawn to scale. Two overhangs face each other across the score, one on each face of the panel. Bending board B up drops its own connector onto board A; bending it down lands board B on board A's connector. Each overhang blocks one direction, so together they block both, and the score can't be snapped. Keep overhangs off breakaway edges, or route the edge and leave a relief cut-out, as in D24.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Panels that are nearly impossible to separate, parts snapped off during depaneling or shipping, and boards that have to be cut apart by hand.

**Example:** An ethernet port on the bottom of one board and a USB port on the top of its neighbor overlapped across the panel rail with no clearance. The boards could not be separated without removing and re-soldering a part. On another design, a module on top and a USB port directly beneath it pinched the panel material; hundreds of boards had to be cut free by hand.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=900)–17:00; [“How Loci Controls automates landfill methane gas collection”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5509702-how-loci-controls-automates-landfill-methane-gas-collection) (Sep 2020), [01:11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5509702?t=4260); [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [01:18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=4680)–01:20:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [39:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=2340)–40:00; [“How to safely and successfully ship assembled PCBs w/ Nicole Poirier”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835-how-to-safely-and-successfully-ship-assembled-pcbs-w-nicole-poirier) (Apr 2021), [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=2040)–36:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1920) and [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=2460)–42:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-011: Mark critical edges on a drawing, and leave room around the board in the enclosure

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-011

**Recommendation:** Don't draw the board to the exact inside size of its enclosure. Leave about 1 mm all round (0.5 mm at the very least). If an edge really must be held tightly, mark it as a critical dimension on a mechanical drawing so the assembler routes that edge instead of scoring or tabbing it.

**Why:** Even good fabs hold board edges to only about ±0.1 mm, and boards change size slightly through reflow and other heating steps. A V-scored edge is less precise than a routed one, and tab stubs stick out past the edge.

**Typical values:** Fab edge tolerance about ±0.1 mm (routed) · enclosure clearance about 1 mm, 0.5 mm minimum.

![D33: Drawn to scale, plan view of a 50 by 30 mm board inside an enclosure with 1 mm of room all round. A 0.5 mm tab stub on the left edge, shown enlarged, fits in that room. The right edge is marked as critical, to be routed to about plus or minus 0.1 mm.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/enclosure-room.svg)

*D33 is drawn to scale, with the left edge enlarged. The board has about 1 mm of room all round inside its enclosure. A breakaway tab can leave a stub of about 0.5 mm, which that room absorbs. The one edge that must be held tightly is marked critical on the drawing, so the assembler routes it to about ±0.1 mm.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards that don't fit their case, or that need every tab stub filed off by hand.

**Applies to:** General practice. Tighter tolerances may be possible but would need to be confirmed with the fab and assembler in advance.

**Sources:** [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=1920)–35:00; [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=2040); [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1740)–30:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-012: If you need tabs and a clean outline, recess the edge where each tab joins

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-012

**Recommendation:** For a tab-routed board that must fit its enclosure closely, add a small notch in the board outline at each tab location. Agree on the tab positions with your assembler.

**Why:** After breaking, the tab stub sits inside the notch, flush with the rest of the outline, so nobody has to file or sand it off.

![D4: Drawn to scale: four close-ups of a board edge at a breakaway tab. Without a recess, the broken tab leaves a stub sticking out past the board outline. With a 1 mm recess, the stub stays below the outline.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/recessed-tab.svg)

*D4 is drawn to scale. The top row shows the board in the panel: a 2 mm routed slot separates it from the panel frame, and a 5 mm tab bridges the slot, joined to the board by a row of 0.5 mm mouse-bite holes. The bottom row shows the board after breaking. Without a recess, the rough stub sticks out past the board outline and has to be filed off. With a recess, the board outline steps 1 mm inward at the tab, so the stub stays below the outline and the board fits its enclosure as it is. The tab, slot and recess sizes are examples.*

**Typical values:** Tabs are typically about 3–6 mm wide. Mouse-bite holes are 0.5 mm non-plated holes, pulled back 0.1 mm from the board edge. Keep traces, pads and plated holes at least 0.5 mm from the mouse-bite holes, which puts them at least 1.1 mm from the board edge. One assembler's guideline.

![D5: Drawn to scale, enlarged: 0.5 mm mouse-bite holes pulled back 0.1 mm from the board edge, with the nearest trace at least 0.5 mm from the holes and 1.1 mm from the edge.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/mouse-bite-clearance.svg)

*D5. The close-up is enlarged and drawn to scale. Non-plated holes 0.5 mm in diameter run along the board edge, each pulled back 0.1 mm from the edge. The nearest trace, pad or plated hole is at least 0.5 mm from the holes, which puts it at least 1.1 mm from the board edge.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Every board needs its tab stubs filed, sanded or ground flush. If your assembler does not have an automated depaneling router, then it's slow manual work, and you pay for it whether or not it's on the quote.

**Example:** A consumer product with a distinctive non-rectangular enclosure, ordered in the thousands. The customer suggested recessing the edge at each tab instead of having every unit filed by hand. The assembler now recommends it to other customers.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=840); [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=2460)–47:00; [“Recessing Your PCB Edge for Perforated Tabs (mouse bites)”](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/blog/2018/6/20/recessing-your-pcb-edge-for-perforated-tabs), Worthington Assembly blog (Jul 2021).

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-013: Agree the number and position of tabs on round or odd-shaped boards

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-013

**Recommendation:** For non-rectangular boards, decide with your assembler how many tabs to use and where they go. Tell them about any keep-out areas, such as an antenna, where a tab must not be placed.

**Why:** Too few tabs and a large board can fall out of the panel during handling or reflow. Too many, or in the wrong place, and separating the board risks damaging it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Example: a 6 in (about 150 mm) round board with only two tabs, which is clearly not enough to hold it securely.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=1980); [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=2460)–47:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-014: Talk to your assembler before panelizing boards thicker than about 2 mm

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-014

**Recommendation:** If your board is 2 mm thick or more, discuss depaneling with your assembler before you order.

**Why:** Standard depaneling tools are made for boards around 1.6 mm thick. Thicker boards are too stiff to snap cleanly along a score, and too thick for the usual round-blade cutter.

**Typical values:** 1.6–1.8 mm depanels normally · 2.0–2.4 mm and up gets difficult.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** If your assembler does not have an automatic depaneling router then boards are broken by hand or cut apart one at a time with special cutters. That's slow, it adds labor cost, and the extra force puts parts near the edge at risk.

**Example:** Boards a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) thick could not be separated by any normal method and had to be cut apart by hand with a rotary tool.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [23:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1380)–25:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=2400)–41:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*
