Source: https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/

## Clearance near board and panel edges

The outer few millimeters of a board are a busy place. Conveyors and clamps grip it, depaneling tools cut and bend it, and the fab's router or scoring blade runs along it. Keeping your parts and copper back from the edge is one of the cheapest things you can do to make a board easier to build.

### Edge clearances at a glance

| What | From | Minimum | Better | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Components and exposed (solderable) copper | Any edge the machines grip, if you want to avoid rails | 3 mm | 5 mm | [PCB-DFA-015](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfa-015-keep-parts-and-exposed-copper-at-least-3-mm-from-the-edges-5-mm-if-you-can) |
| Copper, any layer (traces, pours) | A V-score line | 0.5 mm (20 mil) | 1.0 mm | [PCB-DFM-002](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfm-002-keep-copper-back-from-the-board-edge-further-for-v-score-than-for-routing) |
| Copper, any layer (traces, pours) | A routed edge | 0.25 mm (10 mil) | | [PCB-DFM-002](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfm-002-keep-copper-back-from-the-board-edge-further-for-v-score-than-for-routing) |
| General components | A V-scored or routed edge | 1.3 mm (50 mil) | | [PCB-DFA-016](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfa-016-keep-components-back-from-breakaway-edges-and-ceramic-capacitors-further-still) |
| Ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) | A V-scored edge, or a breakaway tab | 5 mm (0.2 in) | 10 mm | [PCB-DFA-016](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfa-016-keep-components-back-from-breakaway-edges-and-ceramic-capacitors-further-still) |

These come from the podcast episodes and published fab guidelines. Your manufacturer's may differ.

![D3: Drawn to scale: a V-score line between two boards, with copper kept 0.5 mm back, a resistor 1.3 mm or more back and a ceramic capacitor 5 mm or more back, both turned parallel to the line; a capacitor turned across the line 1 mm from it is marked as wrong.](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/images/vscore-clearance.svg)

*D3 is enlarged and drawn to scale. A dashed V-score line separates two boards. Copper is kept at least 0.5 mm from the line, ordinary parts such as resistors at least 1.3 mm, and ceramic capacitors at least 5 mm. The resistor and the good capacitor lie with their long axis parallel to the line. A capacitor lying across the line, only 1 mm from it, is marked as wrong.*

### PCB-DFA-015: Keep parts and exposed copper at least 3 mm from the edges, 5 mm if you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-015

**Recommendation:** Keep every component and every piece of exposed, solderable copper at least 3 mm from the board's long edges, and preferably 5 mm. This is generally not possible, but very convenient when possible. If you manage this, plus fiducials on the board, tell your assembler: they may be able to run the board without rails.

**Why:** Equipment built to the SMEMA conveyor standard (IPC-SMEMA-9851) grips about 3 mm of the board edge, and the standard allows a conveyor to use up to 5 mm. Anything in that strip can be crushed, hidden from cameras or kept from getting solder paste. Without the clearance, the assembler has to add rails, which costs panel material and depaneling time.

**Typical values:** 3 mm minimum · 5 mm recommended. Copper that is covered by solder mask can come much closer (see PCB-DFM-002).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Rails on every panel, a depaneling step on every board, and extra handling stress on the parts near the edge.

**Applies to:** General practice. Most assemblers add rails by default anyway; ask yours whether they'll run your board without them.

**Sources:** [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=1020)–23:00 and [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=1620); [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=1860); [“Conveyers, An Episode You Didn't Know You Needed”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13980495-conveyers-an-episode-you-didn-t-know-you-needed) (Nov 2023), [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13980495?t=2100)–37:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1920)–33:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFM-002: Keep copper back from the board edge, further for V-score than for routing

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-002

**Recommendation:** Keep traces and copper pours, on every layer, at least 0.5 mm (20 mil) from a V-score line, and 1.0 mm if you have room. On routed edges, 0.25 mm (10 mil) is a common minimum. Some fabs can route closer, down to about 0.13 mm (5 mil), if you agree it with them first.

**Why:** The V-score blade cuts a groove into the board, and its position varies by a few tenths of a millimeter. Copper too close to it gets cut, exposed or cracked when the board is snapped apart. Routing is more precise and puts less stress on the edge.

**Typical values:** V-score: 0.45–0.5 mm minimum in published fab rules (one European fab: 0.45 mm on all layers; one US fab: 20 mil), with some fabs asking for up to 1.0 mm · routed: about 0.25 mm on outer layers (some fabs ask 0.4 mm on inner layers). Copper right up to the edge can't be V-scored at all.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** The fab flags the design and puts it on hold, or rejects it.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1560) and [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1680); [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=1020)–23:00; published design rules from several PCB fabs (checked Oct 2026).

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-016: Keep components back from breakaway edges, and ceramic capacitors further still

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-016

**Recommendation:** Keep components at least 1.3 mm (50 mil) from any edge that will be V-scored or tab-routed. Keep multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) at least 5 mm (0.2 in) from a V-scored edge and from each breakaway tab, and 10 mm if you have room. If an MLCC has to sit closer than 5 mm, use a flexible-termination MLCC, or ask for a routed slot between the part and the break line.

**Why:** Breaking a panel apart bends the board along the break line, and the strain is highest right next to it, and highest of all at a tab. Most parts can take it. MLCCs are ceramic: they don't bend, they crack.

**Typical values:** Components 1.3 mm (50 mil) · MLCCs 5 mm (0.2 in) minimum, as two capacitor makers advise · MLCCs 10 mm better, as a third maker advises for board edges, screw holes and connectors. Flexible-termination MLCCs are rated for up to 5 mm of board bending in the standard bend test, against the usual 2 mm minimum. Near an MLCC, a routed slot is a gentler break line than a row of mouse bites. Some assemblers accept MLCCs as close as 3.2 mm (125 mil) on low-volume boards, at higher risk.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Cracked capacitors are hard to catch. Many pass test and fail weeks or months later in the field, sometimes as a short that can overheat. On a run of 50 boards you may never see it; at automotive volumes, you will.

**Example:** Ceramic capacitors placed close to the edge cracked during depaneling, and many boards had to be reworked.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How PCB panelization methods inform depanelization”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685-how-pcb-panelization-methods-inform-depanelization) (Sep 2022), [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11289685?t=1560)–29:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=2580)–44:00; capacitor makers' guidance on preventing MLCC flex cracks (checked Oct 2026), including [“Strain Crack Mechanism and Preventive Measures for Multilayer Ceramic Capacitors”](https://article.murata.com/en-global/article/strain-crack-mechanism-and-preventive-measures-for-mlcc), section 5.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFA-017: Turn ceramic capacitors and other chip parts near a break line parallel to it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-017

**Recommendation:** Where a chip part (especially an MLCC) has to sit near a V-score line or breakaway tab, turn it so its long axis runs parallel to the line, not across it. If you can't, ask your assembler about a routed slot between the part and the line.

**Why:** Snapping a panel bends the board along the break line, and the strain runs across the line. A part lying across the line is stretched end to end, which is how MLCCs crack. A part lying along the line sees much less of that strain. Capacitor makers rank parallel placement as the lowest-stress option.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Cracked capacitors that may pass test and fail later in the field. A cracked MLCC can short and overheat.

**Applies to:** General practice. Distance from the line (PCB-DFA-016) still matters most.

**Sources:** Capacitor makers' layout guidance on preventing MLCC flex cracks (two major makers, checked Oct 2026); [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=1920), for stress from the depaneling knife.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFM-003: If copper must run to the board edge, say so

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-003

**Recommendation:** If your design really needs copper right up to the edge (for example an edge connector or an edge-plated shield), state it clearly in the fabrication notes.

**Why:** Fab engineers are trained to pull copper back from the edge by default, because routing through copper wears out router bits faster. They can do it, but only if they know you mean it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** The fab quietly pulls your copper back, or puts the job on hold with questions.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=3120)–54:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

### Related pages
- [Rails, tooling holes and fiducials](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/02-rails-tooling-holes-fiducials/)
- [Breakaway methods: V-score, tabs and mouse bites](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/03-breakaway-methods/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/05-x-outs/

## X-outs: accepting panels with a bad board

Bare boards are tested at the fab. When one board on a panel fails, the fab can scrap the whole panel or mark the bad board and ship the rest. A marked board is called an **X-out**: it's crossed out with a marker, and a colored sticker is put at an agreed spot on the panel. When the machines see the sticker, they skip that board: no paste, no parts, no inspection.

### PCB-DFM-004: Accept X-outs unless you have a real reason not to

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-004

**Recommendation:** Allow your fab and assembler to use panels with X-outs. If your process truly can't handle them (for example a test fixture that needs every position filled), say so up front and expect to pay for it.

**Why:** The other boards on the panel are perfectly good. Refusing X-outs means the fab scraps whole panels, and that cost is passed on to you.

**Typical values:** Refusing X-outs can cost about 20–30 % more per board (one assembler's estimate, as of 2023).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You pay a premium for every board, often without seeing it on the quote.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=780)–20:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFM-005: Design with margin above the fab's minimums to avoid X-outs in the first place

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-005

**Recommendation:** Don't design right at the fab's stated minimum trace width and spacing. Use 6 mil (0.15 mm) as an everyday minimum and 8 mil (0.2 mm) where you have room. Design for the copper weight you'll actually order: 2 oz copper needs wider gaps than 1 oz.

**Why:** Tight features are fine on one small board but get much harder to make perfectly when they're repeated many times across a large panel. Margin lets the fab hit its tolerances every time, so fewer boards fail.

**Typical values:** Most fabs' practical limit is about 4 mil (0.1 mm) · 6 mil (0.15 mm) everyday minimum · 8 mil (0.2 mm) comfortable, and recommended for 2 oz copper.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** More boards fail at the fab. Panels arrive full of X-outs, the fab has to make extra panels to fill your order, and the cost and delay come back to you.

**Example:** A power-supply board designed with 1 oz spacing but ordered in 2 oz copper came back with so many X-outs that about 400 panels had to be made to deliver an order that should have needed 250. Redesigning to 8 mil trace and gap fixed it. The other way round, a designer who chose 8 mil instead of the fab's 6 mil minimum reported zero X-outs across many thousands of boards.

**Applies to:** General practice. Exact limits vary by fab.

**Sources:** [“Inner Layer Production w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673-inner-layer-production-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [01:09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673?t=4140)–01:11:00; [“Outer Layer Imaging w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857-outer-layer-imaging-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2022), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=2580)–44:00; [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2100)–38:00; [“An EDA Tool Walks Into a CM w/ Fusion 360 Electronics Product Manager, Ben Jordan”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9171908-an-eda-tool-walks-into-a-cm-w-fusion-360-electronics-product-manager-ben-jordan) (Sep 2021), [50:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9171908?t=3000)–53:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

---

### PCB-DFM-006: Prefer smaller panels for designs that are hard to make

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-006

**Recommendation:** If your design pushes the fab's limits, ask for a smaller panel (for example 3- or 4-up) rather than a large one (for example 15-up).

**Why:** A large panel collects more bad boards per panel. Some fabs resist shipping panels with many X-outs, and a panel that is mostly X-outs wastes assembly time.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [01:11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=4260)–01:13:00; [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2100)–36:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-10-28*

### Related pages
- [Why boards are built in panels](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/01-materials-and-stack-up/

## Materials and stack-up

A circuit board is a sandwich: layers of copper foil separated by glass-weave laminate (cores) and bonding sheets (prepreg), pressed together under heat. The stack-up is the recipe for that sandwich: how many copper layers, how thick each copper and dielectric layer is, and what material it's made of. It sets the board's thickness, its stiffness, how it behaves in the reflow oven, and the impedance of every trace.

Most boards need nothing unusual here. The recommendations below are about not asking for more than you need, and saying clearly what you do need.

### PCB-DFM-017: Use standard FR-4 unless the product needs something else

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-017

**Recommendation:** Specify standard FR-4 epoxy-glass laminate unless your product has a real need for something else: sustained high temperature, very high frequencies, or a customer requirement. If you need a particular material or certification, name it by its IPC-4101 specification sheet (the "slash sheet") and confirm with your fab that they stock it.

**Why:** Standard materials are in stock at every fab, in every thickness. Exotic laminates can take about eight weeks to arrive and come with minimum order quantities, and some are harder to drill, plate and laminate. Tg (glass transition temperature) is the temperature at which the laminate starts to soften; a higher-Tg material stays stiffer and flatter through reflow, rework and hot service. UL flammability approval belongs to a particular fab's process with a particular material, so a different material or a custom build may not carry it.

**Typical values:** Standard FR-4 has a Tg of about 135 °C; mid-Tg is about 150 °C and high-Tg about 170 °C. Fabs don't treat mid- or high-Tg as standard, and it usually costs more. If you don't specify Tg, expect the cheapest material, most likely about 135 °C, but the fab may use anything reasonable it has on the shelf. So if your product needs mid- or high-Tg, say so on the drawing; if it doesn't, don't pay for it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Weeks added to the lead time and a higher price for a material the product didn't need; or, the other way round, a board that softens and warps in a hot product.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Bare PCB Materials w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7558222-bare-pcb-materials-w-dave-wilcox) (Feb 2021), [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7558222?t=660)–18:00, [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7558222?t=1860)–35:00 and [57:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7558222?t=3420)–58:00; IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 1-2 (default material: epoxy-glass laminate); a fab-industry engineer, via Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-018: Start from your fab's standard stack-up, or give them what they need to build one

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-018

**Recommendation:** Use your fab's standard stack-up for your layer count and thickness if it meets your needs. If you need a custom one (for controlled impedance, say), don't work it out alone: give the fab the signal frequencies, the target impedances, which layers each impedance trace runs on and references, and how much the material may cost, and let their engineers propose the stack-up before you place the order.

**Why:** The fab knows which cores and prepregs it actually stocks, and how much each one thins when it's pressed. A stack-up built from someone else's materials list will be adjusted anyway. Fabs are allowed to tune dielectric thicknesses (by about ±20%) to hit a stated impedance, but a large change should come back to you for approval.

**Typical values:**
- Minimum dielectric thickness between copper layers, when the drawing doesn't say: 65 µm (2.56 mil) under IPC-6012F.
  Older guidance, including IPC-6012E, gave 3.5 mil (90 µm).
- One sheet of prepreg between the outer layer and the next layer is fine for most boards; use two for products that will see heavy shock and vibration.
- Avoid stacking more than three sheets of prepreg in one gap.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A stack-up that can't be built from stock material, a week lost going back and forth, or impedances that are off because the fab had to change your dielectrics.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer; standard stack-ups are fab-specific.

**Sources:** [“Understanding Controlled Impedance w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer, Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934-understanding-controlled-impedance-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Nov 2022), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=1140)–20:00 and [25:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=1500)–29:00; [“Impedance Control Demo w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746-impedance-control-demo-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Oct 2023), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=1680)–30:00, [01:03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=3780)–01:05:00 and [01:12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=4320)–01:18:00; [“Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=2640); IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 1-2.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-019: Specify controlled impedance fully, make the traces easy to find, and leave room to widen them

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-019

**Recommendation:** For every controlled-impedance requirement, state on the fabrication drawing:
- the structure (for example, surface microstrip, embedded stripline, edge-coupled differential pair, coplanar waveguide with ground);
- the layer the trace is on and the layers it references;
- the target impedance and its tolerance;
- the trace width and spacing you designed with.

Give impedance traces an unusual width, such as 0.159 mm (6.25 mil) instead of 0.15 mm, so the fab can find them among all the other traces. Leave space beside them, so the fab can widen them if their materials need it. Calculate your own design to within about 1% of the target before you send it.

**Why:** Gerbers show trace widths, not which traces are impedance-controlled. An odd width lets the fab select every impedance trace at once. Etching leaves traces narrower at the top than the bottom, and the fab adjusts widths and dielectrics to suit its own materials; if the traces are hemmed in, they can't.

**Typical values:** Tolerance ±10% is common; ±5% costs more. Common targets: 50 Ω single-ended, 90 or 100 Ω differential. Ask for a TDR test of the impedance coupon, or the fab's stack-up calculation, if you want proof.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Traces that can't reach the impedance you need, discovered after the board is built.

**Example:** A board revision added an 85 Ω differential pair in a space that allowed only 3 mil traces with 3 mil gaps; the impedance was physically unachievable in that space, and the design sat stuck for over a week.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Impedance Control Demo w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746-impedance-control-demo-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Oct 2023), [15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=900)–25:00, [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=2100)–37:00, [45:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=2700)–49:00 and [01:10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=4200)–01:11:00; [“Understanding Controlled Impedance w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer, Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934-understanding-controlled-impedance-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Nov 2022), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=1020)–19:00, [37:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=2220)–38:00 and [42:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=2520)–51:00; see also [PCB-DFM-014](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-014-put-everything-the-gerbers-cant-say-on-the-fabrication-drawing).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-020: Size traces and gaps for the finished copper weight

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-020

**Recommendation:** Set your trace width and spacing rules for the copper weight the board will really have, and set the clearance from copper pours to the same values.

**Why:** Copper is etched from the side as well as from the top, so thicker copper needs wider gaps to etch cleanly. Outer layers also gain plated copper on top of the foil. A pour clearance left at a tight default undoes every other rule.

**Typical values:**

| Finished copper | Minimum trace and space | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| 1 oz (35 µm) | 0.1 mm (4 mil) | 0.15 mm (6 mil) |
| 2 oz (70 µm) | 0.2 mm (8 mil) | 0.25 mm (10 mil) |

On 2 oz copper, 6 mil can be built, but with very poor yield, so avoid it. Finer than about 0.075 mm (3 mil) needs thinner starting foil and a fab that specializes in it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Shorts and opens, lower yield, X-outs, and a higher price; heavy-copper boards drawn to 1 oz rules may not be buildable at all.

**Example:** A motor controller needed 2 oz copper for its current but was laid out with fine 1 oz rules; the fab's advice was to open trace and gap up to 8 mil. On another board, trace and space were set to 6 mil, but the pour clearance was left at 2 mil.

**Applies to:** General practice; exact capability varies by fab.

**Sources:** [“An overview of bare PCB fabrication w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663-an-overview-of-bare-pcb-fabrication-w-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2020), [01:01:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663?t=3660)–01:03:00; [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=2580)–46:00; [“Inner Layer Production w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673-inner-layer-production-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [01:09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673?t=4140)–01:11:00; [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [37:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2220)–38:00; [“Outer Layer Imaging w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857-outer-layer-imaging-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2022), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=2460)–45:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=420); Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-021: Use as few layers as the circuit needs

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-021

**Recommendation:** Use two layers when the circuit genuinely allows it, and add layers only when routing, power or signal integrity need them.

**Why:** Every extra pair of layers adds lamination, drilling depth, registration risk and cost. Above about 12 to 16 layers, many fabs reach the limit of their equipment and need very thin cores and tighter process control.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A higher price and a longer lead time than the board needed; at high layer counts, fewer fabs that can build it.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Inner Layer Production w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673-inner-layer-production-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [06:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673?t=360)–11:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-073: Expect thin boards to need a carrier during assembly

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-073

**Recommendation:** Choose the board thickness the product needs; any thickness can be assembled, even double-sided flexible boards. For boards 0.6 mm or thinner, expect the assembler to run them on a carrier (a rigid tray that holds the board through printing, placement and reflow), and ask what it costs.

**Why:** Thin boards sag on conveyors and under the stencil, and warp in the oven. A carrier holds them flat, but it has to be made for the board.

**Typical values:** 0.6 mm or thinner: carrier needed. About 0.8 mm: sometimes needed. 1.0 mm and thicker: generally not needed.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A carrier charge and lead time you didn't plan for.

**Applies to:** Varies by assembler; thresholds from Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub (2026).

**Sources:** Chris Denney (author); [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [01:15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=4500)–01:17:00 (older, stricter limits).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

## Inner layers and lamination

On a multilayer board, each inner layer is imaged and etched on its own core, then the cores are stacked with prepreg and pressed together under heat. In the press, the material moves: each layer shrinks or stretches slightly, and not always by the same amount. The holes are drilled afterwards, through all the layers at once, so every hole has to land on pads that may have moved a little.

Most of what a designer can do here is leave room for that movement.

### PCB-DFM-022: Keep copper 0.25 mm or more from drilled holes on every layer

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-022

**Recommendation:** Keep at least 0.25 mm (10 mil) between the edge of any drilled hole and the nearest copper it isn't meant to connect to, on every layer, including plane clearances. Go down to 0.2 mm (8 mil) only in a tight area, and avoid going below 0.15 mm (6 mil).

**Why:** Layers move during lamination, and the drill has its own positional tolerance. The gap between a hole and nearby copper is what absorbs both. Measure it edge to edge: from the edge of the hole to the edge of the copper.

**Typical values:** 0.25–0.3 mm (10–12 mil): good boards every time. 0.2 mm (8 mil): possible, harder. 0.15 mm (6 mil): in one small, tight area only; below that, few fabs will build it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Shorts between a hole and an inner-layer trace or plane, found at electrical test as scrapped boards, or worse, not found until later.

**Applies to:** General practice; fab capability varies.

**Sources:** [“Inner Layer Production w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673-inner-layer-production-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [01:13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673?t=4380)–01:17:00; fabs' published design rules (about 0.2 mm typical drill-to-copper).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-074: On very large boards, expect the fab to scale the outer layers, and tell the assembler

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-074

**Recommendation:** If your board is very large (about 400 mm or longer), ask the fab whether they had to scale the outer layers, and make sure the stencil is made to match the boards as built.

**Why:** On a large board, the movement in the press adds up from one end to the other. To keep the holes on their pads, the fab may scale the drill data and then scale the outer-layer artwork to match. A stencil cut from your original data is then slightly too small or too large for the board.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Paste prints that are on the pads at one end of the board and off them at the other.

**Applies to:** Large boards; panels are usually kept small enough to avoid it.

**Sources:** [“Inner Layer Production w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673-inner-layer-production-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [01:14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673?t=4440)–01:16:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

- [Drilling](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/03-drilling/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/03-drilling/

## Drilling

Every hole in a board is drilled after lamination: mechanically with carbide drill bits for most holes, or with a laser for the very small microvias in high-density boards. Plated holes are then lined with copper, so the drill is always larger than the hole you end up with. Small holes in thick boards are hard to drill straight and hard to plate all the way down, and every different hole size is another tool change.

How to describe holes in your data, and how to mark the ones that matter, is in [Fabrication data](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/) (PCB-DFM-011 and PCB-DFM-012).

### PCB-DFM-023: Give hole sizes as finished sizes

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-023

**Recommendation:** Give every hole in your design as the finished size you need after plating and surface finish, not the size of drill you think the fab should use.

**Why:** The fab drills plated holes larger, by an amount that depends on its plating process, copper weight and finish, so that the finished hole comes out at your size. They can only do that if your sizes are finished sizes.

**Typical values:** A 1.0 mm finished plated hole is typically drilled at about 1.1 to 1.15 mm. One large fab enlarges plated holes of 0.5 mm and up by 0.15 mm, and non-plated holes by 0.05 mm.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Holes too small for the leads, if you've already allowed for plating and the fab allows for it again.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The basics of the PCB drilling process w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552-the-basics-of-the-pcb-drilling-process-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552?t=1020); one large fab's published hole-size guidance.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-024: Keep the aspect ratio at 8:1 or less, and holes 0.25 mm or larger where you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-024

**Recommendation:** Keep the ratio of board thickness to the smallest plated hole's drill size at 8:1 or less, and no more than 10:1. Use 0.25 mm (10 mil) or larger for the smallest drilled holes where the design allows, and avoid going below 0.2 mm.

**Why:** Plating solution has to flow all the way down a hole to plate its walls. The deeper and narrower the hole, the harder that is, and the thinner the copper in the middle of the barrel. Small drills also bend and break more easily, and fabs can't stack as many panels on the drill at once, which makes drilling slower and more expensive.

**Typical values:** (see D47)

| Aspect ratio (thickness : drill) | What it means |
|---|---|
| 8:1 or less | Recommended; any good fab |
| 8:1 to 10:1 | Possible; pushing the limits |
| Over 10:1 | Difficult; ask first |

For a 1.6 mm board, a 0.2 mm drill is 8:1. At 0.25 mm, a fab can drill two 1.6 mm panels stacked together; some fabs can't drill below 0.2 mm at all.

![D47 is drawn to scale: a 1.6 mm board with a 0.2 mm drilled hole, an aspect ratio of 8 to 1; and top views of a 0.6 mm pad on a 0.3 mm hole, with a 0.15 mm annular ring when centered and 0.05 mm left on one side when the drill is 0.1 mm off center.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/aspect-ratio-annular-ring.svg)

*D47 is drawn to scale. On the left, a 1.6 mm board with a 0.2 mm drilled hole: 1.6 ÷ 0.2 gives an aspect ratio of 8:1, the recommended limit. On the right, a 0.6 mm pad on a 0.3 mm hole has a 0.15 mm annular ring all round when the drill is centered. With the drill 0.1 mm off center, only 0.05 mm of ring is left on one side; the hole is still inside the pad, which is what the margin is for ([PCB-DFM-026](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/03-drilling/#pcb-dfm-026-give-every-plated-hole-an-annular-ring-with-margin-above-the-ipc-minimum)).*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Thin or missing copper in the middle of the hole, which may pass electrical test and then crack open in thermal cycling.

**Applies to:** General practice; capability varies by fab.

**Sources:** [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [38:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2280)–40:00; [“The basics of the PCB drilling process w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552-the-basics-of-the-pcb-drilling-process-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552?t=180)–04:00; fabs' published capability tables (8:1 standard, 10:1 to 12:1 advanced).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-025: Use as few different hole sizes as you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-025

**Recommendation:** Standardize on one or two via sizes, and avoid hole sizes that differ by only a few hundredths of a millimeter.

**Why:** Every hole size is another tool change on the drilling machine. Near-duplicate sizes usually come from footprints made by different people, not from a real need.

**Typical values:** About 40 to 60 seconds per tool change, on every panel.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Longer drilling time and a higher price for no benefit.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [46:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2760)–49:00 and [55:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=3300)–56:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-026: Give every plated hole an annular ring with margin above the IPC minimum

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-026

**Recommendation:** Design every pad on a plated hole with an annular ring (the copper between the edge of the hole and the edge of the pad) of 0.15 mm or more on outer layers where you can. Never end a trace at a plated hole without a pad.

**Why:** The drill never lands exactly in the center of the pad: layers move in the press, and the drill has its own tolerance. The annular ring is the margin that keeps the hole inside the pad. IPC-6012 sets what the finished board must meet; your design needs more than that, so the board still meets it after the drill wanders.

**Typical values:** Design target: 0.15 mm (6 mil) on outer layers; 0.125 mm is a common fab minimum for design; 0.2 mm or more for high-reliability products.
IPC-6012F, finished board, external plated holes:
- Class 2: the hole may break out of the pad by up to 90°, as long as the trace joining the pad isn't narrowed too far; with no teardrop, at least 25 µm of ring where the trace joins.
- Class 3: at least 50 µm of ring all round.

Internal layers, Class 3: at least 25 µm. Teardrops (fillets where a trace meets a pad) are acceptable for Class 2 unless you prohibit them, and must be agreed for Class 3.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Holes that break out of their pads, X-outs, and boards that fail Class 3 inspection.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), section 3.4.2 and Table 3-7; [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=1560)–28:00 and [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=2100)–36:00; [“Inner Layer Production w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673-inner-layer-production-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [01:03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9018673?t=3780)–01:04:00; fabs' published annular ring guidance (0.125–0.15 mm).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-027: Use microvias and blind or buried vias only when you need them

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-027

**Recommendation:** Use plain through-hole vias unless the design really needs blind, buried or micro vias (for example, to fan out a very fine-pitch BGA). If you use laser microvias, make each one span a single layer (layer 1 to 2, for example), and stack them only if you must.

**Why:** Each blind or buried via structure adds drilling and lamination cycles. A laser can only drill a hole about as deep as it is wide, so microvias reach only to the next layer, and need electroless copper plating to cover their walls.

**Typical values:** Laser microvias: below about 0.15 mm; depth about equal to diameter (0.1 mm wide, about 0.1 mm deep).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A board that costs many times what it should.

**Example:** A design expected to cost $30–40 per board was quoted at hundreds of dollars, because it used stacked and blind vias and via fill it didn't need; removing them brought the price down sharply.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The basics of the PCB drilling process w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552-the-basics-of-the-pcb-drilling-process-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Aug 2021), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9091552?t=780)–15:00; [“Understanding Controlled Impedance w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer, Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934-understanding-controlled-impedance-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Nov 2022), [14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11631934?t=840)–15:00; [“Outer Layer Imaging w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857-outer-layer-imaging-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2022), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=1080)–19:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

- [Plating](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/04-plating/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/04-plating/

## Plating

After drilling, the fab makes the hole walls conductive with a thin chemical layer, then electroplates copper onto them. The same plating builds up copper on the outer layers at the same time. That's why outer layers end up thicker than the foil they started with, and why plated holes are drilled larger than the size you asked for.

### PCB-DFM-028: Know what plating does to your holes and outer copper

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-028

**Recommendation:** Design with plating in mind:
- give finished hole sizes ([PCB-DFM-023](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/03-drilling/#pcb-dfm-023-give-hole-sizes-as-finished-sizes));
- set outer-layer trace and space rules for the plated copper thickness, not the starting foil ([PCB-DFM-020](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/01-materials-and-stack-up/#pcb-dfm-020-size-traces-and-gaps-for-the-finished-copper-weight));
- keep the aspect ratio within what plates well ([PCB-DFM-024](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/03-drilling/#pcb-dfm-024-keep-the-aspect-ratio-at-81-or-less-and-holes-025-mm-or-larger-where-you-can));
- if you need more copper in the holes than the standard, say so on the drawing.

**Why:** Plating adds copper to the hole walls and the outer surfaces in one step. Getting the minimum thickness in the middle of a deep, narrow hole means the surface gets more than that. Very small microvias are plated with a slower electroless copper process that covers their walls more reliably than the faster direct-metallization lines.

**Typical values:** IPC-6012F minimum copper in plated holes:

| Copper plating thickness | Class 2 | Class 3 |
|---|---|---|
| Through-holes, blind and buried vias: average | 20 µm | 25 µm |
| Through-holes, blind and buried vias: thinnest spot | 18 µm | 20 µm |
| Microvias: average / thinnest | 12 / 10 µm | 12 / 10 µm |
| Copper cap over a filled via (minimum) | 5 µm | 12 µm |

The outer surfaces gain at least as much copper as the hole walls, often more, so a 1 oz finished outer layer is usually reached from thinner starting foil plus plating.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Outer-layer gaps too tight once the copper has grown, or holes that are too small.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), section 3.6.2.11 and Tables 3-10, 3-11 and 3-13; [“Outer Layer Imaging w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857-outer-layer-imaging-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2022), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=1080)–19:00 and [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=1800)–38:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

Source: https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/05-outer-layers/

## Outer layers

The outer layers are imaged after drilling and plating, usually with a laser that exposes a photoresist directly from your data, and then etched. The CAM engineer prepares the artwork first: compensating trace widths for the etch, adding small fillets, and checking every clearance. Clean, unambiguous geometry in your design leaves less for them to change.

### PCB-DFM-029: Avoid acute angles, keep pour clearances to your trace rules, and fan out fine-pitch parts through vias

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-029

**Recommendation:**
- Avoid acute (sharper than 90°) inside corners in traces and copper pours.
- Set the clearance between copper pours and other copper to at least your trace spacing.
- To escape the inner pads of a fine-pitch BGA or QFN, drop to an inner layer through a via, rather than squeezing a trace between pads on the outer layer.

**Why:** Etchant pools in acute corners and eats into the copper; CAM software fills them in automatically, which changes your copper. A pour clearance tighter than your trace rules becomes the tightest gap on the board. A trace between fine-pitch pads leaves almost no room for etching tolerance or solder mask.

**Typical values:** Pour clearance equal to trace spacing, for example 0.15 mm (6 mil) on 1 oz copper.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Artwork changed by the fab without your knowing; shorts in the narrowest gaps; bridges between fine-pitch pads.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [46:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=2760)–51:00; [“An overview of bare PCB fabrication w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663-an-overview-of-bare-pcb-fabrication-w-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2020), [01:02:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663?t=3720)–01:03:00; [“Outer Layer Imaging w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857-outer-layer-imaging-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2022), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=1620)–28:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

Source: https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/06-via-treatments/

## Via treatments

A via is a plated hole that connects layers. Left alone, it's an open hole lined with copper, with a ring of exposed copper on each side. It can instead be covered with solder mask, partly or completely filled, or filled and plated over flat. Each treatment changes what the via does during assembly, so choose it on purpose.

IPC-4761 names the treatments (drawn in D45):

| Type | Name | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| I | Tented | Solder mask laid over the via, covering its ring and its hole, on one side (Ia) or both (Ib) |
| II | Tented and covered | Tented, with a second coating over the mask; fabs describe a dry-film tent with a liquid mask coat over it. Rarely used |
| III | Plugged | Material pushed partway into the hole, from one side (IIIa) or both (IIIb); about a third of the depth from each side |
| IV | Plugged and covered | Plugged, then covered with mask |
| V | Filled | Hole completely filled, with non-conductive or conductive material |
| VI | Filled and covered | Filled, then covered with mask |
| VII | Filled and capped | Filled, then plated flat with copper, so a pad can sit on top |

![D45 is drawn to scale: cross-sections of a 0.3 mm plated via in a 1.6 mm board, as a fab builds it, with the plating joining the surface and inner-layer pads and solder mask as a liquid coat on the surface: open (not covered), then IPC-4761 Types Ia, Ib, II, III, IV, V, VI and VII. Below, enlarged to true scale, the top of one via: tented, the mask is thickest on bare FR4, thinnest at the copper's corner and sags over the hole; pulled back, its edge is rounded.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/via-treatments.svg)

*D45 shows a 0.3 mm via in a 1.6 mm board for each treatment, with copper and solder mask drawn thicker than true scale so they show. The plating lines the hole and joins the pads on both surfaces and on two inner layers. Solder mask goes on as a liquid and flows before it sets, so it is thickest on bare FR4, thinnest at the copper's corners, and sags where it spans a hole; the enlarged views at the bottom show this at true scale. The first via is open, for comparison. Type Ia is tented on one side only and is marked "avoid", because it traps air and chemistry. Type II, a dry-film tent under a liquid coat, is rarely used. Type III is plugged about a third of the way in from each side, leaving air in the middle; Type V is completely filled, flush with the pads; Type VII is filled and plated flat with copper.*

In this book, "tented" means IPC's Type I: mask over the ring and the hole. Some designers and fabs also say "tented" when the mask covers the ring but leaves the hole open; if a fab's note or a design rule says "tent vias", check which they mean.

### PCB-DFM-030: Tent vias by default, on both sides, if they're 0.3 mm or smaller

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-030

**Recommendation:** Tent every via that doesn't need to be open, on both sides of the board, by leaving it out of the solder mask openings in your data. Keep tented vias to 0.3 mm (12 mil) finished size or smaller; plug or fill larger ones. Tent or plug vias under BGAs, and never leave an open via right beside a solder joint on a different net.

**Why:** A tented via can't steal solder from a nearby pad or bridge to it, lets legend print cleanly over it, and makes the board much easier to inspect. Solder mask can only bridge a small hole; above about 0.3 mm it may not cover, or may crack as it cures. Tenting one side only traps air and process chemistry in the hole (see [PCB-DFA-075](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/06-via-treatments/#pcb-dfa-075-never-put-solder-mask-on-thermal-vias-under-a-qfn)). Tenting is not a seal: if air or liquid must not pass through, plug or fill the via instead.

**Typical values:** Tented: 0.3 mm or smaller, both sides. Larger vias: plugged or filled.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Solder bridges between a pad and a nearby open via; solder drawn away from joints; a busy board that's hard to inspect.

**Applies to:** General practice; check your fab's tenting limit.

**Sources:** [“Vias, Tenting, and Tiny Fireworks”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877-vias-tenting-and-tiny-fireworks) (Oct 2024), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877?t=300)–06:00 and [15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877?t=900)–20:00; [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=600)–14:00; fabs' published via-tenting guidance (0.3 mm or smaller, both sides); Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-031: Plug or fill vias that must be sealed, or that would trap chemistry

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-031

**Recommendation:** Plug or fill a via, rather than tent it, when air or liquid must not pass through the board, or when an open-on-one-side via could trap process chemistry (on boards with a gold finish, for example). Say on the drawing which you want: plugged (partly filled from each side) or filled (completely).

**Why:** A tent is a thin film over a hollow hole; it isn't airtight. A via left open on one side through fabrication can hold plating chemicals that spoil the gold finish nearby ("skip plating"). Plugged and filled are often used as if they meant the same thing, but a plugged via can still have an air gap in the middle.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Leaks through the board where it must be sealed; patches of missing finish on pads.

**Example:** A gas-sensor maker used the board itself as the barrier between the gas being measured and the outside air, so every via had to be filled. In testing, the fill wasn't strong enough to hold back the pressurized gas. So the vias were left open, solder paste was printed over them along with the rest of the board, and reflow filled them with solder. Filling vias with solder is rare, but here it stopped pressurized gas passing from one side of the board to the other.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Mastering Vias: Plugging, Filling, and Best Practices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518-mastering-vias-plugging-filling-and-best-practices) (Nov 2024), [02:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518?t=120)–06:00; [“Vias, Tenting, and Tiny Fireworks”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877-vias-tenting-and-tiny-fireworks) (Oct 2024), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877?t=1320)–23:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFM-032: For via-in-pad, fill with non-conductive epoxy and plate over it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-032

**Recommendation:** If a via sits inside a pad you'll solder to, specify it filled with non-conductive epoxy and copper-capped (IPC-4761 Type VII). Use conductive fill only if you need its extra heat or current capacity and the volume justifies the cost; a larger via with standard fill is often enough. Keep filled vias within your fab's size limit, and if many vias need filling, consider asking for all of them to be filled and capped.

**Why:** An open via in a pad drains solder from the joint and traps gas under the part. Fill and cap gives a flat, solid pad. A plugging compound (similar to solder mask) is fine for vias you won't solder to, but not under a cap. Filling every via can be simpler and barely more expensive than choosing which ones.

**Typical values:** Filled vias up to about 0.5 mm (20 mil), depending on the fab. IPC-6012F limits for a capped filled via: copper cap at least 5 µm (Class 2) or 12 µm (Class 3); dimple no deeper than 127 µm (Class 2) or 76 µm (Class 3); bump no higher than 50 µm.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Voids and starved joints under fine-pitch parts and BGAs; with conductive fill, a higher price for little gain.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Mastering Vias: Plugging, Filling, and Best Practices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518-mastering-vias-plugging-filling-and-best-practices) (Nov 2024), [08:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518?t=480)–20:00; [“Vias, Tenting, and Tiny Fireworks”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877-vias-tenting-and-tiny-fireworks) (Oct 2024), [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877?t=960)–17:00; IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), section 3.6.2.11.2 and Table 3-13.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

---

### PCB-DFA-075: Never put solder mask on thermal vias under a QFN

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-075

**Recommendation:** Never put solder mask on the thermal vias in a QFN's (or similar part's) ground pad, on either side of the board, and never plug them from one side only. Leave them open on both sides, or have them filled and capped (IPC-4761 Type VII). If a part's datasheet recommends tenting or plugging these vias from one side, the datasheet is wrong. If some vias of the same size need a different treatment from the rest, flag them one by one in your design tool, or on a separate layer or note.

**Why:** The top of these vias is the pad you solder to, so it can't be tented. Mask on the bottom closes the hole at one end. In the oven, the air and flux trapped inside expand with nowhere to go: they blow voids into the joint, or lift the part right off the board. Open vias let gas escape; filled and capped vias leave nothing to trap. Many design tools only apply a via treatment by hole size, so a thermal via the same size as your ordinary vias gets tented with them unless you say otherwise.

**Typical values:** Open thermal vias: about 0.3 mm (as in D46).

![D46 is drawn to scale: three cross-sections through a QFN's ground pad on a 1.6 mm board with three 0.3 mm thermal vias: open on both sides (correct), filled and capped (correct), and masked on the bottom with air and flux trapped inside (wrong).](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/qfn-thermal-vias.svg)

*D46 shows a QFN soldered to its ground pad over three 0.3 mm thermal vias in a 1.6 mm board. On the left, the vias are open on both sides, so gas can escape. In the middle, they are filled and capped flat with copper, so there is nothing to trap. On the right, solder mask covers the bottom of the vias; air and flux are trapped inside and expand in the oven.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts that come out of the oven displaced, or pop off the board during rework.

**Example:** A board's large QFN had thermal vias masked on the bottom and open on top. The QFNs came out of reflow scattered, and when the assembler tried to rework them with hot air, they shot off the board like popcorn: the flux trapped in the vias was boiling.

**Applies to:** General practice. One of the few places this book says "never".

**Sources:** [“Mastering Vias: Plugging, Filling, and Best Practices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518-mastering-vias-plugging-filling-and-best-practices) (Nov 2024), [00:30](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518?t=30)–03:00 and [21:30](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518?t=1290)–24:00; [“Vias, Tenting, and Tiny Fireworks”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877-vias-tenting-and-tiny-fireworks) (Oct 2024), [20:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15957877?t=1200)–23:00; two semiconductor makers' QFN assembly notes (one warns that back-side tenting traps air and increases voiding); Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-07*

- [Footprints and the component library](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/)

## Solder mask

Solder mask is the colored coat over most of the board. It goes on as a liquid, is exposed through a pattern and developed away from every pad you'll solder, then cured hard. It stops solder running where it shouldn't, insulates the copper under it, and protects it. How much mask a fab can leave between two pads, and how closely it can line the openings up with the copper, decides how fine your pitch can go.

### PCB-DFM-033: Choose green solder mask and white legend unless you have a reason not to

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-033

**Recommendation:** Use green solder mask with white legend unless the product needs another color. If it does, any common color can be built; expect the effects below, and choose a legend color that stands out against the mask: white on green, blue, red or black, and black on white or yellow.

**Why:** Green mask lets the most ultraviolet light through when it's exposed, so it holds the finest dams between pads. Some fabs can hold a 0.075 mm (3 mil) dam in green, against about 0.1 mm (4 mil) in other colors. Green also gives cameras and people the best contrast with solder and copper. Black mask hides black parts and reflects little light back to optical inspection machines, so it's harder to rework by eye, and 3D inspection machines handle it far better than 2D ones. Red mask can confuse inspection machines that light the board with red LEDs, because the red light coming back from the mask looks like light from a solder joint. Some white masks turn yellow or brown after several trips through the oven, and not every fab stocks white; ask for a white made to survive repeated reflow if appearance matters, as it does on LED boards.

**Typical values:** Smallest dam between pads: about 0.075 mm in green at some fabs, 0.1 mm in black, red, blue, yellow and white; 0.1 mm is recommended for every color (see [PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-032-put-a-solder-mask-dam-between-every-pad-of-a-fine-pitch-part)).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Coarser limits on fine-pitch parts, slower inspection programming, and parts that are hard to see during rework. None of these makes a board unbuildable.

**Example:** Some widely used inspection machines light boards with red LEDs, so red mask adds programming time on them. A designer with two near-identical boards that differed by a couple of parts used a different mask color for each, with matching kit labels, so the two could never be mixed up on the line.

**Applies to:** General practice. Color limits vary by fab and by inspection machine.

**Sources:** [“How sensors.AFRICA empowers citizens to fight against pollution w/ Jack McLeans”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7831030-how-sensors-africa-empowers-citizens-to-fight-against-pollution-w-jack-mcleans) (Feb 2021), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7831030?t=2580)–47:00; [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=2400)–41:00; [“Gloves not Mittens”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842-gloves-not-mittens) (Jun 2026), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=1080)–19:00; [“Stencils: The Unsung Heroes of PCB Perfection Pt. 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15484609-stencils-the-unsung-heroes-of-pcb-perfection-pt-2) (Jul 2024), [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15484609?t=2040)–35:00; [“Impedance Control Demo w/ NCAB Group Field Application Engineer Ryan Miller”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746-impedance-control-demo-w-ncab-group-field-application-engineer-ryan-miller) (Oct 2023), [37:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13789746?t=2220)–39:00; [“Automated Optical Inspection (AOI) for PCB Assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753-automated-optical-inspection-aoi-for-pcb-assembly) (Nov 2020), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753?t=1920); [“The PCB assembly inspection process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750-the-pcb-assembly-inspection-process) (Oct 2020), [45:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750?t=2700)–47:00; [“The importance of having different perspectives in engineering w/ Eli Hughes of Tzero Labs (Part 2)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7118017-the-importance-of-having-different-perspectives-in-engineering-w-eli-hughes-of-tzero-labs-part-2) (Jan 2021), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7118017?t=2580)–45:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=2640)–46:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFA-078: Keep a solder mask web between every via and the pad beside it, or tent the via

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-078

**Recommendation:** Where an open via sits next to a pad, leave a strip of solder mask (a web) between the via's copper and the pad. If there isn't room for the web, tent the via (see [PCB-DFM-030](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/06-via-treatments/#pcb-dfm-030-tent-vias-by-default-on-both-sides-if-theyre-03-mm-or-smaller)) or move it. The exception is thermal vias in a QFN's ground pad, which stay open on purpose (see [PCB-DFA-075](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/06-via-treatments/#pcb-dfa-075-never-put-solder-mask-on-thermal-vias-under-a-qfn)).

**Why:** Molten solder flows over any bare copper it touches. With no mask between them, solder from the pad runs onto the via ring and down the hole, and the joint is left short of solder. A very thin web over a long run is hard for the fab to hold and may break away.

![D49: Drawn to scale, plan views of a 1.0 by 1.2 mm pad joined by a 0.25 mm trace to a via with a 0.3 mm hole and a 0.6 mm ring. Left: the via has its own mask opening, leaving a 0.15 mm web of mask between it and the pad. Middle: the via is tented. Right: the via's opening runs into the pad's, with no web between them.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/via-mask-web.svg)

*D49 is drawn to scale. On the left, pad and via each have their own mask opening, and a 0.15 mm web of mask separates them. In the middle, the via is tented, so only the pad is open. On the right, the openings run together: nothing stops solder flowing from the pad onto the via and down its hole.*

**Typical values:** Web at least 0.1 mm (4 mil) wide, and only over short distances at that width; wider is better.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Starved joints and solder balls on the far side of the board, which need rework.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [01:10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=4200)–01:13:00 and [01:20:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=4800)–01:22:00; [“Reflow soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6175423-reflow-soldering) (Nov 2020), [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6175423?t=2040)–35:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-034: Clear solder mask from non-plated holes by about 0.1 mm, with no thin ring left

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-034

**Recommendation:** Give every non-plated hole a mask opening about 0.1 mm (4 mil) larger than the hole all round. Don't leave a mask opening only a hair bigger than the hole.

**Why:** The fab drills the hole after the mask is on, and the drill and the mask never line up perfectly. A mask opening barely larger than the hole leaves a ring of mask about 0.025 mm wide that either gets drilled into, so mask chips into the hole, or is too thin to stay put.

![D53: Drawn to scale, plan views of a 3.2 mm non-plated hole. Left: the mask opening is 0.1 mm larger than the hole all round, leaving a thin ring of bare board. Right: the opening is only 0.025 mm larger, and with the drill 0.08 mm off center the drill cuts into the mask on one side, leaving chipped mask at the edge.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/npth-mask.svg)

*D53 is drawn to scale. On the left, the mask stops 0.1 mm short of the hole, so the drill never touches it. On the right, the opening is only a hair bigger than the hole; a drill slightly off center cuts into the mask on one side and leaves it chipped and flaking.*

**Typical values:** Mask clearance about 0.1 mm per side on non-plated holes. Copper is kept back from non-plated holes too (see [PCB-DFM-007](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfm-007-dont-put-copper-on-non-plated-holes)).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A query from the fab, or flaking mask in and around mounting holes.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=2460)–43:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-035: Expect the fab to trim pads to keep mask dams, and check what they changed

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-035

**Recommendation:** Expect the fab's CAM engineers to adjust your data so it can be built, most often by shaving a little off fine-pitch pads to keep the dam between them. Ask the fab to send you its questions and changes (an engineering query) before it builds, and check them, especially on a first order. If you plan to tighten mask registration, first ask whether the fab images its mask with a laser.

**Why:** The fab needs a little clearance between each pad and its mask opening, plus a dam between openings. When your pads are too close for both, it either trims the copper or drops the dam, and a dropped dam is worse (see [PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-032-put-a-solder-mask-dam-between-every-pad-of-a-fine-pitch-part)). Changes made in CAM are silent unless you ask to see them, and some (legend resized, pads trimmed, mask opened up) change what the assembler gets. Laser-imaged mask lines up more accurately than mask exposed through film, so it needs less clearance.

![D54: Enlarged and drawn to scale, plan views of three pads of a 0.4 mm-pitch part. Left: pads 0.25 mm wide, 0.15 mm apart, with openings 0.05 mm larger on each side leave a 0.05 mm dam, too thin to hold. Middle: the fab has made one opening round all three pads, with no dam. Right: pads 0.2 mm wide leave room for a 0.1 mm dam.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/dam-room.svg)

*D54 is enlarged and drawn to scale. A dam can only be so thin, so the pads must leave room for it. Pads drawn too wide for their pitch leave the fab two choices: trim the pads, as on the right, or remove the dam, as in the middle, which lets solder bridge from pad to pad. Draw the pads to leave room for the dam in the first place (see [PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-032-put-a-solder-mask-dam-between-every-pad-of-a-fine-pitch-part)).*

**Typical values:** About 0.05 mm (2 mil) between a pad and its mask opening on each side, leaving a dam of about 0.1 mm (4 mil); pads trimmed by tens of microns.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards that don't match your files, discovered at assembly.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=1800)–40:00; [“An EDA Tool Walks Into a CM w/ Fusion 360 Electronics Product Manager, Ben Jordan”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9171908-an-eda-tool-walks-into-a-cm-w-fusion-360-electronics-product-manager-ben-jordan) (Sep 2021), [54:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9171908?t=3240)–56:00 and [01:13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9171908?t=4380)–01:14:00; [“Gloves not Mittens”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842-gloves-not-mittens) (Jun 2026), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=1140)–21:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

### PCB-DFA-079: For BGAs, use copper-defined pads unless the part maker says otherwise

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-079

**Recommendation:** Draw BGA pads as copper-defined (non-solder-mask-defined, NSMD): the copper pad sets the size, and the mask opening is a little larger, so the mask doesn't touch the pad. Use mask-defined pads (the mask overlaps the copper and sets the opening) only where the BGA maker's land pattern calls for them, usually on the finest pitches. Say on the drawing which you've used.

**Why:** A copper pad's size is held by etching, which is more accurate than the mask's position, so every pad comes out the same. Solder wraps around the pad's sides as well as its top, which anchors the joint. Mask-defined pads hold their size by the mask, leave a notch where mask meets ball that can start cracks, but give the most even paste volume at very fine pitch, which is why some makers specify them.

![D50: Enlarged and drawn to scale, cross-sections through one ball of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA after reflow. Left, copper-defined: a 0.35 mm pad with the mask opening larger, so solder wraps round the pad's sides. Right, mask-defined: a 0.45 mm pad with the mask over its edge, leaving a 0.35 mm opening and a notch where mask meets solder.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/bga-pads.svg)

*D50 is enlarged and drawn to scale, with example sizes. On the left, the mask stands clear of a 0.35 mm copper pad, and the solder wraps round the pad's sides. On the right, the mask overlaps a 0.45 mm pad and sets a 0.35 mm opening; the solder meets the mask in a notch, where cracks can start.*

**Typical values:** Mask opening about 0.05–0.075 mm larger than the pad on each side; follow the BGA maker's land pattern where one is published.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Uneven joints across the array, or cracked joints in products that see heat cycling or shock.

**Applies to:** General practice; the part maker's land pattern wins.

**Sources:** BGA makers' land-pattern notes (two semiconductor makers' BGA application notes recommend NSMD pads); fabs' published BGA pad guidance. Not covered in the podcast.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFA-082: Join BGA and leadless pads to copper pours with a short trace, not straight into the pour

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-082

**Recommendation:** Where a pad of a BGA, QFN, DFN or other leadless part connects to a copper pour, keep the pour back from the pad and join them with a short, narrow trace, as you would a pad on its own. Don't let the pour run straight into the pad. This is the BGA and leadless-part version of [PCB-DFA-033](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-033-set-the-solder-mask-expansion-of-fine-pitch-pads-yourself) and D26.

**Why:** A pad inside a pour has no copper edge of its own: the mask opening sets its size instead. Every mask opening is a little larger than its pad, so pads tied into the pour come out bigger than their neighbors, and they sit wherever the mask lands rather than where the copper was etched. On a BGA or leadless part, every joint is under the part and can't be touched up, so those few oversized pads take more solder, pull the part off center, and leave neighboring joints thin. A pad joined by a short trace keeps its copper edge, so all the pads come out the same size.

![D55: Drawn to scale, plan views of the corner of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA with 0.35 mm pads and 0.45 mm mask openings on a ground pour. Left: three ground pads sit straight in the pour, so their whole openings show copper and they come out bigger than the rest. Right: the pour is kept back from every pad and each ground pad is joined to it by a 0.15 mm trace, so every pad shows the same copper.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/bga-pour.svg)

*D55 is drawn to scale. On the left, the ground pads sit straight in the pour, so the mask opening, not the copper, sets their size, and they come out bigger than their neighbors. On the right, a short trace joins each ground pad to the pour, and every pad is the same size.*

**Typical values:** Trace about 0.15–0.2 mm wide, or no wider than about half the pad; pour kept back from the pad by your usual clearance.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Uneven joints, opens or bridges under BGAs and leadless parts, found only by X-ray; it's one of the most common design flaws assemblers see.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** Chris Denney (author); [“Gloves not Mittens”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842-gloves-not-mittens) (Jun 2026), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=1260)–23:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*
