Source: https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/08-surface-finish/

## Surface finish

Bare copper tarnishes within days and then won't take solder. So every pad and hole left open by the solder mask gets a thin protective coat, the surface finish, just before the board is profiled and tested. The finish decides how flat the pads are, how long the boards keep, how well they solder, and part of the price.

| Finish | What it is | Flat enough for fine pitch? | How it ages | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ENIG | Electroless nickel with a thin immersion gold coat | Yes | Slowly: the thin, porous gold keeps the nickel from oxidizing | The common default; costs more than HASL; rare "black pad" defect if the fab's nickel process drifts |
| ENEPIG | ENIG with a palladium layer between nickel and gold | Yes | Like ENIG | For gold or aluminum wire bonding as well as soldering; less prone to black pad; costs more again |
| HASL, lead-free | Board dipped in molten solder, leveled with hot air | No: domed pads | Thin spots, such as hole edges, lose solderability first, typically in 6–12 months; the rest lasts one to two years | Cheapest; fine for through-hole and coarse surface-mount parts |
| OSP | A thin organic coat on bare copper | Yes | Fastest: check solderability after 6 months | Cheap and flat; easily damaged by handling, and weakened by each heat cycle |
| Immersion silver | A thin silver coat | Yes | Spoiled by sulfur and chlorine in the air; needs sulfur-absorbing paper in the bag | Flat; tarnishes if handled or stored badly |
| Immersion tin | A thin tin coat | Yes | Oxidizes relatively quickly, and tin-copper compounds grow through it whatever the packaging | Flat; tin whiskers are a further worry |
| Hard gold | Electroplated gold, hardened, over nickel | n/a | Slowly; thicker and less porous than ENIG | For contacts that slide or wear, such as edge fingers (see PCB-DFM-038); not for soldering |

How finishes age is from IPC-1602A (Nov 2024), section 4.1.3. Dry-packed boards keep at least 12 months, but IPC-1602A asks for a solderability check on boards stored longer than 6 months with OSP, or a year with any other finish.

### PCB-DFM-036: Always name the surface finish on the fabrication drawing

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-036

**Recommendation:** State the surface finish on the fabrication drawing and in the order, every time, even when you'd be happy with the fab's default. For ENIG, ENEPIG, immersion silver and immersion tin, citing the IPC finish standard (IPC-4552, IPC-4556, IPC-4553, IPC-4554) fixes the thicknesses too.

**Why:** Fabs and standards fill gaps with defaults, and those differ. IPC-6012F, the standard most fabs build to, says that if the finish isn't specified, drawings first released on or after 1 October 2023 get ENIG, and older drawings get "X": a solder coating or fused tin-lead. An old drawing reused without a finish can therefore legally come back with tin-lead on it.

**Typical values:** IPC-6012F Table 1-2 default: ENIG (drawings from 1 October 2023), "X" before that.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A finish you didn't expect, which may not suit your parts, your lead-free process or your price.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 1-2 and Table 3-3.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-037: Choose ENIG for most boards; lead-free HASL only for coarse pitch; OSP or immersion silver for high volume with tight process control

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-037

**Recommendation:** Use ENIG unless you have a reason to choose something else. Use lead-free HASL only on boards whose finest parts are about 0.65 mm pitch or 0603 and larger, with no BGAs or QFNs. Consider OSP or immersion silver for high volumes where the assembler controls handling, storage and time between steps closely. Choose ENEPIG for wire bonding, and hard gold only for contacts that wear.

**Why:** Small parts need flat pads: a domed HASL pad lets a tiny part tilt or a QFN rock, and makes paste printing uneven. ENIG is flat, solders well, and keeps for about a year sealed, which suits small batches that may wait between bare board and assembly. OSP and immersion silver are cheaper and flat, but much less forgiving: fingerprints, humidity and time all spoil them, and OSP weakens with every trip through the oven, which matters on double-sided boards.

**Typical values:** HASL: down to about 0.65 mm pitch and 0603. See the table above for shelf lives.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** With HASL on fine pitch, bridges, tombstones and open joints; with OSP stored too long or handled carelessly, poor wetting and open joints on the second side.

**Applies to:** General practice; prices and shelf lives vary by fab.

**Sources:** [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [01:14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=4440)–01:17:00; fabs' published surface-finish comparisons (flatness, shelf life, cost, black pad).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-038: Give edge-connector fingers hard gold and a bevel, with mask and legend kept off them

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-038

**Recommendation:** For fingers that plug into a card-edge connector, specify hard (electroplated) gold over nickel, and a bevel on the inserting edge. Keep solder mask and legend off the fingers, keep plated holes and other pads away from them, and round or chamfer the board corners beside them. Put the gold thickness, bevel angle and bevel depth on the fabrication drawing.

**Why:** Fingers slide in and out of a connector, and the soft, thin gold of ENIG wears through after a few insertions; hard gold is made for wear. A bevel lets the board slide into the connector instead of stubbing on its contacts. The fingers are plated through a strip that's removed at the edge, so the fab needs them to run cleanly to the edge with nothing else in the way.

![D52: Drawn to scale. Plan view of a board edge with six hard-gold fingers, 1.5 mm wide on a 2.54 mm pitch, ending 0.6 mm from the edge, with the solder mask cleared from the whole finger area and the corners beside them chamfered. Below, enlarged 2.5 times, a side view of the 1.6 mm board beveled at 30 degrees on both faces over the last 0.5 mm, with the fingers stopping before the bevel.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/gold-fingers.svg)

*D52 is drawn to scale, with the side view enlarged, and uses example sizes. The fingers are hard gold with no mask over them, and the board's corners beside them are chamfered. The inserting edge is beveled on both faces, and the fingers stop 0.6 mm short of the edge, clear of the bevel.*

**Typical values:** Hard gold at least 0.8 µm (Class 1–2) or 1.25 µm (Class 3) over at least 2.5 µm of nickel (IPC-6012F Table 3-3). Bevel 30° or 45°, commonly 30°, about 0.5–1.0 mm deep; keep other plated features about 1 mm from the fingers.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Fingers that wear through or scratch the connector, boards that won't insert cleanly, and fab queries about mask or holes in the plating area.

**Applies to:** General practice; bevel limits vary by fab.

**Sources:** IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 3-3; fabs' published edge-connector and gold-finger guidelines. Not covered in the podcast.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFA-080: Keep bare boards sealed, use them within the finish's shelf life, and expect a bake if they've taken on moisture

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-080

**Recommendation:** Expect bare boards to arrive dry-packed: heat-sealed in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a humidity indicator card, and only lightly evacuated, not vacuum-packed hard. Keep them sealed until assembly, and build them within a year (six months for OSP). Once a bag is opened, the boards should be built promptly, or go back into dry storage. If the bag was damaged, the card shows moisture, or the boards are older than that, tell the assembler, and expect them to be checked, dried in dry storage or baked just before assembly, or rejected. Don't ask the fab to bake boards before shipping. If your board is unusually sensitive to moisture (polyimide, or thick and many-layered), say so on the drawing; IPC-1602A leaves it to the designer or user to set how much moisture the board can tolerate.

**Why:** Laminate absorbs moisture from the air. In the reflow oven that moisture turns to steam and can blister or delaminate the board. Finishes age too, and solder wets an old finish poorly; dry packing slows the moisture but doesn't stop the finish aging. Squeezing all the air out of the bag stops the desiccant working, can warp boards and lets sharp corners puncture the bag. Baking drives the moisture out but ages the finish further, so it's done only when needed and as late as possible. A humidity card shows the air in the bag, not the moisture in the boards, so a card that has changed color after a short exposure doesn't always mean a bake: dry storage can be the safer fix.

**Typical values:** IPC-1602A, unless you specify otherwise: boards packed with no more than 0.2% moisture by weight, in a moisture barrier bag with desiccant and a three-spot humidity card (5%, 10%, 60% RH); this keeps them at least 12 months at up to 40 °C and 90% RH, and double-bagging at least two years. Check solderability after 6 months for OSP and 12 months for other finishes. An opened bag: boards into dry storage at 10% RH or less within an hour, or resealed with the same desiccant and card within 30 minutes. Handle boards by the edges, with clean gloves if needed. Immersion silver also needs sulfur-absorbing paper in the bag.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Blistered or delaminated boards, and poorly wetted joints, often found only after assembly.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [01:16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=4560)–01:17:00; IPC-1602A, Standard for Printed Board Handling and Storage (Nov 2024), sections 4.1–4.2 and 5.1–5.8; a European PCB industry association's recommendations on IPC-1601 (bake just before assembly, not at the fab).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

## Legend (silkscreen)

The legend is the printed text and outlines on the board: reference designators, polarity marks, part outlines, logos and labels. It used to be screen printed, which is why most people still call it silkscreen; today most fabs print it with an inkjet. Assemblers, inspectors and repair technicians all read it, so it's worth making it legible, accurate and out of the way of the solder. What to mark (pin 1, polarity, outlines) is in [Footprints and the component library](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/); this page is about how it's printed.

### PCB-DFM-039: Make legend text about 1 mm tall, with lines of 0.15 mm or more

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-039

**Recommendation:** Make legend text about 1 mm tall and 1 mm wide, with a line width of 0.18–0.2 mm. Don't go below 0.15 mm line width or about 0.8 mm text height. If text doesn't need to be small, don't make it small.

**Why:** The legend ink spreads and the printer has a resolution limit. Lines thinner than the fab's minimum are removed or come out broken, and small text fills in until it can't be read. Text sized generously costs nothing and is read by people at every step after.

**Typical values:** Line width 0.15 mm (6 mil) minimum, 0.18–0.2 mm recommended; text 1 mm tall, 0.8 mm minimum. Some fabs print down to 0.1 mm lines, but readability suffers below about 0.8 mm text.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Designators and marks that can't be read, so assembly and rework take longer and mistakes get through.

**Applies to:** General practice; minimums vary by fab and printing method.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [20:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=1200)–26:00; [“An overview of bare PCB fabrication w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663-an-overview-of-bare-pcb-fabrication-w-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2020), [56:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663?t=3360)–01:03:00; [“Mastering Vias: Plugging, Filling, and Best Practices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518-mastering-vias-plugging-filling-and-best-practices) (Nov 2024), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518?t=1680)–30:00; fabs' published legend minimums (0.1–0.15 mm lines, 0.8–1.0 mm text).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-040: Send only the legend you want printed, keep it off exposed copper, and expect the fab to clip and resize it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-040

**Recommendation:** Export only the legend layers you mean to print: no component value or name layers unless you want them on the board. Keep the legend off pads, exposed copper and holes, with a small clearance. Expect the fab's CAM engineers to clip legend that runs over pads, holes or off the board, and to resize text too small to print: lots of small legend edits are normal. They aim to keep it legible and printable, and they shouldn't move it; if they must, ask them to check with you first.

**Why:** Ink on a pad stops solder wetting it, so fabs clip any legend that crosses exposed copper. Legend can't print over a hole or past the board edge either. When a designator or polarity mark sits over copper, clipping can cut it in half, so place marks where they'll print whole. Some design tools export value and name layers by default, which crowds the board with text nobody asked for.

**Typical values:** About 0.1 mm clearance from exposed copper and holes.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Unreadable, clipped or missing marks, and a board that doesn't look like your design.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=1320)–24:00; [“An overview of bare PCB fabrication w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663-an-overview-of-bare-pcb-fabrication-w-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2020), [56:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6388663?t=3360)–01:03:00; fabs' published legend clearances.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFA-081: Leave legend out where it won't fit, but keep it complete in your data

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-081

**Recommendation:** Where the board is too dense for legible legend, such as around 0.4 mm-pitch BGAs or on very small boards, leave it off the printed board rather than squeezing it in. Keep every designator and mark complete and correct in your design data anyway, and put them on the assembly drawing. Check designators against the netlist and BOM, not by where the text happens to sit.

**Why:** Tiny legend can't be read and may be printed over pads. The assembler and inspector still need to know which part goes where and which way round, and an assembly drawing gives them that without printing it on the board. When designators are crowded, text drifts onto the wrong part, so only the data can be trusted.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Illegible marks, legend over pads, or the wrong part placed because a designator sat beside the wrong footprint.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=1740)–30:00; [“Mastering Vias: Plugging, Filling, and Best Practices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518-mastering-vias-plugging-filling-and-best-practices) (Nov 2024), [25:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16036518?t=1500)–29:30; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=2940)–52:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-045: Keep legend off vias, even tented ones

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-045

**Recommendation:** Place legend text and marks on flat solder mask, clear of vias. This applies to tented vias as well as open ones. If there's no other room, printing legend over tented vias is acceptable. Avoid printing legend over open vias, because the fab will clip it.

**Why:** A tented via is covered by a thin film of solder mask, and that film sags a little into the hole. Legend printed across the via follows the dip, so the character comes out slightly distorted. It still prints and is usually legible, and a small mark such as a dot works fine. An open via is different. Legend can't print over a hole, and the fab keeps it back from exposed copper (PCB-DFM-040). So the fab cuts the legend away around every open via, and a designator printed across a row of them is cut into pieces.

**Typical values:** Over tented vias, legend can come right up to the via, or even cross it: 0 mm is acceptable. Over open vias, keep legend back from the exposed copper by the fab's clearance, which is about 0.1 mm (PCB-DFM-040). The recommended position is on flat mask, clear of every via.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Over tented vias, designators and marks that look uneven and are harder to read. Over open vias, designators clipped into pieces or removed.

**Applies to:** General practice. Whether a via is tented is set by your data and fab notes (PCB-DFM-030).

**Sources:** [“Small PCB layout decisions that have a significant impact on assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623-small-pcb-layout-decisions-that-have-a-significant-impact-on-assembly) (Aug 2021), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8957623?t=780)–14:00; Chris Denney (author); [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=1320)–24:00.

![D68: Drawn to scale, three plan views of a 0603 resistor, R7, with three vias. Left: the designator sits beside the part on flat mask. Middle: the designator is printed across tented vias. Right: the vias are open and the designator is clipped around them. Below, an enlarged cross-section of a legend line across a tented via: the mask sags into the hole and the ink follows it.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/legend-over-vias.svg)

*D68 is drawn to scale. On the left, the designator sits on flat mask beside the part and prints cleanly. In the middle, it is printed across tented vias: it prints, but the ink dips into each via, so the characters come out wavy and thinner there. On the right, the vias are open, so the fab clips the legend back from their copper and the designator is cut into pieces. The enlarged cross-section below shows why the middle case is distorted: the mask sags into the hole, and the legend ink follows it down.*

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-127: Turn legend text so it reads from only two edges of the board

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-127

**Recommendation:** Keep all horizontal designators and labels the same way round, reading left to right. Where text has to turn 90° to fit, turn all of it the same way. Reading from bottom to top is the most common choice. It matches engineering drawings, where text reads from the bottom or the right-hand side of the sheet, and it's what a 90° turn gives in most design tools. Then a person can read the whole board while holding it in one of only two ways: square on, or turned a quarter turn. Avoid text that reads upside down, or that reads from top to bottom. Bottom-side legend follows the same rule, as seen with the board turned over.

**Why:** Assemblers, inspectors and repair technicians read designators all day. If the text faces all four directions, they have to keep turning the board, which is slow and handles it more. Text read upside down is easy to misread, and some characters such as 6 and 9 swap meaning. Turning a designator to match its part doesn't help, because a person matches a designator to its part by position, not by angle.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Slower assembly, inspection and rework, and more misread designators.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** Chris Denney (author); published silkscreen design guides, which recommend only 0° and 90° text, read from the bottom or right edge of the board; engineering drawing practice (the aligned system, with text read from the bottom or right-hand side).

![D69: Drawn to scale, two copies of the same area of a board with eight 0603 parts, some horizontal and some vertical. Left: horizontal designators read left to right and vertical ones read bottom to top, so the board reads from the bottom and right edges. Right: designators face all four ways, some upside down, so the board must be turned to all four sides.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/legend-orientation.svg)

*D69 is drawn to scale. On the left, every horizontal designator reads from the bottom edge, and every vertical one reads from the right edge. A person only ever holds the board one of two ways. On the right, the same designators face all four ways, so the board has to be turned to every side to read them.*

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-128: Use a callout box where parts are packed too tightly for their designators

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-128

**Recommendation:** Where a group of parts is packed too tightly to fit a designator beside each one, draw a legend box round the group. Then draw a second box nearby, as a map of the group. In the map, put each designator in the same position as its part, turned the same way. Make the map larger than the group, so the designators can be 1 mm tall (PCB-DFM-039). Put it as close to the group as you can, on the same side of the board. Join the two boxes with a legend line. Make the line as straight as you can, and where it has to bend, use 45° and 90° bends. If there's no room for a map either, leave the designators off and put them on the assembly drawing (PCB-DFA-081).

**Why:** Groups of small parts, such as decoupling capacitors round a chip, often leave no room for their designators. Designators squeezed in between the parts end up on pads, where the fab clips them, or beside the wrong part. A callout box keeps every designator on the board and legible. A person finds a part by matching its position in the group to the same position in the map. The line between the boxes shows which map belongs to which group, which matters when a board has several.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Designators clipped, unreadable or next to the wrong part, or left off the board, so everyone has to work from the assembly drawing.

**Applies to:** Dense areas, such as decoupling capacitors beside a BGA or QFN, or parts on the back of a BGA.

**Sources:** Chris Denney (author); published silkscreen design guides, which show designators grouped in a box and arranged to match the parts.

![D70: Drawn to scale, a QFN, U3, with eight 0402 capacitors packed 0.25 mm apart beside it. A legend box surrounds the capacitors. Beside it, a larger legend box holds their designators, C11 to C18, each in the same position and orientation as its capacitor, and a straight legend line joins the two boxes.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/legend-callout-box.svg)

*D70 is drawn to scale. The eight capacitors beside U3 are 0.25 mm apart, so there's no room for a designator beside each one. A box round the group marks them, and the larger box beside it is a map: each designator sits where its capacitor sits in the group, and is turned the same way. A straight legend line joins the two boxes.*

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

## Profiling: routing, scoring, slots and cut-outs

Profiling cuts the board to shape: its outline, internal slots and cut-outs, and any special edges. Most of it is done with a spinning router bit, so every cut has the bit's width and every inside corner its radius. How boards are joined in the panel and broken out of it (V-score, tabs and mouse bites) is in [Part 2: The panel](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/03-breakaway-methods/); this page is about the shape of each board.

### PCB-DFM-041: Draw the outline, slots and cut-outs as closed shapes on one layer

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-041

**Recommendation:** Draw the board outline, and every internal slot and cut-out, as closed shapes on one mechanical layer, and send that layer as its own file. Put nothing else on that layer. Draw plated slots in the drill data, not as outline.

**Why:** CAM builds the router path from the outline layer. Gaps, overlapping lines, dimensions or a title block on that layer make it guess where the edge is. A slot drawn only on a copper or legend layer may never be cut at all.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Fab queries and delay, or a slot or cut-out missing from the finished board.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** Fabs' published outline and Gerber guidelines; the Gerber format's guidance on profile layers. Not covered in the podcast.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-042: Allow for the router: a radius in every inside corner and slots at least 1 mm wide

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-042

**Recommendation:** Give every inside corner a radius of at least half the router bit's width, and design for 1 mm unless you need tighter. Make routed slots at least 1 mm wide. If a part needs a square inside corner, ask the fab for a smaller bit or draw small relief cut-outs at the corner.

**Why:** A round bit can't cut a sharp inside corner: it leaves a radius equal to its own. Fabs route outlines with bits about 2 mm in diameter, which leaves a 1 mm radius, and use smaller bits on request at extra time and risk of breakage. A slot can't be narrower than the bit that cuts it.

![D51: Drawn to scale, plan view of part of a board. A 10 by 6 mm cut-out routed with a 2 mm bit has a 1 mm radius in every inside corner, with the bit drawn in one corner. A slot 1 mm wide has round ends. A cut-out for a square 8 by 6 mm part has a round relief at each corner so the part's corners fit.](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/images/router-corners.svg)

*D51 is drawn to scale. A 2 mm router bit leaves a 1 mm radius in every inside corner of a cut-out, and a slot can't be narrower than the bit. Where a square part must drop into a cut-out, a small round relief at each corner makes room for the part's square corners.*

**Typical values:** Inside corner radius 1 mm with a standard 2 mm bit; about 0.5 mm with a 1 mm bit, on request. Routed slot at least 1 mm wide; non-plated slots 1 mm, plated slots from about 0.5 mm at some fabs. Routed edge tolerance about ±0.1 mm; V-scored edges are looser.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A rectangular part that won't drop into its cut-out, a board that doesn't fit its enclosure, or a fab query.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

**Sources:** [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612?t=2040); [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [01:07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=4020); fabs' published routing minimums (0.4–0.5 mm smallest inside radius, 0.8–1.0 mm smallest slot, ±0.1–0.15 mm).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFM-043: Dimension castellations, edge plating, countersinks and bevels on the drawing, and expect them to cost more

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-043

**Recommendation:** Treat any edge feature beyond a plain routed edge as a special: castellated (half-cut plated) holes, plated edges, countersunk or counterbored holes, and bevels. Show and dimension each one on the fabrication drawing, mention it when you order, and expect extra cost and lead time. If the feature is unusual, talk to the fab and assembler with a sketch before you commit the design.

**Why:** Each one needs an extra process step: castellations are drilled and plated, then routed through the middle of the holes; edge plating is plated before routing; countersinks are cut with a separate tool. None of them shows clearly in Gerber data, so a fab that isn't told may simply route a plain edge.

**Typical values:** Castellated holes about 0.8 mm finished (0.5 mm the usual minimum) with 1.5 mm pads, at least 0.6 mm apart. Countersinks: give the angle (82° or 90° are common) and the top diameter.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Features left off or built wrong, half-holes that tear their plating out, or a quote that changes after you order.

**Example:** An open-source wrist-worn heart-rate monitor needed a notch to hold a watch band's spring pin, with no work after assembly. The designer used a castellated hole as the notch, with a zero-ohm resistor on each side to trap the pin. They talked it through with the assembler first, with drawings, to settle how close to the castellation the resistors could sit.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

**Sources:** [“How Joel Murphy went from visual artist to electronics design engineer”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659-how-joel-murphy-went-from-visual-artist-to-electronics-design-engineer) (Oct 2020), [01:16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659?t=4560)–01:19:00; fabs' published castellation, edge-plating and countersink guidelines.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

- [Edge clearance](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/)
- [Fabrication data](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/11-bare-board-test/

## Bare board electrical test and inspection

Before boards leave the fab, they're tested for opens and shorts and inspected against the standard they were built to. This is the last chance to catch a fault before parts are soldered on, when finding it becomes far more expensive. The assembler's own inspection checks its soldering and parts, not the bare board's copper.

### PCB-DFT-002: Have every bare board electrically tested against your netlist

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-002

**Recommendation:** Ask for 100% electrical test of every bare board, against the netlist you supplied (see [PCB-DFM-009](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/01-fabrication-data/#pcb-dfm-009-always-send-a-netlist-made-from-the-same-revision-as-the-gerbers)). Expect a flying-probe test for prototypes and small batches, and a fixture (bed of nails) for large, repeat orders.

**Why:** Electrical test finds opens and shorts in the copper, including faults hidden on inner layers and in plated holes. Tested against your netlist rather than a netlist the fab extracted from your Gerbers, it also catches a Gerber that doesn't match the design. Assembly inspection can't do this: it looks at parts and solder joints, and assumes the bare board is right. A hole the plating missed, for example, fails electrical test at the fab instead of failing in the field.

**Typical values:** Flying probe: no tooling, slower per board. Fixture: tooling cost and a few days to build, then fast.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A short or open found only after assembly, when the board is full of parts and the fault is much harder to find and fix.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB CAM Process w/ Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431-the-pcb-cam-process-w-dave-wilcox) (Mar 2021), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8226431?t=720)–19:00; [“Outer Layer Imaging w/ CAM Engineer Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857-outer-layer-imaging-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (Nov 2022), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11724857?t=1080); [“Automated Optical Inspection (AOI) for PCB Assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753-automated-optical-inspection-aoi-for-pcb-assembly) (Nov 2020), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753?t=240); [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=540)–11:00; fabs' published electrical-test guidance (IPC-D-356 netlists, flying probe and fixture).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFT-003: Ask for IPC Class 2 unless the product needs Class 3, and know Class 3 is a design standard too

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-003

**Recommendation:** Build to IPC Class 2, which suits nearly all products, unless the product's use truly needs Class 3 (high reliability: medical life support, aerospace, some automotive and military). If you do need Class 3, design for it from the start, not only at ordering, and call out the class instead of writing your own acceptance criteria.

**Why:** The IPC classes set what's acceptable in the bare board (IPC-6012) and the assembly (IPC-A-610): annular ring, plating thickness, solder fillets and much more. Class 3 limits are tighter, so they cost more to make and inspect, and some can only be met if the design allows them: a Class 3 annular ring needs pads big enough for it, for example. Ordering Class 3 for a board designed to Class 2 doesn't make it a Class 3 product.

**Typical values:** Class 1, simple products, about 5% of what's built; Class 2, about 90%; Class 3, the rest, at a much higher cost (one estimate: ten times or more).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Paying far more than you need to, or ordering Class 3 for a design that can't meet it and getting rejects or waivers.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=1020)–20:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=2940)–51:00; [“How IPC helps the global manufacturing ecosystem build electronics better w/ Teresa Rowe and Patrick Crawford”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10444705-how-ipc-helps-the-global-manufacturing-ecosystem-build-electronics-better-w-teresa-rowe-and-patrick-crawford) (Apr 2022), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10444705?t=420)–11:00; IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), Table 3-7.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

---

### PCB-DFT-004: For boards that matter, ask for the fab's evidence

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-004

**Recommendation:** For Class 3 boards, impedance-controlled boards and anything safety-critical, ask the fab to ship its evidence with the boards: a certificate of conformance, the electrical test result, the impedance test report where it applies, and cross-sections (microsections) of test coupons for Class 3. Write what you need on the fabrication drawing or purchase order, so it's quoted from the start.

**Why:** A pass label on its own doesn't say what was tested, against which netlist, or to which limits. A cross-section of a coupon cut from the same panel shows the plating thickness in the holes and the layer build, which no electrical test can. Asking up front costs little; asking after the boards have shipped usually can't be done.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** No proof the boards meet the drawing when a customer, auditor or failure investigation asks for it.

**Applies to:** General practice; report formats vary by fab.

**Sources:** IPC-6012F (Sept 2023), quality conformance testing and coupons; fabs' published electrical-test and quality documents. Not covered in the podcast.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-08*

## Choosing parts that can be bought and built

Every part on your schematic has to be bought, delivered and fitted, possibly for years. A part that's perfect on paper but sold by one maker, stocked by one distributor or near the end of its life can hold up a whole build. This page is about choosing parts with the supply chain and the factory in mind. Package size, footprints and reflow ratings are covered in Part 5 and Part 1.4; links are at the end.

### PCB-DFA-083: Choose parts that are active, widely stocked, and made by more than one maker where you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-083

**Recommendation:** When you choose a part, check three things as well as its electrical fit:
- its lifecycle status is active (not "not recommended for new designs", last-time-buy or obsolete);
- several authorized distributors stock it in quantity;
- for anything but a truly special part, an equivalent exists from another maker.

Check these when you choose the part, not only when you release the BOM ([PCB-DFA-070](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/)). Before moving from prototype to production, look again at any part that was easy to find in tens but may not be in thousands.

**Why:** Parts stocked widely, by more than one maker, keep shipping when one source runs short. A specialty part can carry a lead time of weeks where a mainstream equivalent ships the same day. Parts reused from an old design, or an old library, may already be at the end of their life when the board reaches manufacturing. Distributors sell in small quantities; buying straight from a maker often means minimum orders of thousands.

**Typical values:** Minimum: active, and in stock at two or more authorized distributors. Recommended: also available from a second maker, or listed in a common-parts library chosen for deep supply.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A build held for weeks waiting for one part, or a redesign when it can't be bought at all.

**Example:** For a 200-unit build, an assembler found that only about 204 of one pressure sensor existed in stock anywhere. A simple 4-pin, 0.1 in header from a specialty maker had a two-week lead time, while equivalents from other makers shipped at once.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-1) (Jul 2020), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=2460) and [57:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=3420)–59:00; [“Discussing the Global Electronics Parts Shortage w/ Digi-Key”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8574130-discussing-the-global-electronics-parts-shortage-w-digi-key) (May 2021), [42:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8574130?t=2520); [“The importance of having different perspectives in engineering w/ Eli Hughes of Tzero Labs (Part 2)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7118017-the-importance-of-having-different-perspectives-in-engineering-w-eli-hughes-of-tzero-labs-part-2) (Jan 2021), [48:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7118017?t=2880)–51:00; [“The role of electronic components distributors w/ Digi-key”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8655719-the-role-of-electronic-components-distributors-w-digi-key) (Jun 2021), [14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8655719?t=840).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-084: For parts at risk of shortage, give the board a way to take an alternate

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-084

**Recommendation:** For a part that's scarce, single-source or has been short before, plan an alternate into the layout:
1. First choice: an alternate in the same package and pinout, listed on the BOM ([PCB-DFA-069](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/)), so the board doesn't change at all.
2. If the alternate comes in a different package: use an overlapping footprint only where the part maker publishes one, and name the package you want fitted on the BOM.
3. If the two can't overlap: draw both footprints side by side and mark the one not fitted as DNP (do not place).

**Why:** A board that already accepts a second part can be built from whatever is in stock, without a new revision. Some makers sell the same chip in packages of different sizes with the same pinout, and publish a layout that takes either: a tiny leadless package placed inside the footprint of a leaded one, with each pin joined to its partner by a short trace, as in D57. An overlapping footprint leaves pads unused whichever package is fitted, so the assembler needs to know which package to cut the stencil for. Drawing your own overlap risks pads too close together, the wrong pitch, and bridges.

![D57: Drawn to scale, plan views. Left: a SOT-23-6 footprint with six pads 0.6 by 1.1 mm on a 0.95 mm pitch, in two rows 2.5 mm apart; in the space between the rows sit the six pads of a 1.0 by 0.8 mm leadless package, each joined to the SOT-23 pad beside it by a short trace under the mask. Right: a SOT-23-6 footprint labeled U1 and an SC-70-6 footprint labeled U2 side by side; the BOM fits one and marks the other DNP.](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/images/dual-footprint.svg)

*D57 is drawn to scale, with example pad sizes. On the left, either package fits one footprint, the way some part makers publish it; on the right, two footprints share the same nets and only one is fitted.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A board respin, or a long wait, when the one part it accepts runs out.

**Example:** One designer used an op-amp sold in both SC-70 and SOT-23 packages, and set the board up to take either, so the assembler could fit whichever was in stock.

**Applies to:** General practice; most useful for parts with a history of shortages.

**Sources:** [“How Joel Murphy went from visual artist to electronics design engineer”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659-how-joel-murphy-went-from-visual-artist-to-electronics-design-engineer) (Oct 2020), [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659?t=3120)–53:00; [“When to use through hole vs surface mount components”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410-when-to-use-through-hole-vs-surface-mount-components) (Jul 2021), [39:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410?t=2340)–42:00; a chip maker's application note on dual-footprint layouts (leaded and leadless packages, 2023); Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-085: In production, use the original maker's part on reel, not hobby modules or reseller strips

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-085

**Recommendation:** For anything you'll build in quantity, find the original maker and part number behind a hobby-market product, and buy that part on a reel. Avoid breakout boards, individually bagged modules, and parts sold in short strips by hobby resellers. If a module has no alternative, buy a reel of it yourself and consign it ([PCB-DFA-100](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/05-consignment-and-spares/)).

**Why:** Hobby resellers repackage parts in small bags or strips of ten, which can't be fed to a machine without loading every strip by hand. The original maker's part comes on continuous tape and costs far less in quantity. Hobby products are often hard for a business to buy through normal channels, or have no published maker at all.

**Typical values:** Loading a strip of ten takes 20–60 seconds; a reel of 1,000 or more runs without stopping.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Hours of extra set-up on a large order, a handling charge for every strip, and parts that cost several times more than they need to.

**Example:** A customer specified addressable RGB LEDs sold in strips of ten and needed thousands. The assembler traced the original part, found it on reels of 1,000, and the reel worked out roughly 70% cheaper after shipping.

**Applies to:** General practice; matters most above a few dozen boards.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-1) (Jul 2020), [47:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=2820)–50:00 and [50:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=3000)–51:00; [“The RGB LED Dilemma in Manufacturing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846-the-rgb-led-dilemma-in-manufacturing) (Sep 2024), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846?t=240)–13:00 and [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846?t=960).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-086: Check that board-mount connectors suit your board thickness and the product

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-086

**Recommendation:** For every connector and mechanical part that grips or passes through the board, check its datasheet for the board thickness it's made for, and choose the version that matches your stack-up. Check too that the part is rated for the job: current, mating cycles, temperature, and any approval the product needs (medical, automotive, life-safety).

**Why:** Mid-mount connectors, through-hole tabs, press-fit pins and snap-in parts are designed around one board thickness, often 1.6 mm, sometimes 0.8 mm or 1.0 mm. On a thicker board the tabs don't come through far enough to solder; on a thinner one the part sits at the wrong height or rocks. Two parts that look identical can carry very different ratings.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Connectors that can't be soldered properly or sit crooked, found at first assembly; or a product that fails its approval because one part wasn't rated for it.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Benefits of intrusive soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130-benefits-of-intrusive-soldering) (Jun 2022), [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=1560); [“How Joel Murphy went from visual artist to electronics design engineer”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659-how-joel-murphy-went-from-visual-artist-to-electronics-design-engineer) (Oct 2020), [48:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659?t=2880)–52:00; connector makers' datasheets (mid-mount USB-C receptacles sold per board thickness).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-087: For LEDs and other parts sold in bins, choose the bin, or test each bin and say how to handle it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-087

**Recommendation:** Where brightness or color matters, order the LED with a named bin in its part number, if the maker offers one. If not, get samples from several bins, test them in your circuit, and give the assembler what to do for each bin (for example, which current-limiting resistor to fit). Don't bother for indicator LEDs where brightness doesn't matter.

**Why:** LEDs are sorted after manufacture into bins of brightness and color, and each reel carries a bin code. Two reels of the same part number can look noticeably different side by side.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Products whose LEDs don't match each other, or vary from one batch to the next.

**Example:** A designer whose product depended on LED brightness bought samples of each bin, found the right resistor for each on a breadboard, and gave the assembler a table of bin to resistor.

**Applies to:** LEDs and other parts sold in bins, where appearance or behavior depends on them.

**Sources:** [“How Joel Murphy went from visual artist to electronics design engineer”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659-how-joel-murphy-went-from-visual-artist-to-electronics-design-engineer) (Oct 2020), [53:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659?t=3180)–55:00; LED makers' binning and labeling documents.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-088: Don't name a brand of solder, flux or other process material unless the product needs it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-088

**Recommendation:** Specify process materials by type and standard (for example, "no-clean, lead-free, SAC305, per J-STD-004 and J-STD-006"), not by brand and product name, unless a qualification or customer requirement forces a particular one. If you must name one, list an approved alternative too.

**Why:** Named products are discontinued, reformulated or go out of stock, often after a company is bought. The assembler then can't build to your drawing without your sign-off, and a qualified product may need requalifying.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A build held while you approve a substitute, or the cost of requalifying a process.

**Example:** A government drawing named one flux-core solder wire, which was later discontinued; separately, a favored solder paste disappeared after its maker was acquired.

**Applies to:** General practice; products with a qualified process may have to name a material.

**Sources:** [“The nitty gritty details on solder”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11129008-the-nitty-gritty-details-on-solder) (Aug 2022), [42:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11129008?t=2520)–43:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

## Packaging: reels, cut tape, tubes, trays

Surface-mount parts reach the machine in one of four ways: on a reel of carrier tape, on a cut length of that tape, in a plastic tube, or in a tray. How a part is packaged decides how fast and how reliably it can be placed, and sometimes what it costs. The same part is often sold in more than one packaging, under part numbers that differ by a single character. For supplying your own parts in the right packaging, see [Supplying your own parts](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/05-consignment-and-spares/).

### PCB-DFA-089: Choose tape and reel, and use tubes only as a last resort

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-089

**Recommendation:** Choose parts sold on tape and reel. Treat tubes as a last resort, after every other option is exhausted: a tape-and-reel version of the same part, an equivalent part on tape, or a re-taping service at the distributor. Pay a little more for a part on tape rather than design in one that only comes in tubes. Large or delicate chips in trays are fine. On the BOM, give the maker's full part number including the packaging code (often a suffix such as R for reel or T for tube), so the right packaging is bought.

**Why:** Assemblers like tubes less than any other packaging. Some assemblers, Worthington Assembly among them, are asking component makers to stop using tubes altogether. Carrier tape feeds one pocket at a time, holds thousands of parts per reel, and can only be loaded one way round. Tubes hold far fewer parts, feed by vibration and gravity, and jam more often, even on the best feeders. A tube is symmetrical, so it can be loaded backwards. Its rigid ends puncture moisture barrier bags, and it's too long for most drying ovens. Parts sold only in tubes are often sent to a specialist to be re-taped before they can run well, which adds cost and time.

**Typical values:** A tube holds about 50–100 parts; a reel of the same part, about 2,500. Tape from 8 mm to 24 mm wide is asymmetrical and can't be loaded backwards; wider tape marks its sides with different sprocket holes.

![D56: Four panels, not to the same scale. Carrier tape 8 mm wide, enlarged and drawn to scale, with sprocket holes along one edge every 4 mm, pockets every 4 mm holding chip parts lying across the tape under a clear cover tape, and empty pockets at the leading end as leader, with an arrow for the direction of feed. A 178 mm reel with tape coming off it. A tube about 500 mm long holding a row of SOIC chips, with a stopper in each end. A tray about 323 by 136 mm with a grid of pockets, each holding a large chip with pin 1 the same way.](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/images/packaging-types.svg)

*D56 shows the four ways parts arrive, not to the same scale. Carrier tape has sprocket holes along one edge only, so it can only be loaded one way; on a full reel from the maker, the pockets at the leading end, which goes into the feeder first, are left empty as leader. A tube holds 50–100 parts and looks the same from either end; a tray is for large or delicate chips.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Slower builds, more stoppages, extra handling charges, and the occasional batch of parts placed backwards from a reversed tube.

**Example:** A tube loaded backwards into a feeder put a run of parts on the board the wrong way round, and every one had to be reworked.

**Applies to:** General practice. Tubes do have one advantage: they hold heavy through-hole parts by the body, so the leads don't bend.

**Sources:** [“Stick It Up Your Tube”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259-stick-it-up-your-tube) (Jan 2024), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259?t=240)–05:00 and [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259?t=600)–20:00 and [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259?t=1800)–36:00 and [38:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259?t=2280)–40:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1080)–19:00; [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=1440)–26:00; EIA-481 (tape and reel packaging of surface-mount parts).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-090: Choose connectors packaged for machine placement: on tape, with a flat top or a pick-up cap

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-090

**Recommendation:** For surface-mount and hybrid connectors, choose a version supplied on tape and reel with a flat area for the machine's vacuum nozzle: either a flat top on the body, or a pick-up cap or polyimide (Kapton) pad fitted by the maker. Check the order code: the cap or pad is often a separate option, sold under its own suffix.

**Why:** Placement machines pick parts with a vacuum nozzle, which needs a flat, solid surface near the part's center of mass. Many connectors have open tops, slots or pins where a nozzle can't seal. Some machines have grippers that can pick a part with no flat area, and an assembler can 3D-print a custom tray for loose parts, load it by hand and let the machine place from it. Both work, but grippers are slower and harder to set up than vacuum nozzles, and a custom tray takes time to design, print and load, all of which adds cost. Otherwise, the connector is fitted by hand.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Connectors placed by hand, slowly and less accurately, or a machine that drops them.

**Example:** On one product, electrically identical connectors differed greatly in how quickly and accurately they could be placed, depending only on how they were packaged.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How Loci Controls automates landfill methane gas collection”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5509702-how-loci-controls-automates-landfill-methane-gas-collection) (Sep 2020), [59:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5509702?t=3540)–01:00:00; connector makers' tape-and-reel options with pick-up caps and polyimide pads.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

Source: https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/03-moisture-sensitive-parts/

## Moisture-sensitive parts

Plastic packages absorb moisture from the air. In the reflow oven, which runs far above the boiling point of water, that moisture turns to steam and can crack the package or lift it apart inside ("popcorning"). Each part's moisture sensitivity level (MSL) says how long it can be out of its sealed bag before it has to be soldered or baked. The assembler manages the clock, but the designer chooses the parts, and anyone who holds or sends in their own stock shares the job. The standards are J-STD-020, which sets a part's level, and J-STD-033, which says how to store, bake and use it.

### PCB-DFA-091: Put each part's moisture sensitivity level on the BOM, from its datasheet

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-091

**Recommendation:** Look up every plastic surface-mount part's MSL in its datasheet or the maker's product page, not the bag or a distributor's listing. Give the BOM an MSL column, so the assembler sees the level of every part. Flag anything at MSL 3 or higher, and parts known to be moisture-sensitive even if they aren't labeled that way (some LEDs, for example).

**Why:** Nearly any part that isn't hermetically sealed can take on moisture. The maker's rating is the authority; packaging and listings are sometimes wrong. The assembler can only plan exposure times and baking for parts it knows about. It's very rare for a customer to say which parts are moisture-sensitive, so assemblers usually have to look up every one themselves; an MSL column on the BOM is the easiest way to hand them that information.

**Typical values:** Most chips are rated MSL 3 or higher. MSL 1 parts need no special handling; MSL 2 and above are shipped in sealed bags with desiccant.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts that crack or delaminate in reflow, sometimes without failing until later in the field.

**Example:** A customer sent in moisture-sensitive LEDs in ordinary packaging, with no warning; they were reflowed as received and damaged.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How to Manage Moisture Sensitive Devices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014-how-to-manage-moisture-sensitive-devices) (May 2022), [20:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=1200) and [37:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=2220)–39:00; [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=2160)–38:00; IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020 and J-STD-033.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-092: Prefer a lower moisture level when you have the choice, and remember a double-sided build uses one floor life for both sides

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-092

**Recommendation:** When two parts would do, choose the one with the lower MSL. Avoid MSL 5, 5a and 6 parts unless there's no alternative, and tell your assembler early if you use one. On a double-sided board, plan for both sides being built within one floor life.

**Why:** Floor life is the time a part can spend in factory air, after its bag is opened, before it's soldered. It's set at 30 °C and 60% relative humidity; warmer or damper air shortens it. The clock runs until the part's last reflow, so building the first side doesn't reset it for the second. Short floor lives force small batches, careful scheduling, or a bake.

**Typical values:** Floor life at up to 30 °C and 60% RH, from J-STD-033:

| MSL | Floor life |
|---|---|
| 1 | Unlimited (at up to 85% RH) |
| 2 | 1 year |
| 2a | 4 weeks |
| 3 | 168 hours (1 week) |
| 4 | 72 hours |
| 5 | 48 hours |
| 5a | 24 hours |
| 6 | Bake before use, then solder within the time on the label |

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Builds scheduled around one part's clock, extra baking, and higher cost.

**Example:** An assembler building double-sided boards with MSL 5a parts ran them in batches of 50–100 on trays, so both sides could be reflowed within 24 hours of opening the bag.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How to Manage Moisture Sensitive Devices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014-how-to-manage-moisture-sensitive-devices) (May 2022), [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=1800)–36:00; IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033, Table 1 (floor life), as quoted in a chip maker's application reports (2017, 2018).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-093: Expect cheap addressable RGB LEDs and similar parts to need baking, and budget for it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-093

**Recommendation:** If you use low-cost addressable RGB LEDs, or other parts known to soak up moisture, expect your assembler to bake them before reflow, even when they arrive sealed. Allow for the extra time and cost, or choose a more expensive part that doesn't need it.

**Why:** These LEDs absorb moisture readily, and their packaging often doesn't keep it out. Baking is an extra step outside the normal flow. Damage from moisture can be intermittent: a small delamination opens when the part warms up and closes again when it cools.

**Typical values:** A low-cost addressable LED can cost a quarter of an equivalent from a mainstream maker; part of the difference comes back as baking.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** LEDs that burn out after reflow, or boards that pass a short test and fail in the field.

**Example:** LED matrix boards passed a 30-second bench test, then failed in the sun; the heat opened small delaminations that closed again once the boards cooled.

**Applies to:** Addressable RGB LEDs and other parts with a known moisture problem.

**Sources:** [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=2940); [“The RGB LED Dilemma in Manufacturing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846-the-rgb-led-dilemma-in-manufacturing) (Sep 2024), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846?t=420)–09:00; [“How to Manage Moisture Sensitive Devices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014-how-to-manage-moisture-sensitive-devices) (May 2022), [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=960)–18:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-094: Keep your own moisture-sensitive stock sealed, and let your assembler bake anything that's been exposed

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-094

**Recommendation:** If you hold moisture-sensitive parts yourself:
- after taking parts out, reseal the bag within the hour with fresh desiccant and a humidity indicator card, ideally with a heat sealer;
- push the air out, but don't vacuum-seal tight;
- use bags made for electronics that block both moisture and static;
- if a bag stays open longer than an hour, write on it the date and time it was opened, and how long it was out;
- keep opened bags from being punctured (tube ends and sharp reel edges are the usual cause).

If the humidity card shows the parts have been exposed, don't bake them yourself: send them as they are and tell your assembler.

**Why:** A bag opened briefly and resealed straight away doesn't start the floor-life clock: J-STD-033 lets short exposures, in air no worse than 30 °C and 60% RH, be dried out again by the desiccant in a sealed bag or a dry cabinet. This is how distributors split large packages into smaller ones without logging the few minutes the parts were out. After more than an hour in factory air, resealing doesn't necessarily stop the clock: dry storage pauses or resets it only within the limits in the table below, and beyond them only a bake resets it. The desiccant needs some air in the bag to draw moisture from the parts. Plain static bags don't block moisture, and some moisture bags aren't made for electronics. Some humidity cards change back once they dry out, so a card that looks safe may not be. Baking needs the right temperature and time for each part's level and thickness. Reels and tubes can't go above 40 °C, where a bake takes days or weeks; only trays rated for it can go in at 125 °C.

![D60: Not to scale. A moisture barrier bag heat-sealed across the top, holding a reel of parts, a desiccant pouch and a humidity indicator card with three spots marked 60%, 10% and 5%, all blue (dry). A caution label on the outside reads: moisture-sensitive, level 3, floor life 168 hours at up to 30 °C and 60% RH, with the bag seal date.](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/images/moisture-bag.svg)

*D60 shows what goes in a moisture barrier bag, not to scale. The heat seal, fresh desiccant and humidity card keep the parts dry; the caution label gives the level, the floor life and the date the bag was sealed.*

**Typical values:** For parts that have been out in air no worse than 30 °C and 60% RH (J-STD-033D Table 4-3):

| MSL | Time out of the bag | What restores the floor life |
|---|---|---|
| 2, 2a, 3 | Less than the floor life, in total | Clock paused while stored at 10% RH or less |
| 2, 2a, 3 | 12 hours or less | Reset by dry storage for 5 times the exposure, at 10% RH or less |
| 4, 5, 5a | 8 hours or less | Reset by dry storage for 10 times the exposure, at 5% RH or less |
| Any | Longer than the above, or past the floor life | Bake, then dry-pack |

Bake times for an MSL 3 part past its floor life by more than 72 hours (J-STD-033D Table 4-1):

| Package body thickness | At 125 °C | At 90 °C | At 40 °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under 0.5 mm | 1 hour | 3 hours | 22 hours |
| 0.8 to 1.4 mm | 8 hours | 25 hours | 8 days |
| 1.4 to 2.0 mm | 27 hours | 4 days | 37 days |
| 2.0 to 4.5 mm | 48 hours | 10 days | 79 days |

Higher levels and thicker parts take longer; large BGAs and stacked-die parts can need 96 hours at 125 °C. The floor life starts again from zero after a bake.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts that need baking on arrival, which delays the build, or parts damaged by the wrong bake.

**Applies to:** Anyone holding or consigning moisture-sensitive parts.

**Sources:** [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=2640)–47:00; [“How to Manage Moisture Sensitive Devices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014-how-to-manage-moisture-sensitive-devices) (May 2022), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=1260)–25:00 and [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=2460)–49:00 and [51:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=3060)–56:00; [“Stick It Up Your Tube”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259-stick-it-up-your-tube) (Jan 2024), [14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259?t=840)–15:00 and [38:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14388259?t=2280)–40:00; IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D, sections 4.1–4.1.2 (exposure to factory air) and Tables 4-1 and 4-3 (baking, and pausing or resetting the clock); a chip maker's application reports on floor life and baking (2017, 2018).

## Sourcing, counterfeits and obsolescence

Where parts come from matters as much as which parts they are. Parts bought through the maker's own sales channels can be traced back to the factory; parts that have changed hands several times can't, and that's where counterfeits get in. Lead times also move with the market: they stretched from weeks to most of a year during the 2021–22 shortage, then fell back. This page is about buying parts safely and planning for the ones that are hard to get.

### PCB-DFA-095: Buy parts only from authorized distributors or the maker

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-095

**Recommendation:** Buy from the part maker or its authorized (franchised) distributors. Don't buy from unfamiliar websites, auction sites or marketplaces, however convincing they look. If your assembler buys for you, expect them to do the same, and to tell you before using any other source.

**Why:** Authorized distributors buy straight from the maker, so the parts are genuine and traceable. Counterfeit parts can pass a visual check and still be wrong inside: remarked, used, or made from the wrong materials.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts that don't work, melt in soldering or won't take solder, found after they're on the board.

**Example:** A customer nearly paid a convincing fake distributor website for a hard-to-find part. Terminal blocks that looked right melted into black puddles in selective soldering, or wouldn't wet at all. One designer received 2,000 assembled units with a counterfeit LED that didn't work, and spent a day and a half reworking them by hand.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-1) (Jul 2020), [51:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=3060)–56:00; [“How Joel Murphy went from visual artist to electronics design engineer”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659-how-joel-murphy-went-from-visual-artist-to-electronics-design-engineer) (Oct 2020), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5963659?t=1320)–23:00; [“Catch up with Chris”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13639009-catch-up-with-chris) (Sep 2023), [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13639009?t=2100)–36:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-096: If you must buy from a broker or an unfamiliar source, ask for traceability, have the parts inspected, and try them on a small build first

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-096

**Recommendation:** When a part can only be found outside authorized channels:
- ask the seller for proof the parts came from the maker (an invoice, delivery note or goods-received record tied to the lot);
- ask whether they hold the stock themselves or are offering someone else's;
- have the parts inspected, and tested if they're costly or critical;
- build a few boards with them and check they work before committing the whole order.

**Why:** Brokers trade excess stock, which is often genuine, but every change of hands without records adds risk. Some brokers sell only surplus bought directly from large manufacturers; others search the open market. "Available stock" may be parts someone else holds, with a delivery time the broker doesn't control. Inspection under a microscope can catch sanded and remarked markings or wrong plating that paperwork won't. Two datasheets for the "same" part number can describe different parts.

**Typical values:** Inspection at 50× and 200× magnification, compared against known-good parts. One broker spends about 40 minutes inspecting each part number.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A full production run built with parts that don't match, or don't work.

**Example:** An assembler sourcing addressable LEDs on reel from an unfamiliar distributor found two datasheets for the same part number, in different languages and naming different makers; it got the customer's permission and tested a small build first.

**Applies to:** General practice. Aerospace and defense work follows SAE AS5553 (buyers) and AS6081 (distributors), which require traceability, inspection and notice before any broker purchase.

**Sources:** [“How Component Sense helps components fulfill their destiny w/ Kenny McGee”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15794357-how-component-sense-helps-components-fulfill-their-destiny-w-kenny-mcgee) (Sep 2024), [28:29](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15794357?t=1709)–29:23 and [39:49](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15794357?t=2389)–40:17; [“Navigating the Environmental Impact of Electronics w/ Component Sense Founder, Kenny McGee”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15877892-navigating-the-environmental-impact-of-electronics-w-component-sense-founder-kenny-mcgee) (Oct 2024), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15877892?t=780)–15:00; [“The RGB LED Dilemma in Manufacturing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846-the-rgb-led-dilemma-in-manufacturing) (Sep 2024), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846?t=540)–10:00 and [14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846?t=840)–16:00; SAE AS5553 and AS6081.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-097: Find your long-lead and single-source parts early and buy them ahead, without hoarding

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-097

**Recommendation:** Before production, go through the BOM and find the parts with the longest lead times, a single source, or a history of shortages. Buy those ahead, enough for your next several builds if you can afford it, or arrange for a distributor or your assembler to hold them for you ([PCB-DFA-098](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/04-sourcing/#pcb-dfa-098-tell-your-assembler-or-distributor-your-expected-volumes)). If you hear a part is going out of stock, tell your assembler the same day. In a shortage, don't over-order to win a bigger share of a supplier's allocation.

**Why:** Parts, not boards, set the lead time for most production orders. A large order may only find part of its quantity in stock, with the rest weeks away. In a shortage, stock disappears in hours, and buying early may be the only way to get it. But orders placed in a shortage are often non-cancellable and non-returnable, and when the market turns, buyers who over-ordered are left holding years of stock.

**Typical values:** These move with the market; check them when you plan. Before 2021, typical lead times were about 8–12 weeks; during the 2021–22 shortage, 18–40 weeks was common, and a quoted lead time over about 50 weeks meant the part was on allocation. Suppliers in China shut for the Lunar New Year holiday (late January or February), and lead times take one to two months to recover; order in early December what you'll need through March.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A build stopped for months by one part, or, the other way, cash tied up in stock you'll never use.

**Example:** During the shortage, customers who hadn't planned found 26-week lead times and couldn't build for about 20 weeks. A buyer needing 1,000 of a part found 800 in stock and waited 6–10 weeks for the rest.

**Applies to:** General practice; numbers are date-dependent.

**Sources:** [“Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [23:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=1380); [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=1020)–19:00 and [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=1680)–30:00; [“Discussing the Global Electronics Parts Shortage w/ Digi-Key”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8574130-discussing-the-global-electronics-parts-shortage-w-digi-key) (May 2021), [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8574130?t=1860); [“How Component Sense helps components fulfill their destiny w/ Kenny McGee”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15794357-how-component-sense-helps-components-fulfill-their-destiny-w-kenny-mcgee) (Sep 2024), [12:16](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15794357?t=736)–17:02; [“How Chinese New Year Impacts Manufacturing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955-how-chinese-new-year-impacts-manufacturing) (Jan 2022), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955?t=720)–13:00 and [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955?t=1860)–33:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

### PCB-DFA-098: Tell your assembler or distributor your expected volumes

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-098

**Recommendation:** As soon as you know them, share your expected annual volumes and build schedule with your assembler, or with a distributor directly. For production quantities, ask for quoted prices rather than catalog prices, and for expensive parts, ask whether they can be held and released in batches.

**Why:** With a forecast, buyers can negotiate volume prices, place orders ahead, and warn you when a part is going on allocation. Without one, they can only buy for the job in front of them. Distributors can hold stock against a forecast and release it as you build, so you don't pay for a year of expensive parts up front.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Higher prices, surprises when parts run short, and more cash tied up than necessary.

**Example:** A chip quoted automatically at about $25 each for 5,000 pieces came down to about $8 each through a distributor's quote. A customer alarmed that 15 parts had been pulled from a supply program during a shortage calmed down when shown they added up to $300 a year, and that the distributor was already holding stock for them.

**Applies to:** General practice; most useful once you're past prototypes.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [08:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=480)–10:00; [“Discussing the Global Electronics Parts Shortage w/ Digi-Key”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8574130-discussing-the-global-electronics-parts-shortage-w-digi-key) (May 2021), [37:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8574130?t=2220); [“How Small Manufacturers Manage Large Volume Orders”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426-how-small-manufacturers-manage-large-volume-orders) (Apr 2023), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=1620)–29:00; [“Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=1260)–22:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*
