### PCB-DFA-099: Don't set a fixed date-code limit; store parts well, and have old or doubtful stock tested for solderability

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-099

**Recommendation:** Don't put a blanket date-code limit (such as "no older than 2 years") on your BOM or purchase orders. Instead, store parts sealed and dry, and have the solderability of stock over about 2 years old, or of unknown history, tested to J-STD-002 before a build. If parts won't wet in assembly, suspect contamination of the leads as well as age.

**Why:** Solderability depends on how parts were made, packed and stored more than on their age. Properly stored parts solder well for many years, and some makers guarantee solderability for at least 2 years from shipment. Badly stored or contaminated parts can fail sooner. Makers and distributors, through their trade association (ECIA), recommend against general date-code limits: decades of process improvement removed most age-related failures, and the military specifications that started the practice have dropped it.

**Typical values:** Test stock older than about 2 years, or with no storage history. J-STD-002 covers the test methods for component leads and terminations.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Good parts refused for their age, or bad ones accepted for it.

**Example:** A broker found 2-year-old parts that wouldn't solder because their copper had tarnished, traced in one case to sulfur contamination when they were made, while 30-year-old stock it held still soldered well. Separately, solder refused to wet a manufacturer's parts because silicone release agent from their carrier tape had transferred to the leads.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Navigating the Environmental Impact of Electronics w/ Component Sense Founder, Kenny McGee”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15877892-navigating-the-environmental-impact-of-electronics-w-component-sense-founder-kenny-mcgee) (Oct 2024), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15877892?t=1020)–21:00; [“Board Cleaning w/ Mike Konrad (part 1)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139-board-cleaning-w-mike-konrad-part-1) (Apr 2021), [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139?t=2100)–36:00; ECIA, "Managing Date Code Restrictions on Orders for Electronic Components", GIPC #101 (June 2023); IPC/EIA/JEDEC J-STD-002 (solderability tests for component leads); Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

## Supplying your own parts (consignment) and spares

Most assemblers buy the parts for you ("turnkey"). Sometimes you'll supply some yourself ("consignment"): a part you already hold, one you've had to find from a special source, or a chip you've programmed. Consigned parts arrive alongside dozens of other boxes and have to be identified, counted, matched to your job and loaded onto machines. The more ready they are when they arrive, the faster and safer your build.

### PCB-DFA-100: Let your assembler buy the parts, and consign only the few you must

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-100

**Recommendation:** Let the assembler buy everything it can. Consign only parts it can't get: ones you've secured in a shortage, special-source parts, or parts you program or modify yourself. Don't consign resistors, capacitors and other common parts. Ask before sending a full kit or bare boards; many assemblers don't accept them.

**Why:** Buying, receiving and kitting parts is an assembler's everyday work, done with barcodes and systems built for it. A kit with parts from both you and the assembler on the same job is easy to mix up, especially across several orders. Cheap parts aren't worth the handling, labeling and risk of sending them in. Bare boards bought elsewhere may not suit the assembler's panel and handling needs ([PCB-DFA-001](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/)).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Slower receiving, mix-ups between your parts and theirs, and a quick-turn job that's no longer quick.

**Example:** Before the 2021–22 shortage, about 80–90% of one assembler's builds had no consigned parts at all; during it, that roughly reversed. Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub don't accept full consigned kits by default, and CircuitHub doesn't accept consigned bare boards.

**Applies to:** General practice; policies vary by assembler. Holding stock for you between orders usually carries a fee.

**Sources:** [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=540)–13:00 and [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=2940); [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [38:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=2280) and [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=2400)–42:00; [“How Chinese New Year Impacts Manufacturing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955-how-chinese-new-year-impacts-manufacturing) (Jan 2022), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955?t=240)–05:00; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=1440)–27:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-101: Send consigned parts ready for the machines

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-101

**Recommendation:** Send surface-mount parts in a form a machine can feed:
- reels, or cut tape in one continuous length per part number, not many short strips;
- no cut strip shorter than 50 mm, and preferably 150 mm or more;
- tubes only as a last resort, after reels, cut tape and trays are ruled out, and then with every part facing the same way;
- trays, or protective foam for tray parts, never loose in a bag.

Through-hole and hardware parts can come in labeled bags.

**Why:** Every strip has to be loaded into a feeder, or spliced onto the one before it, by hand. A strip too short to reach through the feeder can't be loaded at all. Cut tape nearly always arrives with a part in every pocket, and no empty leader, so the first and last part of each strip may be lost as it's loaded; the more strips, the more parts lost ([PCB-DFA-105](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/05-consignment-and-spares/#pcb-dfa-105-send-spares-plenty-of-cheap-parts-at-least-one-of-each-expensive-one-and-say-when-you-cant)). Assemblers like tubes less than any other packaging ([PCB-DFA-089](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/02-packaging/)): they feed unreliably, hold few parts and can go in backwards. A tube refilled with parts facing different ways has to be emptied and reloaded. Loose surface-mount parts can't be machine-placed at all.

![D58: Drawn to scale, 8 mm carrier tape seen from above, with a part in every pocket. Top: one continuous strip 240 mm long, round sprocket holes along the top and the direction of feed to the right, so the right-hand end goes into the feeder first; 50 mm is marked as the shortest strip that can be handled and 150 mm as the preferred minimum, and the parts at both ends are marked as the ones that may be lost. Bottom: the same kind of parts sent as five strips of ten, each 40 mm long, shorter than the 50 mm minimum.](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/images/cut-tape-length.svg)

*D58 is drawn to scale. Cut tape should come in strips of at least 50 mm, and preferably 150 mm or more; a strip of ten 0603 parts is only 40 mm long, and each one has to be handled separately.*

![D59: Drawn to scale, part of two tubes of SOIC-8 chips seen from above. Top: every chip has its pin-1 dot at the left. Bottom: a tube refilled by hand, with four of the ten chips turned end for end so their pin-1 dots are at the right.](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/images/tube-orientation.svg)

*D59 is drawn to scale, with the tubes shortened. Every part in a tube must face the same way; a tube refilled with parts turned end for end has to be emptied and reloaded.*

**Typical values:** Shortest cut strip: 50 mm minimum, 150 mm or more preferred (Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub). On 8 mm tape with a 4 mm pitch, 50 mm holds about 12 parts and 150 mm about 37. 1,000 parts sent in strips of ten means 100 strips to load or splice.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Extra handling charges, lost parts, or parts that have to be fitted by hand.

**Example:** A customer sent addressable LEDs as strips of ten; the assembler charged a handling fee for every strip, to cover the time spent loading them.

**Applies to:** General practice. EIA-481 sets leader and trailer lengths for full reels.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=1920)–34:00; [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=2160)–44:00; [“The RGB LED Dilemma in Manufacturing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846-the-rgb-led-dilemma-in-manufacturing) (Sep 2024), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15667846?t=780)–14:00; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=1440)–27:00; Chris Denney (author).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-102: Ship consigned parts in static-shielding packaging, and moisture-sensitive ones sealed

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-102

**Recommendation:** Pack static-sensitive parts in static-shielding bags or boxes, not ordinary plastic bags or plain anti-static bags. Send moisture-sensitive parts in their sealed moisture barrier bag, or resealed with fresh desiccant and a humidity card ([PCB-DFA-094](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/03-moisture-sensitive-parts/)), and say on the packing slip that they're moisture-sensitive.

**Why:** Parts rattling in a plastic bag generate static, which can damage them before they reach the factory. That damage often doesn't show in test; it surfaces as field failures months later, when the cause is hard to trace. Parts that arrive with an open or badly resealed moisture bag have to be baked before use.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Field failures nobody can explain, or a build delayed while parts are baked.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=2100)–38:00; [“How to Protect PCBs from ESD Damage”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936-how-to-protect-pcbs-from-esd-damage) (Mar 2022), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936?t=1320)–23:00; [“How to Manage Moisture Sensitive Devices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014-how-to-manage-moisture-sensitive-devices) (May 2022), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=2460)–42:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-103: Label every package with its part number, and every shipment with your order details

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-103

**Recommendation:** On every bag, reel, tube and tray, put the maker's full part number (the original label is best; handwritten is fine). On every shipment, put your company name, the assembler's order number and your purchase order number, and include a packing slip listing what's inside and which order it's for. If one reel is shared between orders, say how to split it. Send the tracking number as soon as you have it. For a shipment from another country, ask the assembler first about duties, taxes and the product's end use.

**Why:** An assembler may receive about 100 boxes a day. A box with no order reference waits until someone works out what it is, and the job waits with it. A bag separated from its box needs its own label. Import paperwork depends on what the product is for. Unlabeled parts can hold a job up more than late ones: late parts are at least expected.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A job held up, sometimes for days, while unlabeled parts are matched; leftovers that can't be returned with the right order.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=1920)–34:00; [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=1800)–31:00 and [35:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=2100)–39:00 and [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=2640)–48:00; [“Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=1740)–31:00; [“How to safely and successfully ship assembled PCBs w/ Nicole Poirier”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835-how-to-safely-and-successfully-ship-assembled-pcbs-w-nicole-poirier) (Apr 2021), [30:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=1800)–34:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-104: Get consigned parts to the assembler at least the quoted assembly time before the ship date

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-104

**Recommendation:** Deliver consigned parts as early as you can. At the latest, they should arrive as many working days before the ship date as the quoted assembly time.

**Why:** The line can't be set up until every part is there. Most of a quoted lead time is preparation (buying, receiving, kitting, programming), not time on the line. A job waiting for parts can be overtaken by jobs that are ready.

**Typical values:** For a 5-day assembly quote, parts at least 5 days before the ship date. Of a 15–20 day lead time, about 15 days may be preparation and about 5 on the line.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A missed ship date, often by more than the days the parts were late.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [39:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=2340)–40:00; [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=1020)–19:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-105: Send spares: plenty of cheap parts, at least one of each expensive one, and say when you can't

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-105

**Recommendation:** Send more than the exact quantity: generous extra of small, cheap parts and at least one spare of each expensive part. If you can only send the exact number (pre-release samples, very costly parts), say so clearly. When the assembler buys for you, expect it to buy extra for the same reason.

**Why:** Machines reject parts they can't see clearly, lose some loading feeders, and drop parts when a nozzle clogs. The smallest parts scatter easily: an inch of tape can hold 50–100 of them. Cut tape usually has a part in every pocket, so the first and last part of each strip may be lost as it's loaded into a feeder. A board short of one part can't ship.

**Typical values:** Minimum: one spare of every expensive part. Recommended: about 10–20% extra on small, cheap parts (110–120 for 100 boards); a few percent extra on costly chips. Assemblers buying for you typically add 2–3% on expensive parts and buy a full reel or more of cheap ones, since leftovers are usually scrapped.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards missing a part, and a wait for more.

**Example:** About 100 extra 10 kΩ resistors for a job needing 2,010 cost under $1. A customer sent a $5,000 FPGA with no spare and said so up front, which saved a round of emails.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=780)–17:00; [“All about parts purchasing - part 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-2) (Jul 2020), [06:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4704659?t=360); [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=1620)–28:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=600).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-09*

---

### PCB-DFA-106: Tell your assembler before a substitute part number arrives

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-106

**Recommendation:** If you're sending a different part number from the one on the BOM, even an intended equivalent, tell the assembler before it arrives, and update the BOM. When the assembler asks about a mismatch, answer quickly: have an engineer reachable during the build.

**Why:** A part that doesn't match the BOM stops the job until someone confirms it's right. The assembler can't tell an intended substitute from a mistake.

**Typical values:** Aim to answer an assembler's question within about 30 minutes.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A build stopped, or bumped behind other jobs, while a question waits.

**Example:** During the 2021–22 shortage, customers often sent substitutes with different part numbers; each unannounced one held its job until confirmed.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=1140)–24:00.

## Solder paste printing and stencils

Before any part is placed, solder paste is printed onto the board through a stencil: a thin steel sheet with an opening (an aperture) for every pad that needs solder. A squeegee pushes paste across the stencil, the paste fills the apertures, and the stencil lifts away and leaves a small, measured deposit on each pad. Most soldering defects start here, at printing, not later in placement or reflow.

The assembler designs the stencil, not you. They choose its thickness, the shape and size of every aperture, and any special features, from the paste layer in your design files. What your design controls is what they start from: which pads get paste, and how much the smallest and largest parts on the board pull the stencil in opposite directions.

### 5.2 Paste inspection, briefly

Many assemblers measure every paste deposit in 3D right after printing, before any part is placed. A bad print is cleaned off and printed again, which is cheap; a bad print found after reflow is rework, which isn't. There's nothing in your design that paste inspection needs, beyond the recommendations on this page.

### PCB-DFA-018: Send the paste layer 1:1 with your copper pads

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-018

**Recommendation:** Make each pad's paste opening the same size and shape as the copper pad. Don't shrink, reshape or split paste openings yourself. If a part needs something special, say so in a note on the assembly drawing.

**Why:** The assembler uses your paste layer as a map of where solder goes, then redraws every opening for their own stencil thickness, paste and process (for example, cutting a small notch out of the inner edge of each chip-resistor pad). They assume your openings match the pads. If you've already reduced them, they reduce them again, and the pads get too little solder.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Starved joints, or a delay while the assembler works out what you meant.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Solder paste printing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710-solder-paste-printing) (Sep 2020), [01:03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710?t=3780)–01:06:00; [“Stencils: The Unsung Heroes of PCB Perfection Pt.1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360-stencils-the-unsung-heroes-of-pcb-perfection-pt-1) (Jul 2024), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360?t=300); [“Stencils: The Unsung Heroes of PCB Perfection Pt. 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15484609-stencils-the-unsung-heroes-of-pcb-perfection-pt-2) (Jul 2024), [02:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15484609?t=120)–03:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

---

### PCB-DFA-019: Put paste on every pad you want soldered, and only those

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-019

**Recommendation:** Check the paste layer pad by pad before you release the design. Remove paste from pads that must stay bare, such as test points. The exception is a board with an OSP finish, where test points should get paste (see [PCB-DFT-008](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/01-test-points/#pcb-dft-008-make-test-points-surface-mount-pads-at-least-09-mm-in-diameter-and-19-mm-apart-with-no-paste)). Add paste where library footprints leave it out, such as surface-mount standoffs and some battery contacts. For a surface-mount standoff, draw the paste openings the maker's datasheet shows; the assembler then adjusts them for its own stencil and the look you expect, often adding a lot more paste.

**Why:** The paste layer is the only place the assembler learns which pads get solder, and on which side of the board. Footprints downloaded from part makers often have no paste data at all; a surface-mount standoff then looks like a plain mounting hole.

![D34: Drawn to scale except copper and mask thickness, after a maker's datasheet for an M3 surface-mount standoff 5 mm long, with the plated hole most boards use. Plan views of a 7.4 mm round pad around a 4.4 mm plated hole: with no paste in the footprint the pad stays bare; with the maker's stencil, a ring of paste from 4.48 to 7.27 mm in four segments covers it. Cut-away side views after reflow: the standoff's 6 mm body rests on the pad and its 4.2 mm locating collar drops into the hole. With no paste it sits loose; with paste, solder fills under the body, forms a fillet out to the pad's edge, and some drains down the hole round the collar.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/standoff-paste.svg)

*D34 is drawn to scale, except copper and mask thickness, after a maker's datasheet for an M3 surface-mount standoff. The footprint is a round copper pad around a plated hole, so without paste it looks like a through-hole pad and nothing solders the standoff. With the maker's paste openings, a ring in four segments, reflow leaves solder under the standoff's body and a fillet round its base. Some of the solder drains down the plated hole, which is one reason assemblers often print far more paste than the maker shows.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Solder on test points you meant to probe, or a standoff, battery contact or pogo pin soldered on the wrong side or not at all. Assemblers catch many of these, but each catch is a question and a delay.

**Example:** Boards were shipped with solder on every test point. The paste layer asked for it, so that's what was built. The assembler now asks about test points on every new job.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Solder paste printing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710-solder-paste-printing) (Sep 2020), [01:04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710?t=3840)–01:06:00; [“Stencils: The Unsung Heroes of PCB Perfection Pt.1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360-stencils-the-unsung-heroes-of-pcb-perfection-pt-1) (Jul 2024), [06:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360?t=360)–08:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

### PCB-DFA-020: Don't put one very fine-pitch part on a board of large parts

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-020

**Recommendation:** Keep the range of part sizes on one side of the board as narrow as you can. If the board needs one very fine-pitch part (0.4 mm pitch or finer), try to put it on the opposite side from the large, solder-hungry parts (see [PCB-DFA-024](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)).

**Why:** One stencil prints every pad on a side, and its thickness is set mostly by the smallest openings. Large parts want a thick stencil and plenty of paste; fine-pitch parts need a thin one, or the paste won't release from their tiny openings. With both on one side, the assembler has to compromise: a thinner stencil that starves the large parts, or a stepped stencil (thicker or thinner in local patches), a special coating or finer paste, all of which cost more and take longer.

**Typical values:** Stencil thickness about 5 mil (0.13 mm) for most boards, 6 mil for boards of mostly large parts, about 4 mil once 0.4 mm-pitch parts or 0.5 mm-pitch BGAs appear (one assembler's practice). The paste must release from each opening: the opening's area divided by the area of its walls (the area ratio) should be at least 0.66, and a rectangular opening's width at least 1.5 times the stencil thickness (IPC-7525). Below about 0.66 the assembler needs a coated or stepped stencil; below about 0.60, bigger changes. The paste must also fit: at least five of its largest grains across the narrowest opening, which pushes very small openings to finer, costlier paste.

![D6: Drawn to scale, enlarged: two cross-sections through the same 0.25 mm square stencil opening over a copper pad. In a 0.127 mm (5 mil) stencil the area ratio is 0.49 and the paste sticks; in a 0.076 mm (3 mil) stencil it is 0.82 and the paste releases.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/stencil-area-ratio.svg)

*D6 is enlarged and drawn to scale. It shows two cross-sections through a stencil opening 0.25 mm square, sitting over a copper pad. In a 0.127 mm (5 mil) stencil, the area ratio is 0.25 ÷ (4 × 0.127) = 0.49, below the 0.66 minimum, so the paste grips the opening's walls more than the pad and stays in the stencil. In a 0.076 mm (3 mil) stencil, the same opening has an area ratio of 0.82, and the paste releases onto the pad. A thinner stencil helps the small part, but gives every other part on that side less paste.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A pricier stencil with a longer lead time, more defects on either the small part or the large ones, and a higher assembly price.

**Applies to:** General practice. Exact thresholds vary by assembler, stencil and paste.

**Sources:** [“Solder paste printing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710-solder-paste-printing) (Sep 2020), [46:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710?t=2760) and [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710?t=3120)–53:00; [“Stencils: The Unsung Heroes of PCB Perfection Pt.1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360-stencils-the-unsung-heroes-of-pcb-perfection-pt-1) (Jul 2024), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360?t=1080)–20:00 and [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360?t=1620)–30:00; [“Stencils: The Unsung Heroes of PCB Perfection Pt. 2”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15484609-stencils-the-unsung-heroes-of-pcb-perfection-pt-2) (Jul 2024), [08:30](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15484609?t=510)–11:00 and [16:30](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15484609?t=990)–21:00; [“To BGA or Not to BGA”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540-to-bga-or-not-to-bga) (Oct 2026), [22:30](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540?t=1350); IPC-7525C, stencil design guidelines (area ratio and aspect ratio); a solder paste maker's guidance on the "five-ball rule" (checked Oct 2026).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

## Component placement

A placement machine picks each part from its tape, tray or tube with a vacuum nozzle, checks it with a camera and puts it down in the wet solder paste. Modern machines are fast and very accurate, but every part has a target, and smaller targets are harder to hit every time.

What your design controls is the size of those targets and how crowded they are: which packages you choose, and how close together you put them. Footprint shapes, pin-1 marks and polarity marks also matter a great deal, and have their own chapter (Part 1.4, Footprints and the component library).

### PCB-DFA-021: Use the largest package the board has room for

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-021

**Recommendation:** For resistors and capacitors, use 0603 where you have room and 0402 where you need to save space. Go to 0201 or smaller only when the product truly needs it. For chips, use the larger package when the part comes in more than one and the larger one fits: an SO-8 rather than a tiny BGA, for example.

**Why:** Smaller parts need more accurate feeders, nozzles, printing and inspection, and slower machine speeds. They also get less solder (see [PCB-DFA-020](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/)) and are harder to rework and test. 0603 parts are big enough to carry printed value markings, so inspection cameras can check them; 0402 parts aren't.

**Typical values:** 0603: comfortable · 0402: the everyday floor, placed by the million without trouble · 0201: workable, with more care at every step · 01005 and smaller: only when needed.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Lower yield, longer lead times and higher prices, for no benefit when the board had room.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The pick and place assembly process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4928099-the-pick-and-place-assembly-process) (Aug 2020), [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4928099?t=2640)–48:00; [“Solder paste printing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710-solder-paste-printing) (Sep 2020), [01:07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710?t=4020)–01:08:00; [“To BGA or Not to BGA”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540-to-bga-or-not-to-bga) (Oct 2026), [16:43](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540?t=1003)–17:57.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

---

### PCB-DFA-022: At fine pitch, choose a BGA or QFN over a leaded QFP

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-022

**Recommendation:** If a chip comes in a 0.4 mm-pitch QFP and a BGA, choose the BGA. Avoid 0.4 mm-pitch QFPs altogether if you can; 0.5 mm-pitch QFPs are fine. Choose the very finest packages (0.4 mm-pitch chip-scale packages and finer) only when the product needs to be that small.

**Why:** Fine leads are fragile: they bend in packaging and handling, they don't sit flat (poor coplanarity), and the process drifts. A BGA or QFN has no leads to damage, and once the printing process is tuned it stays tuned, so its yield is higher. The drawback is that a defect under a BGA or QFN is harder and more expensive to fix. At the finest pitches the whole job gets harder: routing needs via-in-pad, the stencil needs coatings or steps, and at about 0.3 mm pitch the part may be dipped in flux and placed with no paste at all, which requires special tools that not every assembler has.

**Typical values:** 0.5 mm-pitch QFP: easy · 0.8 and 0.65 mm-pitch BGA: easy, often easier than a QFP · 0.4 mm-pitch QFP: avoid · 0.4 mm-pitch BGA or chip-scale package: expensive, only when needed · about 0.3 mm pitch: flux-dip assembly.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Defects that persist however the process is tuned, and some high-volume assemblers refuse to quote 0.4 mm-pitch QFPs at all.

**Applies to:** General practice. Leaded parts remain the right choice for boards that will be hand-assembled.

**Sources:** [“To BGA or Not to BGA”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540-to-bga-or-not-to-bga) (Oct 2026), [11:21](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540?t=681)–19:32; [“The pick and place assembly process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4928099-the-pick-and-place-assembly-process) (Aug 2020), [50:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4928099?t=3000)–53:00; [“Gloves not Mittens”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842-gloves-not-mittens) (Jun 2026), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19269842?t=1680)–29:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

---

### PCB-DFA-023: Leave room around every part, and keep tall parts away from tiny ones

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-023

**Recommendation:** Aim for about 1 mm from the edge of one part to the edge of the next. Where a board is too dense for that, the absolute minimums are in the table below; check with your assembler before designing to them. Keep tiny parts (0402 and smaller) away from tall ones such as aluminum electrolytic capacitors.

**Why:** A placement nozzle that has just put down a tall part can hit it while placing a tiny part beside it. A small part placed slightly off can end up under a large part placed next to it, such as a BGA. Tall parts also cast shadows that hide their neighbors from 3D inspection cameras, and they make rework harder.

**Typical values:** About 1 mm edge to edge, as an everyday rule of thumb (one assembler's).

| Part size (inch / metric) | Absolute minimum gap, side by side | Absolute minimum gap, end to end |
|---|---|---|
| 01005 / 0402 | 0.13 mm | 0.11 mm |
| 0201 / 0603 | 0.18 mm | 0.17 mm |
| 0402 / 1005 | 0.11 mm | 0.08 mm |
| 0603 / 1608 | 0.21 mm | 0.17 mm |

⚠️ **These minimums are hard to achieve.** They are a leading placement-machine maker's absolute minimums, published by Worthington Assembly. Use them only after you've confirmed your assembler's machines are specified for them, and agreed it with the assembler before layout.

![D8: Drawn to scale: on the left, a top view of small capacitors 1 mm from a BGA and 1 mm from each other; on the right, a side view of a 10 mm tall aluminum capacitor whose shadow hides a small resistor right beside it from an inspection camera's angled light, while a resistor further away is in clear view.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/part-spacing.svg)

*D8 is drawn to scale. On the left, a top view: small capacitors sit 1 mm from the edge of a BGA and 1 mm from each other. On the right, a side view: a 10 mm tall aluminum capacitor blocks the angled light of a 3D inspection camera. A small resistor right beside it is in its shadow and can't be measured; a resistor further away is in clear view. How long the shadow is depends on the camera's angle.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts knocked off or placed on top of each other, defects that inspection can't see, and boards that are hard to rework.

**Applies to:** Everyday spacing: general practice. Absolute minimums: varies by manufacturer; check with yours.

**Sources:** [“The pick and place assembly process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4928099-the-pick-and-place-assembly-process) (Aug 2020), [48:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4928099?t=2880)–50:00; [“Automated Optical Inspection (AOI) for PCB Assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753-automated-optical-inspection-aoi-for-pcb-assembly) (Nov 2020), [45:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753?t=2700)–46:00; [Discrete Component Spacing](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/s/Discrete-Component-Spacing.pdf) (Worthington Assembly, PDF).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

### Related pages
- [Solder paste printing and stencils](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/)
- [Reflow soldering](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)

---

Source: https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/

## Reflow soldering

After placement, the board rides a conveyor through a reflow oven. The oven heats the whole assembly along a set temperature profile until the paste melts, then cools it so the solder sets into joints. A double-sided board goes through twice: the first side is built and reflowed, the board is flipped, and the second side is built and reflowed, with the first side's parts hanging underneath.

The assembler sets the oven profile for each job. What your design controls is how evenly the board heats, which parts must survive the heat, and what happens to the first side during the second pass.

### PCB-DFA-024: On a double-sided board, put small, light parts on one side and heavy parts on the other

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-024

**Recommendation:** Put the small, light and fine-pitch parts (chips, ICs, small passives) on the side built first. Put the heavy and bulky parts (large inductors, connectors, buzzers) on the side built second. Put every part whose leads or pegs go through the board, such as a USB connector with through-hole support pins, on the second side, all together. Check the datasheets of every part on the side that's reflowed twice (the side built first). Some manufacturers recommend reflowing their parts only once.

**Why:** During the second reflow, the first side's solder melts again with its parts hanging upside down. Surface tension holds small, light parts on; heavy parts fall off unless they're glued. Pegs that poke through the board stop the stencil lying flat on the second side, so they can't be printed around unless they're all on the side printed last. Grouping fine-pitch parts on one side also lets each side have the stencil thickness it needs (see [PCB-DFA-020](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/)).

**Typical values:** A common rule of thumb: a part stays on during the second reflow if its weight divided by its total pad area is no more than about 30 g/in² (0.047 g/mm²). Heavier parts on the first side need glue.

![D7: Drawn to scale, side view: a 1.6 mm board on its second pass through the oven. A heavy inductor, a connector with pegs through the board and a large capacitor face up on the second side; a QFN and small resistors and capacitors hang underneath on the first side.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/double-sided-plan.svg)

*D7 is drawn to scale. It shows a 1.6 mm board from the side, on its second pass through the reflow oven. The side built second faces up and carries the heavy and bulky parts: a large inductor, a large capacitor and a connector whose pegs go through the board and poke out of the first side. The side built first hangs underneath and carries only small, light parts, a QFN chip and small resistors and capacitors, which the surface tension of the melted solder holds in place. A part on the first side stays on if its weight divided by its total pad area is no more than about 30 g/in² (0.047 g/mm²); heavier parts must be glued.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Each heavy part on the first side is glued, sometimes by hand on every board, which adds labor that doesn't get cheaper with volume. Some assemblers have automated glue-dispensing equipment, but it's rare. Parts with pegs on both sides may not be buildable by normal methods at all.

**Example:** One design needed a spring-loaded connector on one side and a USB connector with through-hole pegs on the other, because of the enclosure. It was nearly impossible to build by normal methods; the assembler had to invent a special process.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Get to know Melissa and Chris”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9253950-get-to-know-melissa-and-chris) (Sep 2021), [55:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9253950?t=3300)–57:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [25:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1500)–29:00; [“Stencils: The Unsung Heroes of PCB Perfection Pt.1”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360-stencils-the-unsung-heroes-of-pcb-perfection-pt-1) (Jul 2024), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15448360?t=1140)–20:00; “Component Candidacy of Second Side Reflow with Lead-Free Solder” (conference paper, 2006), which reports the weight-to-pad-area rule of thumb (checked Oct 2026 through summaries, not the full paper).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

---

### PCB-DFA-025: Don't put a few parts on the second side just because there's room

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-025

**Recommendation:** If the board can be single-sided, keep it single-sided. If it has to be double-sided, use the same part numbers on both sides where you can.

**Why:** Every side is a separate pass through the printer, the placement machine and the oven, with its own stencil, program and handling. A second side that uses different parts may need a whole second machine setup.

**Typical values:** A second side adds at least about 15 % to assembly cost, even when it has only two parts, both already used on the first side. A second side with entirely different parts can double it (one assembler's estimate, as of 2024).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You pay for a whole extra assembly pass for one or two parts.

**Example:** A board had one resistor on its bottom side, and plenty of room for it on the top.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1740)–32:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

---

### PCB-DFA-026: Check that every part can survive a standard lead-free reflow, and flag any that can't

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-026

**Recommendation:** Check every part's datasheet for its maximum reflow temperature and number of reflow passes, and the bare board's material too. Tell your assembler before the build about any part that can't take a standard lead-free profile, or that asks for an unusual one. Never design batteries to go through reflow, wave or selective soldering; they're soldered by hand. Through-hole parts that will be soldered in the reflow oven (pin-in-paste) need plastics rated for reflow temperatures.

**Why:** Lead-free solder (such as SAC305) melts at about 217 °C, and reflow profiles peak well above that, typically around 240–250 °C. Most parts are rated for it, but some sensors, microphones, LEDs, small solar cells and connector plastics aren't, and a double-sided board puts every part through at least two passes. The assembler only knows a part is special if someone reads its datasheet, and it's cheaper for that to be you.

**Typical values:** Most thin lead-free packages are rated for a 260 °C peak; thicker and larger packages are often rated lower (250 °C or 245 °C), per J-STD-020. There is no single number of passes: every part sets its own, and so does the board's laminate. Count the passes your build needs (two for a double-sided board, plus any rework) and check each part and the board against it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts damaged in the oven, found only when the first boards are tested, or melted connector housings.

**Example:** A tiny surface-mount solar cell was destroyed by a standard lead-free reflow; nobody had checked its datasheet. A lower-temperature solder fixed it, and the rest of the build went fine.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Reflow soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6175423-reflow-soldering) (Nov 2020), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6175423?t=1740)–31:00; [“The nitty gritty details on solder”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11129008-the-nitty-gritty-details-on-solder) (Aug 2022), [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11129008?t=2640)–45:00; [“Benefits of intrusive soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130-benefits-of-intrusive-soldering) (Jun 2022), [02:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=120) and [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=1740)–30:00; J-STD-020 (moisture/reflow sensitivity classification, peak temperatures).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

---

### PCB-DFA-027: Spread the heat load: don't put huge parts right beside tiny ones

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-027

**Recommendation:** Where you can, avoid placing a very large part, such as a big aluminum electrolytic capacitor, right beside very small parts such as 0201s. If the board needs both, expect the assembler to profile the oven with thermocouples on the largest and the smallest parts.

**Why:** A large part soaks up heat and acts as a heat sink, while a tiny part next to it heats much faster. The smallest parts set the highest temperature the oven may reach; the largest set how long it must soak to bring them up to soldering temperature. Modern convection ovens and a measured profile handle most boards, but the bigger the difference, the narrower the window.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A narrower process window: joints on the large part that aren't fully melted, or small parts overheated to get there.

**Applies to:** General practice. Usually a minor concern; the assembler profiles the oven for each board.

**Sources:** [“Reflow soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6175423-reflow-soldering) (Nov 2020), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6175423?t=1680)–29:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

---

### PCB-DFA-028: Talk to your assembler first about very thin boards and large, heavy double-sided panels

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-028

**Recommendation:** If the board is thinner than about 0.6 mm, especially if it's double-sided, ask your assembler before you commit whether it needs a carrier or custom support tooling. Do the same for large panels with heavy parts on both sides.

**Why:** Assembly equipment relies on the board being stiff enough to be its own tooling, which a standard 1.6 mm board is. A very thin board flexes under the squeegee and the placement nozzle. A single-sided thin board can often be taped to a stiff carrier; a double-sided one needs tooling shaped around the parts underneath. A double-sided board rides through the oven on its edges, so a large, heavy panel sags, and in extreme cases falls off the rails.

**Typical values:** 1.6 mm: standard · under about 0.6 mm: a conversation first · 0.2–0.4 mm: custom tooling likely if double-sided.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Tooling charges and delays you didn't plan for, or poor print and placement quality.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Custom tooling to the rescue”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740-custom-tooling-to-the-rescue) (Jul 2022), [08:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740?t=480)–11:00; [“Advanced Drilling w/ CAM Engineer, Dave Wilcox”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991-advanced-drilling-w-cam-engineer-dave-wilcox) (May 2022), [01:16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10611991?t=4560).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-01*

## Optical and X-ray inspection

After reflow, an assembled board is inspected. Automated optical inspection (AOI) machines photograph the board and check that every part is present, the right way round and soldered. 2D machines compare flat images; 3D machines also measure heights, and see solder joints and dark parts on dark boards better. X-ray inspection looks through parts at joints no camera can see, such as the balls under a BGA or the pad under a QFN.

Inspection checks the assembler's work, not the bare board: shorts and opens in the board itself are the fab's job to find. Programming a 3D machine takes time for every new part number, so a small order is often inspected by people instead; on repeat orders, the program is already written and pays for itself. What your design controls is mostly covered elsewhere: footprints and markings that can be checked by eye ([Part 1.4](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/)), space around tall parts so cameras can see their neighbors ([PCB-DFA-023](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/02-component-placement/)), and solder mask color (Part 2.8).

### PCB-DFA-038: Join neighboring pins in copper, and keep a solder mask dam between them

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-038

**Recommendation:** Where two neighboring pins of a part are meant to be connected, connect them in copper, and keep a solder mask dam between the two pads, as you would between any other fine-pitch pads ([PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/#pcb-dfa-032-put-a-solder-mask-dam-between-every-pad-of-a-fine-pitch-part)). Avoid leaving the copper between them exposed.

**Why:** With no mask between the pads, solder flows across the joining copper and forms what looks exactly like a solder bridge. Operators and inspection machines are trained to treat bridges as defects, so an intended connection that looks like one causes confusion. A mask dam keeps two separate, normal-looking joints; the copper underneath still makes the connection.

![D36: Drawn to scale, plan views of four leads of a 0.5 mm-pitch part after soldering, the middle two meant to be connected. Joined by copper under the mask with a dam between their pads, each has its own normal joint. With the copper between them left bare, solder runs across and the pair looks like a solder bridge.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/joined-pins.svg)

*D36 is drawn to scale. Joined under the mask, with a dam between the pads, the two pins solder like any others and inspection sees two normal joints. With the copper between them left bare, solder runs across it and the pair looks exactly like a bridge.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards held while the assembler checks whether the bridge is intended, or a "defect" removed by an operator.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The PCB assembly process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141-the-pcb-assembly-process) (Jun 2020), [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141?t=960)–17:00; [“Automated Optical Inspection (AOI) for PCB Assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753-automated-optical-inspection-aoi-for-pcb-assembly) (Nov 2020), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/6598753?t=240)–17:00, for the chapter opening.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

### Related pages
- [Component placement](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/02-component-placement/)
- [Footprints and the component library](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/05-through-hole-soldering/

## Through-hole soldering

A through-hole part has leads or pins that pass through plated holes in the board. They are soldered in one of four ways: in the reflow oven with the surface-mount parts, using paste printed into and around the holes (pin-in-paste, also called intrusive soldering); by a selective soldering machine, which brings a small fountain of molten solder to each pin from underneath; by a wave soldering machine, which passes the whole underside over a wave of solder; or by hand. Every method except pin-in-paste is an extra step after reflow, and hand soldering is the slowest and least consistent.

What your design controls is how many through-hole parts there are, which parts they are, and how much room they have.

### PCB-DFA-039: Use surface mount by default, and through-hole only where a part takes force

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-039

**Recommendation:** Choose surface-mount parts wherever they'll do the job. Keep through-hole, or hybrid parts (see [PCB-DFA-040](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/05-through-hole-soldering/#pcb-dfa-040-prefer-hybrid-parts-surface-mount-signals-with-through-hole-pegs)), for parts that are pushed, pulled or twisted sideways often, or by people who don't know the product.

**Why:** Surface-mount parts are placed and soldered by machine in the same pass as everything else. Through-hole parts need a separate soldering step, and loose axial and radial parts (resistors, capacitors) often need their leads bent and trimmed by hand first. A through-hole joint is stronger against sideways force, so the failure point becomes the part itself, not its solder joint.

**Typical values:** One assembler's rule of thumb:

| Usually surface mount | Usually through-hole or hybrid |
|---|---|
| Resistors, capacitors, inductors, LEDs, crystals, ICs | Connectors that untrained people plug and unplug, such as field-wired terminal blocks |
| Ribbon-cable connectors; terminal blocks wired once inside a machine | Plugs used thousands of times, such as a phone's charging port |
| Low-voltage DC power jacks plugged in rarely | Mains (AC) power connectors |
| Coin-cell clips changed every few years | Holders for batteries changed every week |
| Push buttons, DIP switches, reset switches (the force is into the board) | On/off toggle switches used often (the force is sideways) |
| Trimmers set once at the factory | Volume and gain knobs that users turn |
| Power transistors and regulators, cooled through the board's copper | |

Where an enclosure holds a connector firmly (with nuts and bolts, for example), a surface-mount connector is usually fine.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You pay for an extra soldering step, often by hand, for parts that didn't need it, or a connector tears off the board in use.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“When to use through hole vs surface mount components”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410-when-to-use-through-hole-vs-surface-mount-components) (Jul 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410?t=600)–39:00; [“Benefits of intrusive soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130-benefits-of-intrusive-soldering) (Jun 2022), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=240)–05:00; [“What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1980)–39:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-040: Prefer hybrid parts: surface-mount signals with through-hole pegs

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-040

**Recommendation:** Where a connector needs strength, look for a hybrid version: surface-mount signal pins, with through-hole pegs or pins that hold it to the board. USB-C connectors are a common example.

**Why:** The pegs take the force of plugging and unplugging; the signal pins only carry signals. Because the whole part can be soldered with pin-in-paste in the reflow oven, it needs no separate soldering step, and the pegs locate it so it can't be fitted crooked or backwards. Some hybrid connectors have half their signal pins as through-holes, which can be routed on inner layers.

![D37: Side view of a USB-C receptacle on a 1.6 mm board. Two pegs on its metal shell go through plated holes and are soldered through the board. Its signal pins come out of the back and are soldered to surface pads.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/hybrid-usbc.svg)

*D37 is drawn to scale, except copper thickness. The shell's pegs are soldered through the board and take the force of plugging and unplugging. The signal pins are surface-mount and solder in reflow with everything else.*

**Applies to:** General practice. On a double-sided board, put hybrid parts on the side built second ([PCB-DFA-024](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)).

**Sources:** [“When to use through hole vs surface mount components”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410-when-to-use-through-hole-vs-surface-mount-components) (Jul 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410?t=600)–11:00; [“The importance of having different perspectives in engineering w/ Eli Hughes of Tzero Labs (Part 2)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7118017-the-importance-of-having-different-perspectives-in-engineering-w-eli-hughes-of-tzero-labs-part-2) (Jan 2021), [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7118017?t=2400)–42:00; [The Best USB-C Port](https://www.worthingtonassembly.com/the-usbc-port) (Worthington Assembly).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-041: Leave room around pin-in-paste parts for extra paste

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-041

**Recommendation:** Around any through-hole part that will be soldered in the reflow oven, leave a few millimeters clear of other parts, so the assembler can print extra paste onto the solder mask around the holes. Check the board thickness the part's maker recommends: some hybrid connectors are designed for boards no thicker than about 1.3 mm.

**Why:** Solder paste is only about half metal by volume, so even a hole packed full of paste gives about half a hole of solder. The assembler makes up the difference by printing paste well beyond the hole onto the mask, sometimes several millimeters; when it melts, it's all drawn into the hole. Parts placed right up against the connector leave no room for it.

**Typical values:** Overprinting of up to about 5–8 mm beyond the hole has been used. Joints soldered this way often look incompletely filled from the far side, but can still meet IPC-A-610J (Table 7-4). It asks for at least 75% vertical fill for Class 2 and Class 3. For Class 2 only, 50% or 1.2 mm, whichever is less, is enough on parts with 14 or more leads, and on a lead tied to an internal plane if the solder has wetted all the way round the lead and barrel on the side the solder came from. It also notes that a pin-in-paste joint may have no fillet between the lead and the land.

![D18: Drawn to scale, cross-sections through a 1.6 mm board. After printing, paste fills the plated hole and is printed well beyond the pad, and the pin is pushed through it. After reflow, the paste has been drawn into the hole, filling it round the pin with a fillet on each side and leaving only flux residue on the mask.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/pin-in-paste.svg)

*D18 is drawn to scale, except copper thickness. Paste is printed well beyond the pad, onto the solder mask, because only about half of it is metal. When it melts, it is drawn into the hole, filling it round the pin with a fillet on each side, and leaves only flux residue behind.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Holes without enough solder, or a second print pass and extra cost to get it there.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Benefits of intrusive soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130-benefits-of-intrusive-soldering) (Jun 2022), [14:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=840)–17:00 and [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=1560)–28:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-042: Choose through-hole parts rated for the soldering process they'll see

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-042

**Recommendation:** Check that each through-hole part's plastic is rated for the way it will be soldered: reflow temperatures for pin-in-paste, and selective or wave soldering for the others. Avoid hobby-grade and unverified parts in production; their plastics are often designed for hand soldering only.

**Why:** Selective and wave soldering heat plastics far more than a hand soldering iron does. High-temperature plastics cost more, so cheap parts often use plastics that soften or melt.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Melted connector housings, and a build switched to slow hand soldering.

**Applies to:** General practice. Batteries are always soldered by hand ([PCB-DFA-026](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)).

**Sources:** [“The selective soldering process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971-the-selective-soldering-process) (Jan 2021), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971?t=2460)–43:00; [“Benefits of intrusive soldering”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130-benefits-of-intrusive-soldering) (Jun 2022), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791130?t=1740)–30:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-043: Keep surface-mount parts away from through-hole pins on the solder side

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-043

**Recommendation:** On the side where through-hole pins come out (the side the solder is applied from), keep surface-mount pads 3 mm from the outer edge of each through-hole pad, and 5 mm on the side where the board leaves the solder wave (ask your assembler which side that is). 2 mm is the absolute minimum; more room is always better. Keep small parts especially well away from pins that will be soldered by hand.

**Why:** A selective soldering machine's nozzle needs room around each pin; the smaller the nozzle the board forces, the harder and slower the job. Too close, and the pins have to be soldered by hand.

**Typical values:** Absolute minimum 2 mm · recommended 3 mm · 5 mm on the side where the board leaves the wave · 4–5 mm all round makes the job easy (one assembler). One selective-soldering machine maker gives 2 mm on three sides of a pin or row of pins and 5 mm on the side leaving the wave as its minimum, with a nozzle at least 3 mm in inside diameter. A second maker's minimum is 1.5 mm from the soldered area to the nearest surface-mount pad for a single pin, and 2 mm for a row of pins, with a 6 mm standard nozzle. If 2 mm isn't possible on three sides, the same maker suggests aligning nearby surface-mount parts in line with the pins.

![D17: Drawn to scale, solder side of the board: a row of three through-hole pads on a 2.54 mm pitch. A white dashed line marks the recommended keep-out, 3 mm beyond the pads on three sides and 5 mm on the side leaving the wave; a red dashed line marks the 2 mm absolute minimum. A small surface-mount part sits outside it, pointing at the pins.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/selective-keepout.svg)

*D17 is drawn to scale and shows the solder side. The white dashed line is the recommended keep-out: 3 mm from the outer edge of the pads, and 5 mm on the side where the board leaves the wave. The red dashed line is the 2 mm absolute minimum. The surface-mount part outside it points at the pins rather than lying side-on to them.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Every board soldered by hand: higher cost, longer lead time and less consistent joints.

**Example:** A board had small diodes placed between its through-hole pins, so every pin had to be soldered by hand. On the next revision the diodes were moved, and the boards went through the factory on the selective soldering machine: cheaper, faster and better soldered.

**Applies to:** General practice. Nozzle sizes vary by assembler; check with yours.

**Sources:** [“The selective soldering process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971-the-selective-soldering-process) (Jan 2021), [47:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971?t=2820)–50:00; [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=1980)–35:00; [Effects of an Appropriate PCB Layout and Soldering Nozzle Design on Quality and Cost Structure in Selective Soldering Processes](https://www.electronics.org/system/files/technical_resource/E8%26S23_02.pdf) (IPC technical paper, PDF); a second selective-soldering machine maker's layout recommendations (2017).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-044: Use thermal relief on through-hole pads connected to planes

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-044

**Recommendation:** Connect through-hole pads to copper pours and planes with thermal relief (a few thin spokes), not solid copper. Use thermal relief on every layer the pad connects to, inner layers as well as outer ones.

**Why:** A plane is a heat sink. A surface-mount part on a plane still gets hot enough in the reflow oven, but a selective nozzle, a wave or a soldering iron can't put heat into a pad faster than a solid plane draws it away.

![D19: Drawn to scale, top side of the board. In both views the copper plane is under the solder mask and only the pad's mask opening is bare. With a solid connection, the opening shows copper right to its edge. With thermal relief, the pad sits in a clearance ring, joined to the plane by four thin spokes.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/thermal-relief.svg)

*D19 is drawn to scale. In both views the plane is under the solder mask; only the pad's opening is bare. Joined to the plane all round, the pad loses heat to it as fast as the soldering tool supplies it. With thermal relief, four thin spokes across a clearance ring keep the heat in the joint.*

**Typical values:** Longer, narrower spokes keep more heat in the joint (a selective-soldering machine maker's guidance).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Cold, poorly filled joints that look bad and may be weak, especially on big connectors and multilayer ground pours.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=2040)–39:00; [“The selective soldering process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971-the-selective-soldering-process) (Jan 2021), [50:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971?t=3000)–51:00; a selective-soldering machine maker's layout recommendations (2017).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-045: Match through-hole lead length to the board and the pitch

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-045

**Recommendation:** Choose through-hole parts whose leads suit your board's thickness: most parts assume a 1.6 mm board. On fine-pitch through-hole connectors (about 1.27 mm pitch and finer), avoid leads that stick out a long way. If leads must be bent or formed, show the bend angle and direction on the assembly drawing.

**Why:** Leads too short for the board don't come through to be soldered; leads too long on a fine-pitch connector bridge to each other in selective soldering. Parts with other lead lengths exist, but often have to be special-ordered.

**Typical values:** For single-nozzle selective soldering, leads sticking out about 1 mm; for multi-nozzle dip soldering, more than 2.5 mm (a selective-soldering machine maker's guidance).

![D38: Side views through two neighboring leads of a 1.27 mm-pitch connector on a 1.6 mm board. Leads sticking out about 1 mm each have a full fillet. Leads that end inside the holes have no fillet on the solder side. Leads sticking out about 4 mm are bridged by solder against the board.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/lead-length.svg)

*D38 is drawn to scale, except copper thickness. About 1 mm of lead through the board gives a full fillet and suits single-nozzle selective soldering. A lead that ends inside the hole leaves no fillet on the solder side. At fine pitch, long leads hold solder between them, and it bridges against the board.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Bridged pins, leads trimmed by hand, or parts that can't be soldered.

**Example:** A design called for a 1.2 mm board, then used hybrid parts with leads made for 1.6 mm boards on both sides. After the first side was built, the leads stuck out through the other side, so that side's stencil couldn't lie flat to print. Later builds used the same connectors with 1.2 mm leads, made for that board thickness.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The selective soldering process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971-the-selective-soldering-process) (Jan 2021), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971?t=2580)–45:00; [“An Answering Your Questions Grab Bag”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902-an-answering-your-questions-grab-bag) (Oct 2023), [42:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13847902?t=2520)–43:00; [“Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [29:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=1740)–31:00; [Effects of an Appropriate PCB Layout and Soldering Nozzle Design on Quality and Cost Structure in Selective Soldering Processes](https://www.electronics.org/system/files/technical_resource/E8%26S23_02.pdf) (IPC technical paper, PDF).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-046: Choose through-hole parts that hold themselves in place

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-046

**Recommendation:** Prefer through-hole parts that snap in or otherwise hold themselves in place. Avoid top-heavy right-angle parts, and parts that must sit at an angle or perfectly flush, unless you've agreed with your assembler how they'll be held.

**Why:** A part that drops loosely into its holes can tilt or lift while it's soldered. Holding it needs either a person or custom tooling.

**Typical values:** A handful of boards can be held and soldered by hand; thousands justify custom tooling; a few hundred is the hardest quantity, too many for hand work and too few for tooling.

![D39: Side views of the same right-angle connector at the edge of a board, before soldering, its housing reaching past the edge. With snap-in pegs it stays flat. Without them it tips forward over the edge under its own weight, lifting its pins in their holes.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/self-holding.svg)

*D39 shows the same connector twice, before soldering. Its housing reaches past the board edge, so most of its weight is in front of its pins. With snap-in pegs it stays flat through soldering with no tooling; without them it tips forward and lifts its pins unless someone or something holds it.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Crooked parts, tooling charges, or slow hand work.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Custom tooling to the rescue”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740-custom-tooling-to-the-rescue) (Jul 2022), [26:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740?t=1560)–27:00; [“The selective soldering process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971-the-selective-soldering-process) (Jan 2021), [45:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971?t=2700)–46:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

### Related pages

- [Press-fit and mechanical parts](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/06-press-fit-and-mechanical/)
