Source: https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/06-press-fit-and-mechanical/

## Press-fit and mechanical parts

Some parts aren't soldered at all, or not only soldered. Press-fit connectors and press-fit nuts are pushed into precisely sized plated holes by a press, and the tight fit makes the electrical and mechanical joint. Heat sinks, standoffs, snap-in sockets and large connectors are often held with screws, nuts or clips as well.

Press-fit is strong and reliable, and needs no heat. But each press-fit part needs its own press tooling and support under the board, so it isn't a standard step for every assembler. What your design controls is which of these parts you choose, and how clearly you tell the assembler what they need.

### PCB-DFA-047: Talk to your assembler before designing in press-fit parts

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-047

**Recommendation:** Before you commit to a press-fit part, ask your assembler whether they can press it with the equipment they have, what tooling it will need and what that will cost. Leave room on the far side of the board around each press-fit part for the support tooling. If you order through an online quoting system, check that it has priced the press-fit parts; many don't detect them.

**Why:** Each press-fit part needs a press head shaped for it and an anvil supporting the board underneath, and the board has to be supported without crushing the surface-mount parts around it. Simple parts such as press-fit nuts are usually easy with existing equipment; large press-fit connectors may need tooling made for them.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A surprise tooling charge, a delay while tooling is made, or an assembler who can't do the job.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Alternative Component Mounting”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=1080)–27:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-048: Give a torque for every screw and nut, and fasten hardware before soldering

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-048

**Recommendation:** List a torque for every screw and nut in your bill of materials or assembly drawing, not just "tight". Ask for hardware that fastens a part to the board (a connector's bolts, a regulator's heat-sink screw) to be tightened before the part is soldered.

**Why:** If a part is soldered first and then bolted down, the bolt pulls the part flat against the board and strains the joints that were made while it sat slightly high. Over time, that strain fatigues and cracks the joints. Fastened first, the joints only carry signals.

![D40: Side views of a connector bolted to the board, with three leads soldered through it. Soldered first and tightened afterwards, the flange is pulled down and bent, straining the solder joints. Tightened first and soldered afterwards, the flange sits flat and the joints carry no strain.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/bolt-first.svg)

*D40. The flange lift is exaggerated. If the leads are soldered first, tightening the bolts pulls the part down after the joints have set, and the joints take the strain. Tightened first, the part is already where it will stay when it is soldered.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Joints that pass test and crack later in the field, or hardware tightened by guesswork.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Alternative Component Mounting”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=1860)–35:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-049: Avoid soldering a connector made only for press-fit

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-049

**Recommendation:** If a connector is designed only to be pressed in, press it in. If you can't, and it has to be soldered, tell your assembler before the build.

**Why:** A press-fit connector's plastic isn't designed for soldering heat. Soldering it needs a process that gets the heat in and out quickly enough to make the joint without damaging the housing.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Melted or warped housings, or a delay while the assembler develops a special process.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The selective soldering process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971-the-selective-soldering-process) (Jan 2021), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/7337971?t=2460)–42:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### Related pages
- [Through-hole soldering](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/05-through-hole-soldering/)

---

Source: https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/07-shields-adhesives-underfill/

## Shields, adhesives and underfill

Some boards need more than solder. RF shields are small metal cans soldered over sensitive circuits. Adhesives hold heavy parts against vibration, or mount parts such as dome switches that have no solder joints. Underfill is a liquid, usually epoxy, run under a BGA and cured, to lock it to the board against shock.

Each of these is an extra step, often done by hand, and not every assembler offers all of them. What your design controls is which of them you need, and which version you choose.

### PCB-DFA-050: Choose a two-piece or clip-on RF shield for low volumes, and a one-piece shield for high volumes

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-050

**Recommendation:** For builds of up to a few hundred boards, use a two-piece shield (a frame soldered to the board and a separate lid) or shield clips, if you can afford them. For thousands of boards, use a one-piece shield, and agree with your assembler how it will be handled before production.

**Why:** A one-piece shield hides everything under it as soon as it's on, so it has to go on after the parts beneath it are soldered and inspected. That means either a second print, place and reflow pass, or hand soldering. With a two-piece shield or clips, the frame is placed and soldered with everything else, the parts inside can still be inspected, and the lid goes on at the end. A one-piece shield costs less to buy and, once the process is set up, is fully automated.

**Typical values:** Two-piece or clips: about 5 to 100 boards · one-piece: thousands (one assembler's guidance).

![D20: Drawn to scale, side views of a 1.6 mm board: a one-piece shield soldered over small parts, hiding them; and a two-piece shield, an open frame soldered around the parts with a separate lid above it.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/rf-shields.svg)

*D20 is drawn to scale. On the left, a one-piece shield: a closed metal can soldered over small parts, which hides them from inspection once it's on. On the right, a two-piece shield: an open frame soldered with the other parts, so the parts inside can still be inspected, and a lid pressed on at the end. Shield clips work the same way as a two-piece shield.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Extra handling and cost at low volume, or a delay while the assembler works out how to build a one-piece shield.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“RF Shields and Restroom Rants”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15565134-rf-shields-and-restroom-rants) (Aug 2024), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15565134?t=540)–20:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-051: Hold heavy parts down against vibration, and fit the hold-down before soldering

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-051

**Recommendation:** If heavy through-hole parts (large capacitors, batteries) must survive vibration, hold them to the board with something other than their solder joints. The most secure options use hardware: a hold-down bracket (injection-molded or 3D-printed) with screws through it and through holes in the board, and nuts on the other side; or a cable tie passed through two holes in the board and around the part. High-strength foam tape or room-temperature-curing (RTV) silicone also work. Plan the holes in your layout, fit screws, brackets and ties before the part is soldered, and agree the method with your assembler before you order.

**Why:** A heavy part shaking on its leads fatigues its solder joints until they crack. A hold-down carries the part's weight so the joints don't have to. Fitted before soldering, it leaves the joints free of strain ([PCB-DFA-048](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/06-press-fit-and-mechanical/)). Ordinary double-sided tape isn't strong or stable enough.

![D41: Side views of a 16 mm capacitor. A hold-down bracket fits over it and is screwed through the board, with nuts underneath. A capacitor lying on its side is held by a cable tie passed through two holes in the board and round it.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/hold-downs.svg)

*D41 is drawn to scale, except the board thickness. A bracket screwed through the board, or a cable tie through two holes, carries the part's weight under vibration instead of its solder joints. Plan the holes in the layout, and fit the bracket or tie before the part is soldered.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Joints that crack in the field, or an assembler who doesn't have the material or process.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Alternative Component Mounting”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [53:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=3180)–57:00; the author's own experience of screwed hold-downs and cable ties.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-052: Check part numbers so you don't order glue-mounted parts by mistake

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-052

**Recommendation:** Check the full part number of every ceramic capacitor and similar chip part to make sure it's the solder-mounted version. If your design really needs parts mounted with conductive epoxy, ask your assembler before you design them in.

**Why:** Some chip parts come in versions with terminations made for epoxy mounting, and the part numbers can differ by a single character. Most assemblers, Worthington Assembly and CircuitHub included, choose not to offer epoxy mounting.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Parts that won't solder properly, found at assembly, and a wait for the right parts.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Alternative Component Mounting”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=660)–18:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-053: Expect adhesive-mounted dome switches to need tooling

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-053

**Recommendation:** If your design uses dome switches held by an adhesive sheet, plan for the tooling, and check that your assembler will take the job at your quantity.

**Why:** The adhesive sheet is usually die-cut to match your board's switch positions, which means custom tooling before the first board.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A tooling charge you didn't plan for, or a low-volume job declined.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Alternative Component Mounting”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=2460)–44:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-054: Consider underfill or corner bonding for BGAs in products that take repeated shock

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-054

**Recommendation:** If the product will take heavy, repeated shock (mining equipment, for example), consider underfill under its BGAs, or corner bonding (adhesive at the BGA's corners only), and agree the process with your assembler.

**Why:** Repeated shock fatigues the solder balls under a BGA. Underfill fills the gap under the part and locks it to the board, so the balls don't carry the whole load.

![D42: Side and plan views of a 0.8 mm-pitch BGA. Underfill fills the whole gap under the package, round every ball, with a rounded fillet along its edges. Corner bonding puts a bead of adhesive at each corner, which wicks a little way under the package but leaves the rest of the gap open.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/underfill-corners.svg)

*D42 is drawn to scale. Underfill fills the whole gap under the package, round every ball. Corner bonding puts a bead of adhesive at each of the four corners; it wicks a little way under the package and leaves the rest of the gap open.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** BGA joints that crack in service.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“IPC APEX EXPO Meetup Recap”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15044769-ipc-apex-expo-meetup-recap) (May 2024), [15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/15044769?t=900)–16:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

### Related pages
- [Press-fit and mechanical parts](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/06-press-fit-and-mechanical/)
- [Cleaning](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/08-cleaning/)

---

Source: https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/08-cleaning/

## Cleaning

Every soldering process uses flux, and flux leaves residue. Most boards today are built with no-clean flux, whose residue is designed to be left on the board: once properly heated it is harmless, and it isn't a coating. Boards built with water-soluble flux, and boards that need to be especially clean, are washed after soldering, usually in batch or conveyor machines with a cleaning chemical, then rinsed.

Cleaning is a reliability process, not a cosmetic one. Residue becomes a problem when moisture, a conductive residue and a voltage all come together, which can grow metal between conductors (electrochemical migration). A board cleaned badly can be less reliable than one not cleaned at all.

### PCB-DFA-055: Use no-clean flux unless your product needs cleaning, and say so if it does

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-055

**Recommendation:** Build with no-clean flux and no washing unless your product needs it. If it does (high reliability, high impedance, high voltage, harsh environments, or conformal coating), say so explicitly when you order; don't assume the assembler will clean.

**Why:** For most designs, no-clean residue is safe once it's properly heated during soldering. Cleaning adds a process step with its own risks, and many assemblers run no-clean as standard and send cleaning to a specialist. Some designs need it anyway: residue matters more in high-impedance circuits, at high voltages, on very small and dense boards, and in wearable, outdoor and other harsh uses, even for an inexpensive product.

**Typical values:** Cleaning is for high-reliability uses such as aerospace, medical implants and other life-critical systems, high-voltage designs (hundreds of volts and up), and dense boards in harsh environments. How clean is "clean enough" is no longer a single pass-or-fail number: J-STD-001 now asks for objective evidence that the process is clean enough for the product, usually from surface insulation resistance (SIR) testing; ionic-contamination (ROSE) testing is a process monitor, and means little on no-clean boards.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards that need cleaning shipped uncleaned, or a cleaning step you didn't need, paid for and added risk to.

**Applies to:** General practice. Whether an assembler cleans in house varies; check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Solder paste printing”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710-solder-paste-printing) (Sep 2020), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5321710?t=720); [“The role of flux in PCB assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791051-the-role-of-flux-in-pcb-assembly) (Jun 2022), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791051?t=1320)–28:00; [“Even Cleaner Cleaning With Cleaning Expert Mike “Mr. Clean” Konrad”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11995563-even-cleaner-cleaning-with-cleaning-expert-mike-mr-clean-konrad) (Jan 2023), [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11995563?t=660)–17:00 and [37:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11995563?t=2220)–46:00; [“Board Cleaning w/ Mike Konrad (part 1)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139-board-cleaning-w-mike-konrad-part-1) (Apr 2021), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139?t=1980); J-STD-001 (cleanliness requirements).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-056: If a product works with no-clean, don't add cleaning or change the flux without a reason

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-056

**Recommendation:** If your boards are built with no-clean flux and aren't failing from residue, keep the process as it is. If you do add cleaning, add it as an extra step, and keep the same flux and soldering profile.

**Why:** The existing process is already qualified by its record. Changing the flux and adding cleaning at the same time changes two things at once, and a new cleaning step done poorly can leave a board less reliable than before.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** New failures, from a change made to fix a problem you didn't have.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Board Cleaning w/ Mike Konrad (part 1)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139-board-cleaning-w-mike-konrad-part-1) (Apr 2021), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139?t=1980)–42:00; [“Even Cleaner Cleaning With Cleaning Expert Mike “Mr. Clean” Konrad”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11995563-even-cleaner-cleaning-with-cleaning-expert-mike-mr-clean-konrad) (Jan 2023), [01:09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11995563?t=4140)–01:12:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-057: Design boards that need cleaning so the fluid can get underneath

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-057

**Recommendation:** On a board that will be washed, give parts as much clearance underneath as you can, especially bottom-terminated parts such as QFNs. Keep a solder mask dam around their pads ([PCB-DFA-032](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/)).

**Why:** Cleaning fluid has to reach under each part and be rinsed out again. A QFN sits only a couple of thousandths of an inch (about 0.05 mm) above the board, which is very hard to clean under; a BGA's balls leave a much bigger gap. At very high volumes, some makers go further and design so the board never needs cleaning: mask dams, controlled spacing and controlled voltages between conductors.

![D21: Enlarged and drawn to scale, side views: a QFN sitting about 0.05 mm above the board on its soldered pads, beside a BGA held about 0.3 mm above the board by its solder balls.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/cleaning-gap.svg)

*D21 is enlarged and drawn to scale; the gaps are approximate. On the left, a QFN sits on its soldered pads only about 0.05 mm above the board, leaving almost no room for cleaning fluid. On the right, a BGA's solder balls hold it about 0.3 mm above the board, leaving a gap the fluid can reach and rinse.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Residue trapped under parts that the wash can't reach.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Board Cleaning w/ Mike Konrad (part 2)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8488862-board-cleaning-w-mike-konrad-part-2) (May 2021), [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8488862?t=3120)–54:00; [“Board Cleaning w/ Mike Konrad (part 1)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139-board-cleaning-w-mike-konrad-part-1) (Apr 2021), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8399139?t=1980)–34:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-058: Flag parts that can't be washed, and don't wash rigid-flex boards with chemicals

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-058

**Recommendation:** If a board will be washed, list any parts that mustn't get wet, so the assembler can mask them or fit them after washing. Ask for rigid-flex boards not to be cleaned with chemicals.

**Why:** Washing gets everywhere. Parts that can't take it have to be masked, or soldered by hand after the wash, which the assembler can only plan for if they know. Chemical cleaning can damage the materials that join the rigid and flexible parts of a rigid-flex board.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Damaged parts, or a rigid-flex board that comes apart.

**Example:** A rigid-flex board cleaned with chemicals was ruined.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How New Solder Products Are Developed w/ AIM Solder Content Marketing Specialist, Gayle Towell”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14215618-how-new-solder-products-are-developed-w-aim-solder-content-marketing-specialist-gayle-towell) (Jan 2024), [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14215618?t=2160)–37:00; [“Flex & Rigid-Flex PCB Assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19401881-flex-rigid-flex-pcb-assembly) (Jun 2026), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19401881?t=720)–13:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-059: Keep small boards that need washing in their panel

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-059

**Recommendation:** If small boards need to be washed, leave them in a panel until after washing.

**Why:** Washing machines are built to hold panels of about a half to a whole sheet of paper. A board an inch square tumbles around inside one.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Back from the Dead and Back from APEX”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19107985-back-from-the-dead-and-back-from-apex) (May 2026), [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19107985?t=2160)–37:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

Source: https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/09-conformal-coating/

## Conformal coating

Conformal coating is a thin protective film (acrylic, silicone, urethane, parylene and others) applied over an assembled board to keep out moisture, dust and chemicals. It's applied by spraying, dipping, brushing or vapor deposition, often by a specialist coating contractor, and it adds cost to every board.

Coating keeps bad things off the board, but it also seals in whatever is already on it. What your design controls is whether the board is clean underneath, and which areas must stay uncoated.

### PCB-DFA-060: Clean boards before they're coated, where you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-060

**Recommendation:** If a board will be conformally coated, cleaning it first is recommended. Coating over no-clean flux residue without cleaning is common, and many boards built that way are proving reliable; if you choose it, qualify that flux and coating together for your product (for example with surface insulation resistance testing, [PCB-DFA-055](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/08-cleaning/)) rather than assuming it. Avoid treating coating as a substitute for cleaning.

**Why:** Electrochemical migration needs three things: a voltage, a conductive residue and moisture. Coating a board over residue seals the residue in, with any moisture already there, right where the voltage is. Properly heated no-clean residue is far less active than other fluxes' residue, which is why coating over it often works.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Residue trapped under the coating, and the failures you coated the board to prevent.

**Applies to:** General practice. Coating over no-clean flux is not unusual; cleaning first is still the safer choice.

**Sources:** [“Board Cleaning w/ Mike Konrad (part 2)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8488862-board-cleaning-w-mike-konrad-part-2) (May 2021), [01:06:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8488862?t=3960)–01:08:00; [“The role of flux in PCB assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791051-the-role-of-flux-in-pcb-assembly) (Jun 2022), [22:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10791051?t=1320), on no-clean residue; the author's own experience of coated no-clean boards.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

---

### PCB-DFA-061: Mark on the drawing the areas that must not be coated

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-061

**Recommendation:** On the assembly drawing, mark every area that must stay free of coating: connector mating areas, switches, test points you'll probe, and anything adjusted or contacted after assembly. Leave a few millimeters between keep-out areas and parts that must be coated.

**Why:** The coater masks or avoids exactly what the drawing shows. Selective coating machines can't hold an edge right up to a keep-out, so they need some room.

**Typical values:** About 2–3 mm is usually the closest a selective coating process can reliably hold to a keep-out edge (one industry article).

![D43: Plan view of a 60 by 40 mm board as it would appear on an assembly drawing. Areas outlined in red and labeled do not coat cover a connector's mating area, a push switch and a row of test points. The nearest part that must be coated sits 2 to 3 mm from the connector's keep-out.](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/images/coating-keepouts.svg)

*D43 is drawn to scale. Each area that must stay free of coating is outlined and labeled on the assembly drawing. Parts that must be coated sit 2–3 mm from a keep-out edge, about the closest a selective coating process can reliably hold.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Coated connectors that won't make contact, or test points that can't be probed.

**Applies to:** General practice. Whether test points are coated varies by customer; some require them coated.

**Sources:** Industry guidance on conformal coating drawings and keep-outs, including IPC-HDBK-830 (checked Nov 2026; not from the podcast).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

## Depaneling

After assembly and testing, the boards are separated from their panel. V-scored panels are snapped by hand or run through a round-blade cutter; tab-routed panels are cut at each tab with a router, nibbler or hand tool; flexible boards are cut with scissors at low volume or with a laser at higher volume. Depaneling bends and cuts the board right next to your parts, so it's where brittle parts crack.

Almost everything your design controls here is decided when the panel is designed, so the recommendations live in Part 2:

- Breakaway methods, overhanging parts, tabs and thick boards: [Breakaway methods](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/03-breakaway-methods/) (PCB-DFM-001, PCB-DFA-010 to 014).
- Distances from break lines, and ceramic capacitors: [Clearance near board and panel edges](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/) (PCB-DFA-015 to 017).

### PCB-DFA-062: Ask how flexible boards will be separated

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-062

**Recommendation:** For flexible boards, agree with your assembler how they'll be separated from their panel or carrier, and design the outline to suit.

**Why:** Routers and V-score cutters are for rigid boards. Flexible boards are cut with scissors or a knife at low volume, and with a laser at higher volume; each needs a suitable outline and access.

**Applies to:** Varies by manufacturer. Check with yours.

**Sources:** [“Flex & Rigid-Flex PCB Assembly”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19401881-flex-rigid-flex-pcb-assembly) (Jun 2026), [25:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19401881?t=1500)–26:00; [“PCB Depaneling”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8035612-pcb-depaneling) (Mar 2021), for the chapter opening.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

## Rework and repair

Rework is removing and replacing parts on an assembled board, by hand with a soldering iron, or with a hot-air or infrared rework station for BGAs and other parts with hidden joints. It's slow, skilled work, and every rework heats the board and its neighbors again.

Much of what makes a board reworkable is decided elsewhere: space around parts ([PCB-DFA-023](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/02-component-placement/)), package choice ([PCB-DFA-021 and 022](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/02-component-placement/)), and reflow ratings that allow another heat cycle ([PCB-DFA-026](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/)). This page covers sending boards back to be fixed.

### PCB-DFA-063: Before sending boards back for repair, find the failing part and get a return number

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-063

**Recommendation:** Before you send failed boards back to your assembler, narrow the failure down to a part if you can, and tell them which part to replace. Get a return authorization (RMA) number first, and pack the boards the way they were sent to you, in proper static-shielding packaging.

**Why:** An assembler has the tools to replace parts you can't, such as a BGA, but boards that arrive with no explanation can't be fixed efficiently. If every board fails the same way, the cause has to be found before anything is replaced. Boards repacked in unshielded bags can be damaged by static on the way back.

**Typical values:** For an inexpensive board (around $20), replacing a fine-pitch BGA can cost more than the board, so a refund or replacement may be offered instead.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Delays, boards repaired without the real fault being found, or new damage in shipping.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Debugging PCB Assemblies”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945-debugging-pcb-assemblies) (May 2022), [15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945?t=900)–19:00; [“How Blue Robotics is enabling the next generation of ocean exploration robots w/ Rustom Jehangir”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597-how-blue-robotics-is-enabling-the-next-generation-of-ocean-exploration-robots-w-rustom-jehangir) (Mar 2021), [53:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597?t=3180)–55:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-04*

## Design for test: test points and access

Every assembled board has to be tested to prove it works. That's much easier if the designer planned for it. A tester needs places to touch the board, a way to program it, and somewhere to hold it. None of these can be added after the board is made, but most of them cost almost nothing if they're in the first layout. For small builds, under about 1,000 boards, most customers test the boards themselves. For larger volumes, it's normal for the assembler to test the boards on the customer's behalf. Either way, the test plan has to start with you, because only you know what the board is meant to do.

### PCB-DFT-005: Decide how each board will be tested while you design it, and test boards before they go into anything expensive

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-005

**Recommendation:** Make testing one of the product's requirements from the first day of design. Decide who will test each board: you, your assembler or a test house. Decide how it will be tested: by flying probe, in a fixture, by a functional test or by boundary scan. Test each board before it goes into a finished product, a chassis or any other step that takes real time or money. Bring your firmware engineers in early, because the test usually needs help from the firmware.

**Why:** Test points, a programming connection, room for probes and tooling holes are all part of the layout. If they're missing, adding them means a new board revision. Firmware engineers write their code differently when they know from the start that it needs a test mode. Test code added at the last minute tends to have bugs, and those bugs show up as boards failing test when nothing is wrong with them. A bad board found after it's built into a product costs you the assembly time as well as the board. It's also much harder to find the fault once the board is inside the product.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You end up with a design that works but can't be tested without a redesign. Or the test fixture costs thousands more than it needed to. Or faulty boards are found only after hours of final assembly.

**Example:** One customer's finished product took about 17 hours to assemble after the boards arrived, and the boards weren't being tested before that work started. Another built boards into a chassis that took about three hours to assemble before anything was powered. In both cases a simple board test first would have caught faults before the expensive part of the build. A purchasing manager once asked an assembler to guarantee that every board would work, for a design with no test of any kind. There was no way to do it.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [01:02:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3720)–01:06:00; [“Debugging PCB Assemblies”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945-debugging-pcb-assemblies) (May 2022), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945?t=300)–06:00; [“Inevitable Failures”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984-inevitable-failures) (Aug 2025), [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984?t=1860)–38:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-006: Write the test plan yourself, as numbered requirements tied to named test points

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-006

**Recommendation:** Write a test plan for every board, even a short one, and keep it with the design files. Make each step a numbered requirement that either passes or fails. Tie each step to a named test point, connector pin or function. For example: "Step 3.1: TP4 reads 3.3 V, within 3%." "Step 4.2: firmware version 2.1 loads." "Step 5.1: LED D3 lights during boot." Write the plan as plain text that anyone can open, not only inside one test system's software. When a board fails in the field in a way the plan didn't catch, add a step that would have caught it.

**Why:** You know what the board is meant to do, but the assembler and the fixture builder don't. That's especially true when you've used a common part in an unusual way. A step tied to a test point can be built into any fixture, by anyone. When a board fails, the report can name the step it failed. A vague check like "it works" can't be repeated, and it doesn't tell anyone where to look. A plain-text plan is easy to review, easy to compare between revisions, and easy to move to a different tester later.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** The assembler or fixture builder has to guess what matters. They may test the wrong things, or nothing at all. Failed boards come back marked "doesn't work".

**Example:** One fixture builder says only about half of its customers arrive with a test plan. It would much rather start from one, because the designer knows the product best.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Smarter Test Plans for Inevitable Failures w/ Blue Clover CEO & Co-founder, Pete Staples”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982-smarter-test-plans-for-inevitable-failures-w-blue-clover-ceo-co-founder-pete-staples) (Oct 2025), [21:30](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=1290)–23:00 and [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=1980)–36:30; [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [56:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3360)–01:00:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-007: Put a test point on every net you want to test, and on every net if you want in-circuit test

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-007

**Recommendation:** Give every net in your test plan its own test point. If the board will get an in-circuit test, by flying probe or in a bed-of-nails fixture, aim for a test point on every net. Make a list of any nets you leave without one on purpose. Place test points while you lay out the board, not after the routing is finished. Give the fixture builder a list of the test points, with each one's net name, its X and Y position from the board's origin, and which side of the board it's on. Don't tie a part's control pins, such as enable or output-enable, straight to ground or to the supply. Connect them through a resistor, so the tester can override them.

**Why:** In-circuit test checks each part by measuring between nets with the power off. If the tester can't touch a net, it can't check that net or any part on it. Probing a part's own pad or lead instead is less reliable, because the probe can slip, mark the joint or miss it. Test points are cheap to place early, and very hard to squeeze into a finished, dense layout. A control pin tied straight to ground or the supply can't be changed by the tester, so it can't run its standard test on that part.

**Typical values:** For full in-circuit test, one test point on every net. IPC-2221C asks for a test land on every node, and says fewer are needed when boundary scan is used. For functional test, a test point on each net the test plan measures.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Faults on nets the tester can't reach go undetected. If too many nets are missing, in-circuit test stops being worth paying for.

**Example:** At one consumer-products company, the boards were so small that not enough test points would fit for in-circuit test to be worth doing, so they relied on functional test alone.

**Applies to:** General practice. How close to full coverage is worth paying for depends on volume and on what a missed fault would cost.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=1260)–22:00 and [57:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3420); IPC-2221C (December 2023), sections 3.6.5.1 and 3.6.5.2; fixture makers' and test houses' published design-for-test guides.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-008: Make test points surface-mount pads at least 0.9 mm in diameter and 1.9 mm apart, with no paste

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-008

**Recommendation:** Make each test point a surface-mount copper pad with the solder mask pulled back from it. Make it at least 0.9 mm in diameter, and 1.0 mm if you can. Round pads are the usual choice, but square pads are fine too and give the probe more room to land. For a square pad, use the same numbers for the length of each side. Space test points at least 1.9 mm (75 mil) apart, center to center, and 2.54 mm (100 mil) if you can. Leave paste off the test points (see [PCB-DFA-019](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/#pcb-dfa-019-put-paste-on-every-pad-you-want-soldered-and-only-those)). The one exception is a board with an OSP finish, where you should put paste on the test points so they're solder-coated. Print the net name in silkscreen beside each pad. If someone needs to clip a meter or scope probe on by hand, use a surface-mount test point (a small metal loop made for reflow), not a through-hole one. Tell your assembler on the assembly drawing whether the test points must stay free of flux and solder. If the test points won't be used in production, say that too.

**Why:** A probe never lands exactly on target, because the fixture and the board both have tolerances. A bigger pad means the probe still hits it. A square pad has about 27% more area than a round pad whose diameter equals the square's side. IPC-2221C asks for test points to be solder-coated, or to have a surface finish that doesn't oxidize. ENIG, HASL, immersion silver and immersion tin don't oxidize the way bare copper does, so on those boards the finish is enough. Solder on a test point makes a dome that a probe can slide off, so avoid it on boards with those finishes. OSP is different, because it leaves bare copper that oxidizes, and probes can't make good contact through the oxide. So on an OSP board, a thin coat of solder on each test point is better than bare copper. Spacing decides which probes will fit. At 2.54 mm, the fixture can use standard probes, which are the sturdiest and cheapest. Closer spacing needs thinner probes, which cost more, bend more easily and wear out faster. A flying-probe tester can reach much smaller pads than a fixture can. So a board laid out for a fixture can always be flying-probed, but not the other way round. A surface-mount test point is placed by the machine and soldered in reflow with everything else, so it adds almost nothing to the cost. A through-hole test point has to be fitted by hand and soldered afterwards, often by selective soldering, which is slower and harder than reflow. Test points that must stay clean also have to be protected during selective soldering, and that can get in the way of soldering nearby through-hole parts. If the assembler knows the test points won't be used, it doesn't have to protect them, and selective soldering is much easier.

**Typical values:**

| Test point | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| Pad diameter | 0.9 mm | 1.0 mm or more |
| Center-to-center spacing | 1.9 mm (75 mil) | 2.54 mm (100 mil) |

IPC-2221C says a test land used for probing should be at least 0.9 mm in diameter. It says 0.6 mm is possible on boards smaller than 7,700 mm². It also asks for test lands on 2.5 mm centers where possible, so standard probes can be used. One test-equipment maker's fixture specification asks for test points at least 1.0 mm in diameter and at least 2.0 mm apart. The fixture builder on the podcast gives 0.8 mm as its minimum. Some published guides say 1.27 mm (50 mil) spacing is possible, but it costs more. Flying-probe testers can usually probe pads of 0.5 mm or smaller, but check with yours.

![D61: Plan view of the corner of a board, drawn to scale. Three round test points, each a copper pad 1.0 mm in diameter with the mask cleared, sit 2.54 mm apart. An 0603 resistor sits 1 mm from the first. A fourth test point is kept 5 mm from a tall radial capacitor, and the 5 mm zone around the capacitor is shaded. The strip along the edge of the board is marked at 3 mm and 5 mm.](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/images/test-points.svg)

*D61 is drawn to scale. The test points are pads 1.0 mm in diameter, 2.54 mm apart, each with its name in silkscreen. The nearest short part is 1 mm away. The tall capacitor has a 5 mm zone around it where a probe can't reach. No test point is within 5 mm of the edge of the board.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Probes miss their pads, and good boards fail the test. Or the fixture costs more because it needs fine probes.

**Applies to:** General practice. Check the minimum sizes with whoever builds your fixture.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [57:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3420)–58:00; [“All the Tricks and Gotchas in Surface Mount Assembly (Repost from the Coriolis Effect)”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453-all-the-tricks-and-gotchas-in-surface-mount-assembly-repost-from-the-coriolis-effect) (Jul 2022), [01:20:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11006453?t=4800); [“When to use through hole vs surface mount components”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410-when-to-use-through-hole-vs-surface-mount-components) (Jul 2021), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410?t=1080)–22:00; Chris Denney (author); IPC-2221C (December 2023), section 3.6.5.1; a test-equipment maker's in-circuit test fixture specification (April 2020); fixture makers' and test houses' published design-for-test guides.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-009: Keep test points on one side, clear of tall parts and the board edge, and off connector solder joints

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-009

**Recommendation:** Put all the test points on one side of the board, top or bottom. Choose the side with fewer or shorter parts. Keep each test point at least 1 mm from the body of a short surface-mount part. Keep it 5 mm away from tall parts such as connectors, electrolytic capacitors and transformers. Keep test points at least 3 mm from the edges of the board, and 5 mm if you can, because conveyors and fixtures grip the edges (see [PCB-DFA-015](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/04-edge-clearance/#pcb-dfa-015-keep-parts-and-exposed-copper-at-least-3-mm-from-the-edges-5-mm-if-you-can)). If a signal goes to a through-hole connector, add a test point on that net instead of probing the connector's solder joint. Don't use gold edge-connector fingers as test points, because probes damage them. Avoid using vias as test points. A dedicated pad is more reliable, and a tented via can't be probed at all. Spread the test points evenly over the board, rather than bunching them in one area.

**Why:** A fixture that probes one side needs only one plate of probes. Probing both sides needs a second plate, lined up with the first. That costs more, and it's less reliable over the life of the fixture. A probe is a long, thin pin held in a plate. Next to a tall part, the plate has to be cut away and the probe made much longer, if it fits at all. After wave or selective soldering, the joints on a through-hole connector are covered in flux. Probes that land on flux get dirty quickly and stop making good contact. IPC-2221C allows through-hole pins to be used as test points to save space, but a dedicated pad is more reliable. When the test points are bunched in one area, the probes push harder there, so the board flexes and the vacuum seal in the fixture can leak.

**Typical values:** IPC-2221C gives a simple rule for the space around a test point. The clear space should be 80% of the height of the nearest part. It should never be less than 0.6 mm, and it never needs to be more than 5.0 mm. For example, next to a part 2 mm tall, keep 1.6 mm clear. On the side being probed, IPC-2221C says parts shouldn't be taller than 5.7 mm. Taller parts need cut-outs in the fixture, and test points should be 5.0 mm away from them. Keep test points at least 3 mm from the edge of the board, and 5 mm if you can. IPC-2221C also says 3.0 mm. One test-equipment maker's fixture specification asks for at least 2 mm between a test point and any part, and between a test point and the edge of the board.

![D62: Side views, drawn to scale. Left, marked good: a 1.6 mm board with its parts on top and all its test points underneath, probed by short spring probes rising from one 10 mm plate. Right, marked to avoid: the same board with a test point on top, 1 mm from an 11.5 mm tall capacitor, reached by a long probe from a top plate that needs a cut-out over the tall parts.](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/images/probe-access.svg)

*D62 is drawn to scale. On the left, all the test points are on the side with no parts, so one plate of short probes reaches them all. On the right, a test point on top sits 1 mm from a tall capacitor. To reach it, the fixture needs a second plate cut away around the parts, and a probe longer than the capacitor, squeezed into the 1 mm gap.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** The fixture costs more and wears out faster. Some nets may not be reachable at all.

**Example:** One fixture probed the flux-covered leads of through-hole parts with cup-tipped probes. It worked on the first day. Within a week, flux had built up in the probe tips, and good boards kept failing. The probes had to be wire-brushed several times a day and replaced every couple of weeks, instead of every six months.

**Applies to:** General practice. A flying-probe tester can reach both sides, but testing one side is still faster and cheaper.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=2040)–38:00, [58:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3480) and [01:06:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3960)–01:07:00; IPC-2221C (December 2023), section 3.6.5.1 and Figures 3-2 to 3-4; IPC-SMEMA-9851 (conveyor edge grip); one contract manufacturer's published design guidelines for in-circuit testability (2020); a test-equipment maker's in-circuit test fixture specification (April 2020).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-010: Avoid potentiometers, DIP switches and jumpers that someone has to set by hand

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-010

**Recommendation:** Avoid parts that someone has to adjust or set by hand during production, such as trimming potentiometers, DIP switches and jumpers. Set the value in firmware, with a fixed resistor, or with a digital potentiometer that the test can adjust. If you can't avoid a mechanical part, give its setting in the test plan and on the assembly drawing.

**Why:** Every hand adjustment is a step someone can forget or get wrong, and a test can't easily check it. Setting a potentiometer means probing and turning it at the same time, one board at a time. These parts are often through-hole too, which adds a soldering step. Switches can also get knocked out of position after the board has been tested.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards ship with switches in the wrong position, or with trimmers never set. Testing is slow, and the result depends on who did it.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Smarter Test Plans for Inevitable Failures w/ Blue Clover CEO & Co-founder, Pete Staples”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982-smarter-test-plans-for-inevitable-failures-w-blue-clover-ceo-co-founder-pete-staples) (Oct 2025), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=1440)–25:00; [“When to use through hole vs surface mount components”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8803410-when-to-use-through-hole-vs-surface-mount-components) (Jul 2021).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

- [Flying probe and in-circuit test](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/02-flying-probe-and-ict/)
- [Functional test and fixtures](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/05-functional-test-and-fixtures/)
- [Conformal coating](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/09-conformal-coating/) (keeping test points free of coating)

Source: https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/02-flying-probe-and-ict/

## Flying probe and in-circuit test

In-circuit test (ICT) checks that the right parts are fitted, the right way round, and soldered. It does this by measuring between nets with the power off. It finds shorts, opens, wrong values, and missing or backwards parts, and it says exactly where they are. It doesn't prove the board works. That's the job of a functional test. There are two ways to do it. A flying-probe tester moves a few probes around the board from point to point, and needs no tooling. A bed-of-nails fixture has a probe for every test point and touches them all at once.

### PCB-DFT-011: Choose flying probe or a bed-of-nails fixture by volume, and design for the one you'll use

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-011

**Recommendation:** For prototypes, small batches and designs that are still changing, plan on a flying-probe test, or none. For steady production in the thousands, consider a bed-of-nails fixture. If you do, lay the board out for it from the start. That means a test point on every net (PCB-DFT-007), pads big enough and far enough apart for a fixture (PCB-DFT-008), all on one side (PCB-DFT-009), and tooling holes in the board (PCB-DFT-001). If you're not sure which you'll use, lay the board out for a fixture anyway, because it can always be flying-probed too. Before you finish the layout, ask your assembler or test house what equipment they have and what they'd recommend for your volume.

**Why:** A flying-probe tester only needs a program made from your design data, so it costs little to set up. It can probe both sides of the board and reach small pads. But it moves its probes one point at a time, so it can take minutes to test each board. A fixture tests a board in seconds, because it touches every test point at once. But it has to be designed and built for one revision of the board, and changed whenever a test point moves. So a fixture is only worth its cost when it's spread over a lot of boards. Both kinds of tester learn what a good board looks like by measuring known-good boards, so they work best once the design has settled.

**Typical values:** Fixtures come in two grades. A development fixture is made of acrylic or MDF and lasts for a few hundred boards. A production fixture is made of FR4 about 10 mm thick and lasts for tens or hundreds of thousands of boards. A custom production fixture can cost tens of thousands of dollars. In 2025, one test company put a fixture at about $50,000 and a high-end in-circuit tester at about $1,000,000. Prices vary widely and will change. Between a home-made fixture and a high-end tester, there are simpler production test systems built around your test plan.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You pay for a fixture before the design has settled, and then pay again to rebuild it. Or a high-volume board spends minutes on a flying-probe tester. Or the layout doesn't allow either kind of test.

**Example:** One fixture builder starts by asking every customer how many boards they'll build a year. At 1,000 a year, a $100,000 fixture doesn't make sense. At a million a year, it does.

**Applies to:** General practice. What's available varies by assembler and test house.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=780)–14:00, [20:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=1200)–24:00 and [59:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3540)–01:00:00; [“Smarter Test Plans for Inevitable Failures w/ Blue Clover CEO & Co-founder, Pete Staples”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982-smarter-test-plans-for-inevitable-failures-w-blue-clover-ceo-co-founder-pete-staples) (Oct 2025), [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=1020)–18:00; test houses' published comparisons of flying-probe and fixture test.

Source: https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/03-boundary-scan/

## Boundary scan

Boundary scan is test circuitry built into many processors, FPGAs and other large chips. It's defined in the standard IEEE 1149.1, and it's often called JTAG, after the group that wrote it. Through four or five wires, a tester can take control of every pin on those chips. It can drive the pins and read them, so it can check the connections between chips without a probe on each net. It's useful on dense boards where test points won't fit, and under BGAs, whose pins nobody can touch.

### PCB-DFT-012: Where test points won't fit, use boundary scan: choose parts that support it and bring the chain to a connector

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-012

**Recommendation:** If the board is too dense for a test point on every net, plan for boundary scan from the start of the design. Where you have a choice, pick parts that support boundary scan. Get each part's boundary-scan description file (called a BSDL file) from its maker. Link the parts into a chain: each part's TDO pin goes to the next part's TDI pin. The TCK and TMS signals go to every part in the chain. Bring the chain out to a connector or a set of test pads, with a ground pin beside the signals. Follow each chip maker's advice on pull-up and pull-down resistors, and on terminating TCK. If the advice isn't clear, leave pads for both a pull-up and a pull-down, so either can be fitted. Make sure nothing on the board stops a chip from going into test mode, such as a pin that has to be held high or low, or a part that needs firmware before its pins work.

**Why:** Each boundary-scan part can drive and read its own pins. So a tester can check every connection between two of these parts without touching the nets at all. It can also check many connections to simpler parts, such as memory. That can replace some or all of an in-circuit test fixture. But it only works if the parts support it, the chain is complete and can be reached, and the board lets the chips go into test mode. None of that can be added after the layout is done. The same connector is often used for programming and debugging too (see [Programming](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/04-programming/)).

**Typical values:** Boundary scan uses four signals: TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO. Some parts add a fifth, a reset called TRST. The connector also needs ground. Chip makers commonly suggest pull-up resistors of 1 kΩ to 10 kΩ on TMS and TDI. They also want TCK and TRST held at a set level, but they don't all agree on how, so follow each part's datasheet.

![D64: Block diagram, not to scale. A six-pin connector carries TCK, TMS, TRST, TDI, TDO and ground. TDI runs into U1, U1's TDO into U2, U2's TDO into U3, and U3's TDO back to the connector, forming one chain; TCK, TMS and TRST run to all three chips. TMS and TDI are pulled up and TRST pulled down. A memory chip without boundary scan is wired to U1.](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/images/boundary-scan-chain.svg)

*D64 is a block diagram, not to scale. The test data runs through each boundary-scan part in turn, from TDI to TDO, and back to the connector. The clock and control signals go to every part at once. The memory has no boundary scan of its own, but its connections to U1 can still be tested through U1's pins.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** On a dense board, the only way left to test the connections under the BGAs is a functional test. A functional test often can't tell you which joint has failed.

**Applies to:** Boards with large digital parts that support boundary scan, such as processors, FPGAs and CPLDs. Boundary scan needs its own software and controller, and the first project takes some setting up.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=1440)–27:00; IEEE 1149.1; chip makers' JTAG pin and termination guidance; boundary-scan tool makers' design-for-test guides.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

- [Programming](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/04-programming/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/04-programming/

## Programming

Most boards have at least one part that needs software before it will work, such as a microcontroller, an FPGA's configuration memory or a programmable clock. There are three times the software can be loaded. It can go into the loose parts before assembly, done by a distributor, a programming house or the assembler. It can go into the finished board through a connection on the board. Or you can load it yourself after the boards arrive. Whichever you choose, the board and the paperwork have to allow for it.

### PCB-DFT-013: Give every programmable part a programming connection the assembler can reach: pads for a spring-pin cable, or a test fixture

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-013

**Recommendation:** If the parts aren't programmed before assembly, bring the programming signals to one place on the board that can be reached after assembly. Include ground, and power and reset if the part's programming interface needs them. Use a footprint of plain pads made for a spring-pin programming cable, with its locating holes, rather than fitting a connector. Better still, put the programming signals on test points, so the test fixture programs the board as part of its test. Put the pads on the same side as the test points (PCB-DFT-009). Keep parts, tracks and vias out of the area the cable maker marks as a keep-out. Leave paste off the pads. Say on the assembly drawing or in the test plan whether the programmer powers the board, or whether the board needs its own power.

**Why:** A pad footprint adds nothing to the BOM and no step to assembly. The cable's locating pins line it up the same way every time. A header costs a part and a placement, often needs through-hole soldering, and stays on the board for its whole life for a job done once. A fixture that touches every test point can reach the programming pads at the same time. So the board is programmed and tested in one step, in one place, which is the quickest and most repeatable way of all. A programming connection hidden under a part, behind a tall connector, or on the other side from everything else has to be reached by hand, one board at a time.

**Typical values:** Each cable maker publishes its own footprint. D63 shows one maker's six-pin footprint, for a cable without retaining legs. It has six round pads 0.787 mm in diameter, in two rows of three on a 1.27 mm (50 mil) grid. Three non-plated holes 0.991 mm in diameter locate the cable. There's one hole at one end and two at the other, so the cable only fits one way. The maker asks for no tracks or vias between the two rows of pads. Nothing else should come within 0.5 mm (0.020 in) of a pad. The pads get no paste. Use the exact footprint for the cable you'll use. List it on the BOM as do-not-fit, so nobody tries to buy a part for it.

![D63: Plan view, drawn to scale. Six round copper pads 0.787 mm in diameter in two rows of three on a 1.27 mm grid, numbered 1, 3, 5 along the bottom and 2, 4, 6 along the top, with traces leaving each pad outwards. Three non-plated holes 0.991 mm in diameter: one at the pin-1 end on the center line, and two at the far end, 2.03 mm apart. The area between the rows is a shaded keep-out, and a dashed circle shows the 0.5 mm clearance round one pad.](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/images/spring-pin-pads.svg)

*D63 is drawn to scale, from one cable maker's published footprint. The cable's spring pins land on the six pads, and its three locating pins drop into the holes. The holes are placed so the cable only fits one way.*

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Every board has to be programmed by hand, with a clip or flying leads. Or you pay for a connector on every board. Or nobody can reach the part once the board is built.

**Applies to:** Varies by assembler, so ask yours which method and cable it uses. Parts programmed before assembly don't need a connection on the board, but one is still useful for updates and repairs.

**Sources:** Chris Denney (author); a spring-pin programming-cable maker's published footprint for its six-pin cable without legs (Rev B); chip makers' programming-interface guidance. Not covered in the podcast.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-014: Say where each chip gets programmed, and give the exact file, version and checksum

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-014

**Recommendation:** For every programmable part, say who programs it and when. That could be before assembly, on the finished board by the assembler, or by you. Give the exact file to load, its version number and its checksum. Also give any settings that go with it, such as fuse or option bytes, read-out protection, and serial numbers if each board gets its own. Mark pre-programmed parts on the BOM with the file version, so a blank part can't be fitted by mistake (see [PCB-DFA-071](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/#pcb-dfa-071-mark-do-not-place-and-customer-supplied-lines-clearly)). Before the production run, have whoever will do the programming send you a few samples, and approve them.

**Why:** "Load the latest firmware" leaves the programmer guessing which file you mean. A checksum is the only quick way to prove the right file went in. Programming loose parts needs a socket made for that exact package. If the programming house doesn't have one, buying it is expensive and slow. Settings outside the main file, such as protection bits, are easy to forget, and some can't be changed once they're set. Checking a few samples before the run stops a wrong or old file being loaded into a thousand parts.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A thousand chips get the wrong file. Or read-out protection is left off. Or blank chips are fitted where programmed ones should be.

**Example:** One distributor's programming service checks the code first, then checks it has the right socket for the package. It programs a few samples for the customer to approve before it programs the rest. It doesn't want to program 1,000 controllers and then find out the code was wrong.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“The role of electronic components distributors w/ Digi-key”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8655719-the-role-of-electronic-components-distributors-w-digi-key) (Jun 2021), [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8655719?t=2580)–46:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-015: Build a test mode into the production firmware rather than a separate test image

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-015

**Recommendation:** Give the production firmware a test mode that the test fixture can switch on. For example, the fixture could hold a pin low at power-up, or send a command. In test mode, the fixture should be able to read sensors, drive outputs and get results back. Program each board once, with the production firmware, and test it in that state. Make sure the test mode can't be switched on by accident in use.

**Why:** With only the normal firmware, the board does things on its own schedule. A relay switches or a sensor is read when the firmware decides, so the test can't predict what to measure, and it checks much less. Separate test firmware solves that, but then every board has to be programmed twice: once to test, and again to ship. Each pass can take 30 seconds or more in the fixture, and you pay for both. A test mode puts the board in a known state with only one programming pass. Firmware engineers need to know about it from the start, because a test mode added late tends to have bugs that make good boards fail.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You pay for every board to be programmed twice. Or the test can't check much, because the board won't do what it's told.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [53:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3180)–55:00 and [01:03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3780)–01:04:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

- [Consignment and spares](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/05-consignment-and-spares/)
- [Boundary scan](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/03-boundary-scan/) (the same connector often serves for both)

Source: https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/05-functional-test-and-fixtures/

## Functional test and fixtures

A functional test powers the board up and checks that it does its job. The power supplies come up, the firmware loads, the inputs read correctly and the outputs work. It's usually done in a fixture that holds the board and touches its test points with spring-loaded probes. The fixture then runs through the test plan automatically. A good fixture tests a board in seconds and says exactly what failed. A poor one fails good boards and wears out quickly.

### PCB-DFT-016: Make every test failure point to a place on the board

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-016

**Recommendation:** Write each test step so that a failure names the part of the circuit involved, not just "fail". Report the step number and where on the board the problem is. For example, "Step 3.1 failed: 3.3 V rail low, check U4, L2 and C17" is far more useful than "power failure". "USB port 3 of 12 failed" is far more useful than "USB failure". Where you can, make each step a simple electrical check, such as a voltage, a current or a reply from a chip. Don't recreate real-world conditions, such as spraying water on a water sensor, unless the product truly needs it.

**Why:** The person repairing a failed board needs to know where to look. If a board with 400 parts just "fails the test", the fault could be in any of them. If the failure names three parts, it can be fixed in minutes. Simple electrical checks are fast, repeatable and cheap to build into a fixture. Recreating real-world conditions is slow, and it adds more things that can go wrong in the fixture itself.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Failed boards take hours to diagnose, or get set aside and never fixed.

**Example:** One customer built a test fixture with a small screen that listed the parts involved in each failure, such as U1, R13, C43 and J4. The assembler called it "solid gold", because every failed board came back with the likely parts already named.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“Debugging PCB Assemblies”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945-debugging-pcb-assemblies) (May 2022), [08:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945?t=480)–10:00; [“Smarter Test Plans for Inevitable Failures w/ Blue Clover CEO & Co-founder, Pete Staples”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982-smarter-test-plans-for-inevitable-failures-w-blue-clover-ceo-co-founder-pete-staples) (Oct 2025), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=1620)–30:30; [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=1680)–31:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-017: Match the fixture to the volume, and send spare boards to the people building it

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-017

**Recommendation:** Choose the fixture to suit the number of boards it will test. Use a simple development fixture for prototypes and the first few hundred boards. Use a production fixture for steady volume. Have it built by people who build fixtures for a living. Ask for the probes to sit in sockets (receptacles), not soldered in, so worn probes can be swapped. Send the fixture builder several assembled boards, not just one. Send the schematic, the fabrication data and a 3D model of the board too. Allow time, because a custom fixture takes weeks to design and build, and often needs a revision or two.

**Why:** A fixture is a machine that has to work thousands of times. Its probes wear, collect flux and stick, and they need replacing. A cheap, improvised fixture works at first, but in the end it costs more in repairs and failed good boards than a well-built one. Boards sometimes get damaged while a fixture is being developed, so the builder needs spares. The same goes for other custom production tooling, such as carriers and holding fixtures for assembly. Often nobody finds out it's needed until the first larger build.

**Typical values:** A development fixture is made of acrylic or MDF and lasts for a couple of hundred boards. A production fixture is made of FR4 plates about 10 mm thick and lasts for tens or hundreds of thousands of boards. Probes last about six months when they land on clean pads, but as little as two weeks on flux-covered joints. Custom tooling takes about two weeks to design, plus time to make it, try it and revise it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Good boards fail, or bad boards pass because a probe isn't really touching them. A poor fixture can even damage the boards it tests.

**Example:** At one company, a spring-loaded probe in the fixture kept sticking. When it stuck, the board's ground was left floating during the test, and the same diode burned out on board after board. Once someone spotted the pattern, the repair became routine: "replace D1, check probe 13". But the fault was in the fixture, not the boards. Another customer's home-made fixtures were held together with wires and hot glue. They worked, but they needed constant repair.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“How to develop a PCBA functional test system w/ FixturFab”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478-how-to-develop-a-pcba-functional-test-system-w-fixturfab) (Feb 2022), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=780)–14:00, [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=2040)–38:00, [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3120) and [56:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10100478?t=3360); [“Inevitable Failures”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984-inevitable-failures) (Aug 2025), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984?t=1440)–28:00; [“Custom tooling to the rescue”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740-custom-tooling-to-the-rescue) (Jul 2022), [15:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10804740?t=900)–17:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFT-018: Agree with your assembler what happens to boards that fail

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-018

**Recommendation:** Before the first production run, agree with whoever tests the boards what happens to a board that fails.
- Label it straight away with the step it failed, on a printed label rather than a note on masking tape.
- Put it in an ESD-safe bin, away from the good boards.
- Tell you about each failure straight away, not in a batch at the end of the run.
- Record every repair, even when nobody knows why replacing a part fixed the board.
- Keep any parts that were removed, so they can go back to the supplier.
- Keep a shared log of each failure and what fixed it, so the next board with the same failure is quick to repair.

When you send boards back for repair, get a return number (RMA) first. Find the cause yourself first if you can. Pack the boards as carefully as they came to you, in ESD-shielding bags (see Part 7).

**Why:** Anyone can diagnose a board later if it's labeled with the step it failed. Nobody can diagnose "doesn't work". One failure on its own often doesn't tell you much. Several boards with the same failure usually point to one cause, such as a wrong part value, a bad reel, a stencil problem or the fixture itself. So if failures are rare, it usually pays to let a few identical ones build up and look at them together. If a lot of boards in one batch fail, look at them straight away. A part that's replaced and thrown away without a record hides the pattern, and loses the evidence the supplier needs. Boards sent back loose, or in the wrong bag, can be damaged again on the way. The assembler then has to record that damage before it can repair them.

**Typical values:** In one example, 30 failures out of a batch of 500 was enough to investigate straight away. Otherwise, collect 20 to 40 similar failures before digging in. For a cheap board with a fault that's hard to repair, such as a failed fine-pitch BGA, replacing the board may cost less than repairing it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Failed boards get mixed back in with good ones. The same fault is diagnosed from scratch every time. Or a whole batch is sent back with no idea what's wrong with it.

**Example:** In one investigation, 35 of 40 failed boards turned out to have the same cause. At one contract manufacturer, technicians used to swap out a part that fixed a failing board, throw the old part away and say nothing. Nobody could spot the pattern or send the part back to the supplier. The company's rule became "share bad news immediately".

**Applies to:** General practice. It matters most for repeat production. Small builds are often tested by the customer, but at larger volumes the assembler usually does the testing.

**Sources:** [“Smarter Test Plans for Inevitable Failures w/ Blue Clover CEO & Co-founder, Pete Staples”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982-smarter-test-plans-for-inevitable-failures-w-blue-clover-ceo-co-founder-pete-staples) (Oct 2025), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=1620)–33:00 and [39:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=2340)–41:00; [“Debugging PCB Assemblies”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945-debugging-pcb-assemblies) (May 2022), [09:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10713945?t=540)–22:00; [“Inevitable Failures”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984-inevitable-failures) (Aug 2025), [24:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984?t=1440)–28:00; [“How Blue Robotics is enabling the next generation of ocean exploration robots w/ Rustom Jehangir”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597-how-blue-robotics-is-enabling-the-next-generation-of-ocean-exploration-robots-w-rustom-jehangir) (Mar 2021), [53:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597?t=3180)–55:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*
