Source: https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/06-burn-in-and-stress/

## Burn-in, stress testing and early failures

Even a well-designed, well-built batch has a few boards that fail early. The cause might be a weak solder joint, a part with a hidden flaw, or a little moisture damage. Most of these boards fail in the first hours or weeks of use. After that, the failure rate drops to a low, steady level for the rest of the product's life. Engineers draw this as the left-hand side of a "bathtub curve". A production test proves a board works today. Stress screening tries to make the weak boards fail in the factory, before they reach a customer.

### PCB-DFT-019: Decide whether your product needs thermal cycling or burn-in, ask for it by name, and don't mistake a line test for validation

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFT-019

**Recommendation:** For each product, decide whether the boards need stress screening before they ship. If they do, decide which kind, for how long, and to what limits. Write it in the test plan, and agree it with your assembler before they quote. Thermal cycling takes boards hot and cold over and over, with a pause at each end. It's usually the better screen for assembly defects. Burn-in runs boards powered up at a raised temperature for hours. It's aimed at weak parts. Don't treat a pass on the production test as proof that the design is reliable. Proving the design, with environmental testing, life testing and qualification, is a separate job done before production. Check that boards built on the production line perform like the ones you tested in the lab.

**Why:** A production test checks each board for the faults in the test plan, at room temperature, for seconds or minutes. Some faults only show up after heat, cold, vibration or hours of running. Cracked joints, moisture damage inside a part and marginal parts are examples. Screening isn't included unless you ask for it. It needs test chambers, time and power, so it's quoted separately. Products used outdoors, in vehicles, in medical equipment or in industrial plants usually need it. Low-cost products used indoors often don't, but even they can benefit from a short thermal-cycling screen.

**Typical values:** There's no single standard for commercial boards. The limits come from the parts' ratings and where the product will be used. Production stress screens commonly take a few hours. Burn-in commonly takes 24 to 48 hours, and longer when it's used to qualify a design. Plan for a few early failures in any batch. For example, if you need 100 good boards, order 105 to 110.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Weak boards pass the test and fail weeks later in the field. Each of those failures costs far more than one caught in the factory.

**Example:** A part with moisture damage passed a 30-second bench test, then failed in the field after running hot for a while. One company launched a product that had only been proven in its engineering lab. The production units shipped with problems nobody had checked them for, and the company changed how it launches products. A maker of sensors for power plants puts its boards through its own environmental testing, on top of the assembler's functional test, because a production test alone isn't enough for that use. One test engineer expects to find around ten more problems after the "golden sample" is signed off, once real production volumes start.

**Applies to:** Depends on the product's use and reliability needs.

**Sources:** [“Inevitable Failures”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984-inevitable-failures) (Aug 2025), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984?t=1260)–23:00 and [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984?t=1860)–35:00; [“Smarter Test Plans for Inevitable Failures w/ Blue Clover CEO & Co-founder, Pete Staples”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982-smarter-test-plans-for-inevitable-failures-w-blue-clover-ceo-co-founder-pete-staples) (Oct 2025), [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=2640)–51:00; [“How to Manage Moisture Sensitive Devices”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014-how-to-manage-moisture-sensitive-devices) (May 2022), [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=960)–18:00; [“How Blue Robotics is enabling the next generation of ocean exploration robots w/ Rustom Jehangir”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597-how-blue-robotics-is-enabling-the-next-generation-of-ocean-exploration-robots-w-rustom-jehangir) (Mar 2021), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597?t=1680)–29:00; published reliability-test practice (environmental stress screening, burn-in, HALT and HASS).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

Source: https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/07-first-articles/

## First articles

A first article is the first panel of a production run. It's built and checked before the rest of the run goes ahead. It proves that the parts, the bare boards, the stencil and the machine programs all come together correctly on this assembler's line, before hundreds or thousands of boards are built. It isn't a prototype, because it checks the build, not the design.

### PCB-DFA-107: Use first articles to check a proven design before a big run, not as a prototype

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-107

**Recommendation:** Ask for first articles when a design that already works is about to be built in quantity. That includes scaling up from prototypes, moving a product to a new assembler, and making a small change, such as adding one resistor, before a large or expensive run. For a new design or a big change, build another round of prototypes instead. Expect at least one full panel of first articles, and a set-up charge for them. After that, expect the volume to ramp up in steps, not jump straight to full volume.

**Why:** First articles find build problems, such as a wrong reel, a part fitted backwards, a stencil that clogs, or a footprint the assembler has to work around. They can't tell you whether the design works, because the production run follows straight after. A design problem found at that point means boards are already built. Setting up the line always builds at least one full panel, so "one first article" usually means one panel's worth. Later batches go faster as the assembler learns the board, so the first few hundred boards of a big order are the slowest.

**Typical values:** At least one panel, which is often around 200 × 150 mm. A typical ramp-up is 20 boards, then 200, then 1,000 or more.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A whole run gets built with the same mistake. Or a "first article" order for an untested design turns into an expensive prototype run.

**Example:** A customer with a well-proven product placed a $200,000 order for 3,000 boards with several changes. The first articles showed that a resistor the customer expected was missing, and that the stencil clogged. The assembler ordered a new stencil and improved the process before building the rest.

**Applies to:** General practice. An assembler may refuse first articles for an unproven design and ask for prototypes first.

**Sources:** [“When to request first articles”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335-when-to-request-first-articles) (Dec 2021), [04:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335?t=240)–07:00, [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335?t=780), [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335?t=960)–19:00 and [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335?t=1680)–30:00; [“How Small Manufacturers Manage Large Volume Orders”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426-how-small-manufacturers-manage-large-volume-orders) (Apr 2023), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=1920)–40:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

---

### PCB-DFA-108: Check first articles against a known-good board, and don't expect the line to wait while you do

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-108

**Recommendation:** Test first articles the way you test your own boards. Compare them side by side with a known-good working board, not only with the drawings. Plan to have them shipped to you and test them at your own site. Don't expect the assembler to keep its line set up and waiting while you test at their factory. If you find a simple problem, send clear photos and instructions for the fix. You often won't need another full round of first articles. For a first build, send a photo of a working prototype. This matters most for parts that need a particular orientation, height or lead bend.

**Why:** If the silkscreen or the part's own marking is unclear, a part fitted backwards can seem to match both and pass the assembler's inspection. Only a working board shows the truth. An assembly line is set up for one job at a time. Every hour it waits for a decision is an hour of expensive equipment and people standing idle. A photo of the fix gets it right on the rest of the run without a second set-up.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A mistake that looked right to everyone gets built into the whole run. Or a line is held up for hours waiting for an answer.

**Example:** A customer moved a mature product to a new assembler and asked for first articles. A voltage regulator was fitted turned 180°, because both the part's marking and the board's marking seemed to agree with that way. The customer thought it looked right too. It was caught only when the customer compared it with known-good boards at its own site. About 300 boards were then built correctly. Each board had two of these regulators, so about 600 would otherwise have needed rework. The same assembler has tried four or five times to let a customer test the first board at the factory while the line waited. It went badly every time. Once, a restart agreed for 2:30 pm didn't happen until 8 pm.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** [“When to request first articles”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335-when-to-request-first-articles) (Dec 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335?t=600)–12:00 and [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9645335?t=1140)–23:00; [“The PCB assembly inspection process”](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750-the-pcb-assembly-inspection-process) (Oct 2020), [51:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5713750?t=3060)–52:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-10*

- [Footprints](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/04-footprints/) (PCB-DFA-034, pin-1 marks)

## Static (ESD) protection

Static electricity is made whenever two materials touch and then separate. Walking across a floor does it. So does peeling tape off a roll, sliding a board into a bag or shuffling paper. A discharge you can see, such as the spark from a doorknob, is already about 3,000 V. Many semiconductors can be damaged by less than 100 V, so a part can be harmed by a discharge nobody felt. Some damage kills the part at once. Other damage only weakens it, and the board passes test and fails later in the field. Assemblers control static inside the factory. This page is about what happens to boards before and after they're in a controlled area: how they're packed, and how they're handled once they reach you.

### PCB-DFA-109: Ship and store assembled boards in static-shielding bags, not in plain anti-static bags

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-109

**Recommendation:** Put every assembled board that carries semiconductors in a static-shielding bag for shipping and storage. Use a metallized shielding bag, usually silver-gray and slightly see-through, and close it by folding the top over and taping it. Wrap the board in anti-static (usually pink) bubble wrap first, because that is safe against the board, and then put it in the shielding bag, as in D65. Don't rely on a pink or blue anti-static bag on its own. Never put boards or loose semiconductors in an ordinary plastic bag. Boards that carry no semiconductors, such as a board with only connectors and passive parts, can ship in anti-static bubble wrap alone if you agree it with your assembler.

**Why:** Packaging can do three different jobs. An anti-static (low-charging) material doesn't build up much charge itself when it rubs against the board. A dissipative material lets any charge drain away slowly. A shielding material has a metal layer that stops a discharge from outside reaching the board inside, like a Faraday cage. A pink anti-static bag does only the first job. If a charged hand or box touches it, the discharge goes straight through to the board. ANSI/ESD S541, the static control packaging standard, says that inside a static-controlled area, packaging must be low-charging and dissipative or conductive. Outside that area, in a warehouse, a truck or your office, it must also shield. A shielding bag only shields while it is closed and has no holes. An ordinary plastic bag is worse than nothing, because it makes static every time it moves.

**Typical values:** A discharge you can see is about 3,000 V. Many semiconductors are damaged by less than 100 V, and some by far less. The ESD Association's tests for shielding bags are ANSI/ESD STM11.31 for discharge shielding and STM11.11 for surface resistance.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards arrive working, or seem to, and then fail weeks or months later. That kind of failure is very hard to trace back to how the boards were packed.

**Example:** A maker of underwater robots found that a board damaged by static in transit might work for about six months before it failed. An assembler's shipping team packs every board in anti-static bubble wrap and then a shielding bag. The only exceptions are a few customers whose boards carry only through-hole connectors and no semiconductors, and who asked for bubble wrap alone.

![D65: Cross-section of two packed boxes, drawn to scale. Left, marked good: a 100 mm board 1.6 mm thick with parts on top is wrapped in pink anti-static bubble wrap, then sealed in a metallized static-shielding bag whose top is folded over and taped, in a corrugated box with paper filler above and below. A spark from outside the box stops at the shielding bag. Right, marked avoid: the same board in a pink anti-static bag on its own, and the spark passes through the bag to the board.](https://opendfx.org/07-handling-packaging-and-shipping/images/packed-board.svg)

*D65 is drawn to scale, except that the bags are drawn thicker than they are. The pink bubble wrap touches the board, and the shielding bag goes round the outside. A pink anti-static bag on its own makes little static, but it doesn't stop a discharge from outside.*

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** ["How to Protect PCBs from ESD Damage"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936-how-to-protect-pcbs-from-esd-damage) (Mar 2022), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936?t=420)–08:00 and [16:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936?t=960)–22:00; ["How to safely and successfully ship assembled PCBs w/ Nicole Poirier"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835-how-to-safely-and-successfully-ship-assembled-pcbs-w-nicole-poirier) (Apr 2021), [10:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=600)–13:00; ["How Blue Robotics is enabling the next generation of ocean exploration robots w/ Rustom Jehangir"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597-how-blue-robotics-is-enabling-the-next-generation-of-ocean-exploration-robots-w-rustom-jehangir) (Mar 2021), [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597?t=2940)–52:00; ["The PCB assembly process"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141-the-pcb-assembly-process) (Jun 2020), [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4364141?t=2400); ESD Association, *ESD Fundamentals*, Part 1 (sensitivity and latent failure) and Part 3 (packaging and material handling containers), esda.org; ANSI/ESD S541, *Packaging Materials for ESD Sensitive Items*.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-110: Open and handle boards only at a grounded workstation, and hold them by the edges

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-110

**Recommendation:** Wherever your boards are unpacked, tested or fitted into the product, set up a grounded workstation. At the least, that means a static-dissipative mat, a wrist strap and a cord to a known ground. Open the shielding bag on the mat, and keep the board on the mat until it is inside its enclosure. Keep cardboard, paper and ordinary plastic off the mat. Hold boards by their edges, and touch the plastic bodies of parts rather than their leads or solder joints. Tell everyone who handles your boards to do the same, including your own customers if they receive bare boards.

**Why:** A person is the most common source of a damaging discharge. A wrist strap and a grounded mat keep the person, the mat and the board at the same voltage, so no discharge can pass between them. The cord of a wrist strap has a resistor built in, most commonly 1 MΩ, so that the wearer isn't directly connected to ground. Charge reaches a part through its metal leads and the copper joined to them, so holding a board by its edges keeps your fingers away from that path. Once a board is inside its enclosure, it is far less exposed, because hands no longer touch its joints.

**Typical values:** A complete mat kit with a wrist strap and grounding cord costs about $50 (2022 price). The resistor in a wrist strap cord is most commonly 1 MΩ. Don't wear a wrist strap when working on circuits at 250 V or more.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards your assembler built and shipped correctly are damaged on your own bench. They fail in the field, and the failure looks like a manufacturing defect.

**Applies to:** General practice, wherever boards are handled outside an assembler's static-controlled area.

**Sources:** ["How to Protect PCBs from ESD Damage"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936-how-to-protect-pcbs-from-esd-damage) (Mar 2022), [39:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936?t=2340)–40:00 and [50:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936?t=3000)–52:00; ["Inevitable Failures"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984-inevitable-failures) (Aug 2025), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984?t=1140)–21:00; ESD Association, *ESD Fundamentals*, Part 3 (wrist straps and workstations), esda.org.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-111: Choose an assembler with a documented static control program, such as one that meets ANSI/ESD S20.20

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-111

**Recommendation:** When you choose an assembler, ask whether it runs a written static control program. Ask whether that program follows ANSI/ESD S20.20, or the equivalent IEC 61340-5-1, and how it is checked.

**Why:** Static control only works as a complete system. Grounded floors need grounded footwear, and wrist straps and mats need to be tested. S20.20 sets out what a program must contain: a written plan, training, grounding of people and equipment, packaging, marking and regular checks. An assembler that follows it can show you the plan and its test records.

**Typical values:** In a typical program, people check their wrist straps or footwear at least once a day. Floors, mats and workstations are tested on a regular schedule.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards are damaged before they ever leave the factory, and nobody can tell you how or when.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** ["How to Protect PCBs from ESD Damage"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936-how-to-protect-pcbs-from-esd-damage) (Mar 2022), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936?t=720)–13:00 and [41:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10275936?t=2460)–44:00; ["ESD Flooring w/ SelecTech CEO Tom Ricciardelli"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13534129-esd-flooring-w-selectech-ceo-tom-ricciardelli) (Sep 2023), [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/13534129?t=1140)–21:00; ANSI/ESD S20.20, *Protection of Electrical and Electronic Parts, Assemblies and Equipment*; ESD Association, *ESD Fundamentals*, Part 2 and Part 3, esda.org.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-112: Put ESD protection on every connector that people or cables can touch, as close to the connector as you can

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-112

**Recommendation:** Give every signal that reaches a connector, button or other exposed metal its own ESD protection device, usually a TVS diode array. Place the device as close to the connector as your design rules allow. Route each protected line straight from the connector pin to the protection device's pin, with no via between them and no branch. Then route on to the chip being protected. Connect the protection device's ground pin to the ground plane through the shortest path you can, with its own via or vias. Keep unprotected traces away from the short stretch between the connector and the protection device. Choose a device rated for at least the IEC 61000-4-2 level your product must pass.

**Why:** Once a board is in a product, the connectors are where static gets in. A user touches a USB plug, or a cable that has picked up charge is plugged in. The protection device clamps the voltage and steers the current to ground before it reaches the chip. An ESD pulse rises in less than a nanosecond, so even a tiny inductance in the path adds a large voltage. That is why the device must be close to the connector and well grounded. If the chip is close to the connector and the protection device is further away, the current takes the path to the chip instead. This can only be done while laying out the board. A board without room for protection devices near its connectors can't have them added later.

**Typical values:** IEC 61000-4-2 Level 4 is 8 kV by contact discharge and 15 kV through the air. In an 8 kV contact discharge, the current rises at about 40 A per nanosecond. At that rate, 0.25 nH of inductance in the path adds about 10 V to the voltage the chip sees. As a common rule of thumb, a thin trace has an inductance of about 1 nH for each millimeter of length. A via through a 1.6 mm board has an inductance of about 1 nH.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Products fail ESD testing for certification, or fail in the field after a user touches a connector. Moving or adding protection devices then means a new revision of the board.

**Applies to:** Products with connectors, buttons or exposed metal that users touch.

**Sources:** Texas Instruments, *ESD Protection Layout Guide*, SLVA680A (Feb 2015, revised Apr 2022), section 2; IEC 61000-4-2, *Electrostatic discharge immunity test*.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

## Moisture and storage

Moisture matters at three stages. Bare boards absorb it before assembly, and that is covered by [PCB-DFA-080](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/08-surface-finish/). Moisture-sensitive parts absorb it before they're soldered, and that is covered by [PCB-DFA-091 to 094](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/03-moisture-sensitive-parts/). This page covers the boards and parts you keep yourself: spare bare boards, spare parts and finished boards waiting to be used.

### PCB-DFA-113: Store spare boards and parts sealed in bags that block both static and moisture, with desiccant and a humidity card

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-113

**Recommendation:** Keep spare bare boards, moisture-sensitive parts and assembled boards you store for months in a moisture barrier bag made for electronics. The bag should also protect against static. Put fresh desiccant and a humidity indicator card in the bag, and heat-seal it, as in D60 in [Part 4](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/03-moisture-sensitive-parts/). Don't use a moisture barrier bag made for other goods, such as machine parts. Don't use a plain static-shielding bag for long storage, because it doesn't keep moisture out. Label each bag with what is inside and the date it was sealed. When you send stored boards or parts to an assembler, send them in the sealed bag and say on the packing slip how long they have been stored.

**Why:** Bags made for electronics combine a moisture barrier with a static-safe inner layer and a metal layer that shields. Moisture barrier bags made for other goods may block moisture but generate static. A plain shielding bag blocks static but lets moisture through over weeks. The humidity card shows whether the bag has kept the moisture out. Bare boards take on moisture and their finish ages, so they may need baking or a solderability check before use (PCB-DFA-080). Parts that have taken on moisture need baking before reflow (PCB-DFA-094).

**Typical values:** IPC-1602A says bare boards dry-packed this way should keep for at least a year below 40 °C and 90% relative humidity. It recommends against drawing a full vacuum on the bag, because that can damage the desiccant, warp boards and puncture the bag. For moisture-sensitive parts, J-STD-033 sets the floor life and the bake times.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Stored boards or parts need baking before they can be built, which adds days to the job. Or they're built without baking, and parts crack or joints fail in reflow.

**Applies to:** General practice, for anything you store for more than a few weeks.

**Sources:** ["How to Manage Moisture Sensitive Devices"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014-how-to-manage-moisture-sensitive-devices) (May 2022), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=1260)–22:00 and [54:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10522014?t=3240)–56:00; IPC-1602A, *Standard for Printed Board Handling and Storage* (Nov 2024), section 4; IPC/JEDEC J-STD-033D, *Handling, Packing, Shipping and Use of Moisture/Reflow Sensitive Surface Mount Devices*.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

- [Surface finish](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/08-surface-finish/) (PCB-DFA-080, bare-board shelf life)
- [Moisture-sensitive parts](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/03-moisture-sensitive-parts/) (PCB-DFA-091 to 094)

## Packaging and shipping assembled boards

Most assembled boards travel at least twice. They go from the assembler to you, and often on to a test house, a coating house or your own customer. Some come back for repair. Each trip is a chance for static, a crushed box or a customs hold-up to undo good work. Packing is the assembler's job, but the designer decides things that make it easy or hard: parts that hang over the board edge, very heavy boards, and whether boards ship in the panel.

### PCB-DFA-114: Agree with your assembler how boards will be packed: in the panel or separated, how many to a bag, and in what box

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-114

**Recommendation:** Before the first order ships, agree with your assembler how the boards will be packed. Say whether you want them in the panel or separated. Say how many boards go in each bag, and whether each board is wrapped on its own. For heavy boards, or boards going a long way, ask for a double-wall box and foam lining. If boards will go from the assembler to another company first, such as a coating or cleaning house, say where they go and how they should be packed for that trip. For boards with parts that hang over the edge, such as an antenna or a connector, ask whether they should ship in the panel to protect those parts. If your assembler is close by and you order often, ask about reusable static-safe boxes with partitions.

**Why:** The assembler packs to a standard method unless told otherwise. That suits most boards, but not all of them. Heavy parts near the edge of a board can break off in transit if the box isn't lined. A part hanging over the edge can snap off during depaneling or in the box (PCB-DFA-010). Leaving boards in the panel protects those parts, but then you must separate them yourself. Boards that go on to another company must be packed for a second trip, and it may cost less to ship them there directly. Reusable partitioned boxes protect boards well and cut out most of the single-use packing.

**Typical values:** The usual pack is anti-static bubble wrap against the board, inside a static-shielding bag (PCB-DFA-109), in a box with filler, as in D65. A single-wall box is usual for light boards sent within one country.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards arrive with broken parts, or in a form you didn't expect, such as still in the panel when you wanted them separated.

**Example:** One board carried a radio module with its antenna hanging off the board edge, held to the panel only by a breakaway tab underneath. Separating it without snapping the antenna off took several people. It didn't always succeed.

**Applies to:** General practice; agree it once for each product.

**Sources:** ["How to safely and successfully ship assembled PCBs w/ Nicole Poirier"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835-how-to-safely-and-successfully-ship-assembled-pcbs-w-nicole-poirier) (Apr 2021), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=420)–09:00, [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=720)–17:00 and [34:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=2040)–36:00; ["What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [50:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=3000)–51:00; ["IPC's Leadership on Sustainability in Electronics w/ Dr. John W. Mitchell and Dr. Kelly Scanlon"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16624642-ipc-s-leadership-on-sustainability-in-electronics-w-dr-john-w-mitchell-and-dr-kelly-scanlon) (Feb 2025), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/16624642?t=1080).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-115: For international shipments, give the right tariff code, a plain description of the goods and a contact telephone number

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-115

**Recommendation:** When boards or parts cross a border, work out the correct tariff code for them with your assembler or customs broker. Choose the code from what the boards are for in the end product, not from a quick search for "circuit board". Use a different code for boards returned for repair or under warranty. On the customs paperwork, also write a plain description of what is in the box and why it is being sent. For a return, say that it is a repair return of no commercial value, and give the tracking number of the original shipment. Give a telephone number that someone will answer. Before you send parts in from abroad, agree with your assembler who pays the duties and taxes.

**Why:** Customs officers read the paperwork, not just the codes. The tariff system classifies an assembled board mostly by the kind of equipment it goes into. A code chosen from a search can sit under the wrong heading, and that holds the shipment up. A repair return sent without the right code or note can be charged duty a second time. When customs has a question, they call the number on the paperwork, and an unanswered call means a held shipment.

**Typical values:** Bare boards and assembled boards fall under different tariff headings. Bare boards come under heading 8534. Assembled boards usually come under the heading for parts of the equipment they go into, which depends on the product. Codes, duty rates and rules change, so check them for every new product and from time to time after that.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Shipments sit in customs for days, you pay duty you didn't owe, or a delivery date you promised is missed.

**Example:** An assembler once picked a code for "assembled circuit board" from a search. It later found the code sat several levels down under a heading for nuclear equipment.

**Applies to:** International shipments; rules vary by country and change over time.

**Sources:** ["How to safely and successfully ship assembled PCBs w/ Nicole Poirier"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835-how-to-safely-and-successfully-ship-assembled-pcbs-w-nicole-poirier) (Apr 2021), [25:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=1500)–29:00 and [44:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8309835?t=2640)–50:00; ["The Open Source Ventilator Project with Dugan Karnazes and Nadim Conti"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5109637-the-open-source-ventilator-project-with-dugan-karnazes-and-nadim-conti) (Aug 2020), [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/5109637?t=2160); ["How to Send Consigned Material to Your CM"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930-how-to-send-consigned-material-to-your-cm) (Mar 2022), [46:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10182930?t=2760)–48:00; Harmonized System heading 8534 (printed circuits) and US Customs rulings classifying printed circuit assemblies by end use.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

Boards sent back for repair are covered by [PCB-DFA-063](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/11-rework/): get a return number first, and pack the boards the way they came to you.

## What drives cost and lead time

Most of the cost of an assembled board is decided in layout, long before anyone asks for a quote. Most delays are decided by how quickly questions get answered, and by when orders are placed. This page gathers the cost drivers that earlier parts of the book cover one by one, and adds what a designer or buyer can do about price and schedule when ordering. Prices on this page are examples from particular dates, and will change.

### PCB-DFA-116: Know what drives the price of an assembly, and design with it in mind

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-116

**Recommendation:** Before you release a design, check it against the cost drivers in the table below. Each one has its own recommendation elsewhere in the book. Where the product needs one of them, keep it, but know that you are paying for it. Where it doesn't, design it out.

**Why:** An assembler's price is mostly set-up time and labor. Set-up is paid once for each batch, so it matters most on small orders. Labor is paid for every board, so it matters most on large orders. Anything that adds a machine set-up, a manual step or a slower process adds cost.

**Typical values:**

| Cost driver | Why it costs more | Where it's covered |
|---|---|---|
| Many unique BOM lines | Each unique part takes about 3 to 5 minutes to load onto a feeder, however few boards you build. | [PCB-DFA-072](https://opendfx.org/01-design-package/03-bom/) |
| Parts on both sides | A second side costs at least 15% more, even if it carries only two passive parts already used on the top. It can cost about twice as much if the bottom parts are all different from the top. | [PCB-DFA-024 and 025](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/03-reflow-soldering/) |
| Through-hole parts | Each one is placed and soldered by hand or on a separate machine. | [PCB-DFA-039](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/05-through-hole-soldering/) |
| Parts in tubes or loose | They're slower to load and to place than parts on tape. | [PCB-DFA-089](https://opendfx.org/04-components-and-materials/02-packaging/) |
| Very small or very fine-pitch parts | They need tighter process control and more inspection, and fail more often. | [PCB-DFA-021 and 022](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/02-component-placement/) |
| Hardware such as heatsinks, screws and brackets | Each piece is fitted by hand. | [PCB-DFA-048](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/06-press-fit-and-mechanical/) |
| Conformal coating | It needs masking, coating and inspection, usually by hand. | [PCB-DFA-061](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/09-conformal-coating/) |
| Cleaning | Many assemblers run no-clean flux only, so cleaning may be sent out to another company. | [PCB-DFA-055](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/08-cleaning/) |
| IPC Class 3 | Inspection is stricter, and some boards built to a Class 2 design can't meet it. | [PCB-DFT-003](https://opendfx.org/03-bare-board-fabrication/11-bare-board-test/) |
| Tin-lead solder | Many assemblers now run lead-free only. One assembler solders tin-lead through-hole parts entirely by hand. | |
| Stepped or etched stencils | A simple laser-cut stencil cost about $300 in 2024. Stepped or chemically etched stencils cost more, up to about $900 or more. | [Solder paste and stencils](https://opendfx.org/05-assembly/01-solder-paste-and-stencils/) |
| Small, odd or thin panels | They need special handling, carriers or extra set-up. | [Part 2](https://opendfx.org/02-the-panel/01-why-panels/) |

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You get a quote far higher than you expected, for reasons that are hard to change once the board is laid out.

**Example:** One customer new to fine-pitch BGAs designed overlapping blind and buried vias, with laser-drilled vias much smaller than they needed to be. The assembler put them in touch with the fab's engineers, who showed them what was driving the cost. A couple of weeks later the customer sent a redesigned board. Its bare-board price came down to about $30 each, about a twentieth of what the first design would have cost.

**Applies to:** General practice; prices vary by manufacturer and over time.

**Sources:** ["What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=1080)–31:00, [47:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=2820)–48:00 and [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=2940)–52:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-117: Get your quote from real design data, and expect a repeat build to be priced differently

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-117

**Recommendation:** Ask for a quote only when you have the real BOM and board files, or something very close to them. Don't ask for a ballpark price from a description. When you reorder, expect the price to change a little. If the board hasn't changed, programming and stencil costs drop out. If the board revision has changed, expect them to come back.

**Why:** An assembly quote is built from the actual parts, the number of unique lines, the number of sides and the processes the board needs. Without the real data, the assembler can only guess, and a guess is no use to you. On a first build, the assembler sometimes finds the job took longer than quoted, and the repeat price is adjusted, usually upwards. But the one-off work of the first build, such as machine programming and approving the stencil, isn't repeated for an unchanged board.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A budget built on a ballpark figure that turns out to be wrong, or surprise at a repeat price.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** ["What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [13:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=780)–14:00 and [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=2580)–45:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFM-044: Ask your board fab how many boards its minimum lot charge buys

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFM-044

**Recommendation:** When you order a small number of bare boards, ask the fab what its minimum lot charge is and how many boards it covers. Then order that number, rather than asking for prices at several small quantities.

**Why:** Most board fabs charge a fixed minimum for any order, however few boards are in it. Up to some quantity, more boards cost nothing extra. Asking for prices one quantity at a time hides where that point is. Assemblers use the term less often than fabs, and some don't have a minimum lot charge at all.

**Typical values:** In one example, a fab quoted $300 for 5 boards, and the same $300 for 7, 10 and 11 boards. The minimum lot charge covered 13 boards. Twenty boards cost $430.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You pay the same price for fewer boards than you could have had.

**Applies to:** Bare-board fabrication, mainly prototypes and small orders.

**Sources:** ["What are fiducials and why you should use them"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465-what-are-fiducials-and-why-you-should-use-them) (Oct 2021), [03:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9355465?t=180)–04:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-118: Order a few more boards than you need: 105 to 110 when you need 100

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-118

**Recommendation:** When you need a certain number of working boards, order about 5% to 10% more. For example, order 105 to 110 boards when you need 100. If the boards go into a test fixture, add the spares the fixture builder needs as well (PCB-DFT-017).

**Why:** Even a good design built well has a small failure rate. A few boards will fail test, or fail early in a stress screen (PCB-DFT-019). Some will be damaged in handling. Spares cost little when they're built with the rest of the batch. Building a handful more later costs a full set-up.

**Typical values:** About 5% to 10% extra, which is 105 to 110 boards when you need 100.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** You end up a few boards short, and a small top-up order costs almost as much in set-up as the first one.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** ["Inevitable Failures"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984-inevitable-failures) (Aug 2025), [21:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17722984?t=1260).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-119: Leave at least two weeks of margin in your schedule, and plan round long factory holidays

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-119

**Recommendation:** Plan for boards to arrive at least two weeks before you need them. Ask each supplier when it will close for long holidays, and the last day it will take an order that ships before it closes. Ask domestic suppliers too, because their own suppliers may close. Place orders before that date. For the Lunar New Year, which falls in late January or February, place orders for February and March in early December where you can. When an order is urgent, tell your manufacturer so, and say why. Use holiday closures for work that doesn't need a factory, such as finishing designs and tidying your parts library.

**Why:** Lead times slip for reasons outside anyone's control: a late part, a question that waits, a holiday or a delay in transit. Many factories in China slow down a week or two before the Lunar New Year, because staff travel home for the longest holiday of the year. After the holiday, it takes time to clear the backlog. Domestic suppliers get busier at the same time, as customers turn to them instead. An assembler that knows an order is urgent can warn you early if something threatens the date.

**Typical values:** At least two weeks of margin. Expect delays for about one to two months after the Lunar New Year.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A missed launch or delivery date, or an expensive rush order to recover it.

**Applies to:** General practice; holiday dates change every year.

**Sources:** ["How Chinese New Year Impacts Manufacturing"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955-how-chinese-new-year-impacts-manufacturing) (Jan 2022), [12:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955?t=720)–13:00, [17:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955?t=1020)–18:00 and [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9863955?t=1860)–36:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-120: Answer your manufacturer's questions quickly, and keep an engineer reachable by telephone

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-120

**Recommendation:** While your order is being built, answer your manufacturer's questions within the hour, and within about 30 minutes once the job is on the assembly line. Give the manufacturer the telephone number of an engineer who knows the design, not only an email address. If you'll be away during a first or critical order, name someone who can answer for you. Keep the questions about each order in one place, such as the order's own message thread, so that everyone sees the same answers.

**Why:** When an assembler finds a problem, such as a part that doesn't match the BOM, the line often stops until it has an answer. If no answer comes, the job is taken off the line and has to wait for the next free slot. At the fab, an unanswered question about the panel or the drawing stops the job too.

**Typical values:** Aim to answer within about 30 minutes. An idle surface-mount line costs from several hundred to several thousand dollars an hour (2021 figure). The machines on one line can cost $1 million to $2 million and are expected to last about 10 years. A 48-hour fab turn can become 3 or 4 days while questions wait for answers.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Your job comes off the line and loses days. Or the assembler has to guess, and the guess is wrong.

**Applies to:** General practice; most important for first builds and fast turns.

**Sources:** ["Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [20:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=1200)–24:00; ["Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=1620)–28:00 and [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=2160)–39:00; ["What factors influence PCB quotes w/ Brett Babilonia"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855-what-factors-influence-pcb-quotes-w-brett-babilonia) (Feb 2024), [07:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/14580855?t=420)–10:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-121: Check your order before you place it, and report a mistake at once

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-121

**Recommendation:** Before you place an order, check that the options you choose on the order match your fabrication drawing and files. Check the board thickness, the solder mask color, the surface finish and any special processes such as via-in-pad. If you find a mistake after ordering, report it straight away. If the order was placed only minutes ago, ask whether it is simpler to cancel it and place a new one.

**Why:** Many manufacturers build to the options on the order, so an option that disagrees with your drawing may win. Once fabrication has started, or parts have been bought, a change costs money and time. A change made by hand on a placed order is also a chance for a new mistake. A fresh order goes through the normal checks.

**Typical values:** In one assembler's experience, an order can usually be canceled and replaced at no cost within about 30 minutes, before work starts. After about 24 to 48 hours, fabrication or parts buying has usually started, and changes get harder and dearer.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Boards built to the wrong option, or a change fee that grows the longer you wait.

**Applies to:** General practice; how orders are placed varies by manufacturer.

**Sources:** ["Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [40:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=2400)–48:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

- [Prototype versus production](https://opendfx.org/08-working-with-a-manufacturer/02-prototype-to-production/)

Source: https://opendfx.org/08-working-with-a-manufacturer/02-prototype-to-production/

## Prototype versus production

A prototype proves the design works. Production proves it can be built the same way, many times, at a cost you can sell it for. These are different jobs. Parts that were placed by hand on five prototypes need feeders, nozzles and machine programs for five thousand boards. A process that was fine for a few boards can show its weak spots at volume. This page covers how to plan the step from one to the other. First articles, which check a proven design before a big run, are covered in [Part 6.7](https://opendfx.org/06-test-and-programming/07-first-articles/).

### PCB-DFA-122: Plan the move from prototype to production as a ramp, not a jump

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-122

**Recommendation:** Don't go straight from a few prototypes to a full production order. Build in steps, such as 20 boards, then 200, then 1,000, and then the full volume, as in D66. Before the first large build, talk to your manufacturer about your volumes and anything that was done by hand on the prototypes. Replace hard-to-find parts, hobby modules and hand-fitted parts with mainstream parts on tape where you can (PCB-DFA-083 and 085). If anything in the design or BOM has changed since the last build, expect new first articles (PCB-DFA-107). Check that boards built on the production line perform like the ones you tested in the lab. Expect the first production batch to run slower than later ones, and expect to find a few more issues. If the volume is far beyond what your manufacturer has built for you before, consider splitting the first large order between two manufacturers.

**Why:** Each step shows up problems while they're still cheap to fix. The first large batch is where the assembler learns the board's quirks: a via in an awkward place, a part that has to be hand-soldered because of its neighbors, a polarity mark that is easy to misread. Later batches run faster because those quirks are known. Problems that a few prototypes never showed only appear once hundreds of boards are built.

**Typical values:** A typical ramp is 20, then 200, then 1,000, then 2,000 or more. After a design reaches a signed-off golden sample, expect to find about ten more issues once it reaches real production volume.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A large first order with a fault that affects every board. Or a launch that slips while the manufacturer works out how to build the board at volume.

**Example:** In one case, about 8 months of engineering went into reaching a golden sample. About ten more issues were still found once the product moved into production volume.

![D66: Flow diagram, not to scale. Five boxes run left to right, each wider than the last: 5 boards, prototypes; 20 boards, a pilot build; 200 boards, with first articles first; 1,000 boards, the first large batch; and 2,000 or more boards, full volume. Inside the full-volume box, small squares in groups of three show batches released as whole panels.](https://opendfx.org/08-working-with-a-manufacturer/images/production-ramp.svg)

*D66 is not to scale. Each step builds about ten times as many boards as the one before, up to the full volume. First articles come at the start of the first step after anything has changed. Full volume is released in batches of whole panels, such as 27 boards from three 9-up panels.*

**Applies to:** General practice, whenever volume rises sharply.

**Sources:** ["How Small Manufacturers Manage Large Volume Orders"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426-how-small-manufacturers-manage-large-volume-orders) (Apr 2023), [32:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=1920)–33:00 and [36:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=2160)–40:00; ["Smarter Test Plans for Inevitable Failures w/ Blue Clover CEO & Co-founder, Pete Staples"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982-smarter-test-plans-for-inevitable-failures-w-blue-clover-ceo-co-founder-pete-staples) (Oct 2025), [47:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/17955982?t=2820)–48:00; ["How Blue Robotics is enabling the next generation of ocean exploration robots w/ Rustom Jehangir"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597-how-blue-robotics-is-enabling-the-next-generation-of-ocean-exploration-robots-w-rustom-jehangir) (Mar 2021), [28:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8139597?t=1680)–30:00; ["Soft Skills of Engineering w/ Being an Engineer Host, Aaron Moncur"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12593633-soft-skills-of-engineering-w-being-an-engineer-host-aaron-moncur) (Apr 2023), [52:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12593633?t=3120)–54:00; ["All about parts purchasing - part 1"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040-all-about-parts-purchasing-part-1) (Jul 2020), [59:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/4540040?t=3540).

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-123: For large orders, release boards in batches matched to the panel, and agree who holds the parts and the risk

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-123

**Recommendation:** For a large annual volume, agree a schedule of batch releases with your manufacturer, rather than one delivery of the whole quantity. Make each batch a whole number of panels. Agree which parts the manufacturer buys up front and which are held by a distributor and released batch by batch (PCB-DFA-098). Before a very large order, agree in writing who carries which risks. That includes insurance for parts held in the factory, and who pays if boards fail in the field months later.

**Why:** A batch schedule matches deliveries to how the product sells, and keeps less money tied up in parts and finished boards. A batch of whole panels uses every board the machines build. The costly part of a changeover is setting up the surface-mount machines, so batches are sized to spread that set-up over enough boards. On a large order, most of the money is in parts, and someone has to hold that stock and its risk until the boards are built.

**Typical values:** In one example, a 9-up panel of 3 by 3 boards meant batches of 27 boards. Each surface-mount feeder costs about $1,000 or more (2023 figure), which is why surface-mount set-up dominates changeover cost. In one example of a $200,000 order, about $150,000 was parts and about $50,000 was labor. Orders of about $100,000 often run without a formal contract. Orders of $400,000 to $500,000 usually need one.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Cash tied up in a year of stock, partial panels that waste boards, or a dispute about who pays after a fire, a flood or a field failure.

**Example:** One product has been built at about 2,000 boards a year for 20 years. The customer never takes all 2,000 at once. For years it called them off in batches of 27, a whole number of its 9-up panels, every few days.

**Applies to:** Production volumes; contracts and insurance vary by manufacturer and country.

**Sources:** ["How Small Manufacturers Manage Large Volume Orders"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426-how-small-manufacturers-manage-large-volume-orders) (Apr 2023), [05:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=300)–08:00, [11:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=660)–13:00, [19:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=1140)–22:00 and [27:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12586426?t=1620)–29:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

## Design reviews and communicating intent

A manufacturer can only build what the design data and drawings tell it. Part 1 covers what goes in that data. This page covers the conversation around it: when to bring the manufacturer in, how to learn from each build, and when to talk before you commit to something unusual. The common thread is to talk early, while changes are still cheap.

### PCB-DFA-124: Bring your manufacturer into the design review before the design is final

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-124

**Recommendation:** Share the design with your fab and assembler while you can still change it, at about 60% to 80% complete. Ask them what will be hard to make, test or ship. Review in small steps as the design develops, rather than in one large review at the end. Before each release, compare the schematic, the board and the BOM with the previous version, so you can see exactly what changed. Let the mechanical engineers and others who depend on the board comment on the design files themselves, not only on a summary.

**Why:** At 60% to 80%, the layout is far enough along to show real problems, and still open enough to fix them. Small reviews get read properly, and their actions get done. A large review at the end produces a long list, and much of it never gets done. A comparison of versions catches changes nobody meant to make.

**Typical values:** Review with suppliers at about 60% to 80% complete.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** Problems the manufacturer would have spotted in minutes turn into a board revision. Or a review list so long that half of it is never acted on.

**Example:** One design review produced 327 items and 557 actions. Only about half of them were ever dealt with.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** ["Soft Skills of Engineering w/ Being an Engineer Host, Aaron Moncur"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12593633-soft-skills-of-engineering-w-being-an-engineer-host-aaron-moncur) (Apr 2023), [47:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/12593633?t=2820); ["The Benefits of Asynchronous Design Review for Engineers & Manufacturers w/ AllSpice.io"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11886751-the-benefits-of-asynchronous-design-review-for-engineers-manufacturers-w-allspice-io) (Dec 2022), [31:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11886751?t=1860)–37:00 and [43:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/11886751?t=2580)–45:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-125: Ask for feedback after every build, and fix recurring problems before you reorder

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-125

**Recommendation:** After each build, ask your assembler and fab what gave them trouble. Make the changes they suggest before you reorder, not after. If the same problem comes up on more than one build, treat it as a design problem and fix it in the next revision.

**Why:** The people who built the board know exactly where the time went: a through-hole connector that could have been surface-mount, a part that had to be hand-soldered, a polarity mark that was easy to misread. A manufacturer will often work round a problem without telling you, and keep paying for it on every build. The next revision is the cheapest place to fix it.

**What goes wrong if you don't:** The same problem costs you money on every build, and sometimes causes the same defect again.

**Applies to:** General practice; most valuable on products that are reordered.

**Sources:** ["Our top suggestions for customers w/ CircuitHub Account Manager, John Jacquinet"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604-our-top-suggestions-for-customers-w-circuithub-account-manager-john-jacquinet) (Jul 2021), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=1080)–21:00 and [49:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/8884604?t=2940); ["Showstoppers that delay PCB assembly w/ Production Manager, Rob OConnell"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439-showstoppers-that-delay-pcb-assembly-w-production-manager-rob-oconnell) (Dec 2021), [33:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/9741439?t=1980)–34:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*

---

### PCB-DFA-126: Talk to your manufacturer before designing in anything unusual, and don't assume standard pricing

**Permanent address:** https://opendfx.org/PCB-DFA-126

**Recommendation:** Before you commit to anything outside a standard surface-mount build, ask your manufacturer whether it can do it, and what it will cost. Ask every time, whether it's a first prototype or a product moving to higher volume. If you choose a very fine-pitch BGA or chip-scale package, choose a manufacturer that has built that kind of part before.

**Why:** Unusual processes may need tooling, a different machine, a subcontractor or skills the manufacturer doesn't have. None of that is in a standard price. Experience with a fine-pitch part comes only from building it, and a manufacturer still learning will have lower yields. The earlier you ask, the more choices you still have, including changing the design.

**Typical values:** Unusual processes covered elsewhere in this book include:
- press-fit parts (PCB-DFA-047)
- one-piece RF shields (PCB-DFA-050)
- boards thicker than about 2 mm (PCB-DFA-014)
- very thin boards and large, heavy double-sided panels (PCB-DFA-028)
- conformal coating and cleaning (PCB-DFA-055 and 061)
- adhesive-mounted parts and underfill (PCB-DFA-052 to 054).

**What goes wrong if you don't:** A quote far above what you expected, a lead time with tooling added, or a manufacturer that can't build the board at all.

**Applies to:** General practice.

**Sources:** ["Alternative Component Mounting"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215-alternative-component-mounting) (Feb 2022), [18:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=1080)–25:00 and [57:00](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/10030215?t=3420)–59:00; ["To BGA or Not to BGA"](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540-to-bga-or-not-to-bga) (Oct 2026), [19:30](https://www.buzzsprout.com/1066066/episodes/19944540?t=1170)–22:00.

*Last reviewed: 2026-11-12*
